News.title: New ISA rules mean 'new charge' for savers paid to HMRC
News.content:
New ISA rules mean 'new charge' for savers paid to HMRC

Experts have said the new rules are more complicated than they first seem

View 4 Images HMRC will soon take a chunk of some interest on ISAs (Image: tupungato via Getty Images)

New ISA rules are “a complete dog’s dinner”, experts have warned.

‌



From April 2027, someone aged 65 or over will still be able to put up to £20,000 into cash ISAs and transfer money from a stocks and shares ISA into a cash ISA. Those under 65, however, will be restricted to £12,000 of new cash ISA subscriptions and will not enjoy the same flexibility to move money into cash ISAs.

‌



This is despite 65 no longer being the State Pension age and many people of that age will still be working and waiting to receive their pension. The changes were announced by former Chancellor Rachel Reeves in the November 2025 Budget and she said the aim of reducing the limit from £20,000 was to encourage more people to invest their money in stocks and shares instead.

‌



“Someone who has invested £1,000 a year in an average stocks and shares ISA every year since 1999 would be £50,000 better off today… than if they’d put the same money into a cash ISA,” Ms Reeves told the Commons at the time.

Even those aged 65 and over will face the new 22% tax charge on interest payable to HMRC earned from cash deposits held inside a stocks and shares ISA. The government says the charge is intended to prevent people from using investment ISAs primarily as cash savings accounts.

However, older savers will be able to transfer those assets into a cash ISA, while being penalised if they simply retain the cash within their existing stocks and shares ISA. The published guidance also appears to contain no obvious transitional provisions for investors who already hold fixed-term cash deposits within stocks and shares ISAs that do not mature until after April 6, 2027.

‌



View 4 Images Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves (Image: Bloomberg, Bloomberg via Getty Images)

They may have entered into those arrangements entirely legitimately under the current rules, but could find themselves caught by a change they have little or no practical ability to avoid. Scott Gallacher, director of Leicester-based Rowley Turton described it as “a complete dog’s dinner” that showed “a remarkable lack of joined-up thinking by the government”.

He said: “If the government had aligned the cut-off with State Pension age, it would at least have had some logic. Instead, it has chosen the outdated age of 65. The government is effectively saying you are too young to receive your State Pension, but old enough to receive preferential ISA treatment. If there is a clear policy rationale for selecting age 65 rather than State Pension age, the government has yet to explain it.”

‌



Gallacher added: “You seriously have to question the ministers, special advisers and civil servants whose fingerprints are all over this policy. Rather than creating a coherent system that encourages sensible long-term saving, they have produced different allowances, transfer rights and tax treatment based on an arbitrary birthday. Savers should not need a flowchart and their birth certificate to understand what they can do with an ISA.”

Rob Mansfield, Independent Financial Advisor at Tonbridge-based Rootes Wealth Management, said ISAs were becoming unnecessarily complicated.

He added: "Given all the problems the country faces, is this really the best use of the government's time? There's the ominous promise of a list of cash-like investments that will incur these charges to follow. The whole beauty of the ISA was that it's a simple concept. Tax free savings up to a limit.

‌



"Government's keep faffing around with it and are undermining saving. People tend to default to cash because they don't know any different and investments seem scary. These attempts to cajole people into investments is never likely to work well."

David Stirling, Independent Financial Adviser at Belfast-based Mint Wealth, said the new rules would cause "chaos"

He added: "The new ISA rules are a masterclass in government policy that sounds coherent in a press release and disintegrates on contact with reality. Under-65s get a £12,000 cash ISA allowance, over-65s get £20,000, and the cut-off is not the State Pension age of 67 but the apparently magic number of 65, selected for reasons the government has yet to share with anyone.

‌



"You are simultaneously too young for your State Pension but old enough for preferential ISA treatment. Savers will need their birth certificate and a flowchart just to work out what they are allowed to do. The 22% charge on cash interest inside stocks and shares ISAs completes the chaos.

"Older savers can sidestep it by transferring into a cash ISA. Younger ones cannot. Anyone locked into a fixed-term deposit inside an investment ISA maturing after April 2027 gets penalised for something they did entirely legally under rules since rewritten around them."

View 4 Images ISAs are tax-free, but soon one aspect won't be (Image: Laurence Berger via Getty Images)

‌



Nouran Moustafa, practice principal & IFA at Roxton Wealth, said the 65-year-old cut-off didn't make sense.

She added: "The age-65 line is difficult to defend because it has no clear relationship with retirement, income or financial need. Two savers with identical circumstances could face different limits and transfer rights purely because one had a birthday last week. The 22% charge is even more problematic.

"Cash inside a stocks and shares ISA is not always avoidance; it can be a temporary holding while an adviser rebalances, waits for markets to settle or prepares withdrawals. Penalising all interest risks turning sensible cash management into a compliance trap. Existing fixed-term deposits are the clearest fairness issue.

‌



"Where someone entered a legitimate arrangement before the rules were announced and cannot exit without penalty, those holdings should be grandfathered. Otherwise advisers will need to review cash positions much earlier, providers may reduce available options, and ordinary savers will face rules that are harder to understand than the behaviour they are meant to stop."

Harvey Dhillon, founder and CEO at Zmartly, urged people to check what cash is in their stocks and shares ISA.

He added: "The only money this tax touches is the cash you were keeping safe. Your provider pays it to HMRC. You cannot claim it back. Picture a woman of 68 living on a small pension. Outside an ISA her £400 of interest is tax-free, covered by allowances she is not using. Inside the ISA she loses £88 of it, the full 22 per cent, even though she pays no income tax at all.

‌



"The draft would also cut under-65s to £12,000 of new cash ISA savings a year, while over-65s keep £20,000. So her age protects her allowance, not her interest. Nobody reaches State Pension age at 65 any more, so that line is hard to defend. Nothing in the draft protects a fixed-term cash deposit ending after April 6, 2027, either. The draft is not law yet. In my experience nobody spots a deduction taken before the money arrives. Check what cash is sitting in your stocks and shares ISA before April 6, 2027."

View 4 Images Harvey Dhillon (Image: Newspage)

Evren Ergin, founder and developer at ValuQ, said the new rules would mean savers were nudged towards unnecessary risks.

‌



He added: "Everyone is arguing about the age line. Look at what it does to house deposits. Under 65s are the people saving to buy. Over 65s are overwhelmingly already in a home, often mortgage-free. So the group still trying to get on the ladder has its cash allowance cut to £12,000, while the group that already owns keeps the full £20,000.

"That is the wrong way round. A deposit cannot sit in equities. If you are buying in two years, cash is not timidity, it is the only responsible place for that money. These rules nudge deposit savers toward risk they should not be taking.

"And the alternative on offer is a Lifetime ISA capped at £4,000 a year, with a £450,000 property limit frozen since 2017 and a 25% charge if you buy above it. It is also due to be replaced in 2028. So save hard now and you still cannot be sure of the rules on the day you buy. First-time buyers already face the hardest deposit hurdle in decades. This quietly makes it harder."

‌



Antonia Medlicott, founder and MD of London-based Investing Insiders, said more clarity was needed.

She added: "The government has overcomplicated ISAs to the point where people with little financial knowledge feel they are inaccessible. ISAs have traditionally been one of the UK's simplest financial products, but these changes risk undermining that simplicity. Behavioural finance research consistently shows that complexity reduces participation.

"The cash ISA limit should be higher for those approaching retirement, so that it provides them a chance to lower the risk to their money. Less disruption from market volatility allows for firmer retirement plans, and you can already access your private pension by then. As you approach your later years, the appetite for investment risk should naturally reduce, which is the same with a pension.

Article continues below

"More clarity must be provided for people who have their money locked away until after the new financial year begins; it would be a travesty for them to have to pay tax. This requires a clear exemption from tax, or else even more faith will be lost from consumers."

News.title: More than half of England officially in drought, Environment Agency says
News.content:
The combination of low rainfall and prolonged high temperatures - meaning greater evaporation of moisture - has quickly depleted water reserves in soils, vegetation and rivers.

These conditions have led to a "flash drought", the EA has said. This is where drought conditions begin suddenly rather than over many months or years.

Today's announcement means there have been three droughts in the past five years â 2022, 2025 and now 2026.

While droughts happen naturally, scientists say that climate change is raising the risks, with higher summer temperatures drying out soils more quickly.

This can lead to more severe and longer-lasting droughts, which have had noticeable effects on wildlife and farming.

Paul Tompkins, deputy president of the National Farmers' Union of England and Wales (NFU), said: "Farmers and growers have always had to contend with the weather, but what they are experiencing now is climate change in action. More extreme conditions [are] making it harder, riskier and more costly to produce the nation's food."

He added the issue of drought is something that "should matter to everyone" as it affects the country's food security.

Some areas of the country have now entered their fourth heatwave of the year.

Amber and yellow heat health alerts have come into force for parts of the UK, with temperatures potentially peaking at 35C in parts of south-east England on Wednesday.

The hot, dry weather has created ideal conditions for wildfires to spread. The National Fire Chiefs Council has warned that wildfire risk "remains elevated across the UK".

More than 200 wildfire incidents have been reported in England and Wales over the past two weeks, it said.

The Met Office has separately announced that the new June temperature record set last month was even higher than previously thought, following verification processes.

The previously-reported figure of 37.7C in Lingwood, Norfolk, on 26 June 2026 has been updated to 38.0C â smashing the UK's previous June high of 35.6C.

Additional reporting by Jess Carr

News.title: Boy, 7, dies in hospital after beach tragedy
News.content:
A seven-year-old boy involved in a beach tragedy that killed his teenage cousin and her mother has died in hospital, his family has said.

Musa Ahmed was on a day trip to West Mersea, Essex, on 22 July, when he and five relatives got into difficulty in the water.

While he was pulled from the water and airlifted to hospital, Shelina Rahman, 41, and 15-year-old Sameeha, died at the scene.

Musa's family said he died "in a state of ease and peace" at the Royal London Hospital on Tuesday evening.

The family had travelled to the island, near Colchester, from Ilford in east London that morning.

Three others were also taken to hospital by ambulance after the incident, first reported to Essex Police at 17:35 BST, and were said by the force to be "recovering".

Musa's father, Shahin Ahmed, has said they were swept away by a "very strong" tide and police said they made "significant efforts to help each other".

News.title: Teenage Norwegian 'hitman' guilty of UK murder plot
News.content:
A teenager who travelled from Norway to the UK to carry out a "hit" for a Swedish organised crime group has been found guilty of conspiracy to murder.

An Old Bailey jury heard how Johannes Natland, 19, was arrested in a hotel room in Huddersfield with two working guns and 19 rounds of live ammunition in March 2025.

He pleaded guilty to possession of the firearms and ammunition but had denied the conspiracy charge.

Following a retrial, Natland showed no emotion as the jury brought in a unanimous guilty verdict after deliberating for just over 17 hours.

During the trial opening, prosecutor Alistair Richardson said the teen was "recruited" by the Foxtrot Network, which was described as a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.

Natland had claimed rather than carry out the attack, he had planned to shoot himself in the foot, telling jurors he had found himself in "a major pickle".

The court heard how the Foxtrot Network had been sanctioned by both the UK and the US for its close links to the Iranian government.

The group is infamous for pioneering the relatively new phenomenon of hiring teenage killers that Europol has called "violence-as-a-service" (VaaS).

Natland flew into Manchester Airport on an emergency passport on 17 March and was guided by videos on the messaging app Signal to Huddersfield, where the guns, a stolen car and a stash of cash were hidden.

News.title: OpenAI says its rogue AI tried to hack other companies
News.content:
OpenAI has revealed a cyber-attack carried out by rogue ChatGPT agents went further than just one company.

Hugging Face was thought to be the only victim of the unprecedented hack - but OpenAI now admits its bot attacked several "publicly-available services".

The out-of-control AI found four logins online which allowed it to access four separate, unnamed services.

Meanwhile, in an emergency briefing with hundreds of cyber security professionals, Hugging Face has described what it was like to be on the receiving end of the world's first fully autonomous AI hack.

The firm described how the AI worked at superhuman speed but also made strange decisions and mistakes that no human hacker would have made.

Hugging Face, which is like an app store for AI tools, said the hacking agents worked relentlessly with thousands of different methods trialled simultaneously.

The company first revealed that it had been hacked, external by someone using powerful autonomous AI on 16 July and reported it to police.

Nearly a week later, OpenAI admitted it was its AI that had escaped a closed environment and attacked Hugging Face on its own during a test.

It was trying to find the answers to a hacking exam it had been set by OpenAI, and targeted Hugging Face.

On Wednesday OpenAI updated its statement to include the extra detail that the hack went further than first thought.

"The models identified and used publicly exposed credentials at the account-level on other publicly-available services. This includes four accounts on four services as part of the Hugging Face incident," the company said.

OpenAI did not clarity whether "publicly-available services" means companies.

News.title: 'Apocalyptic' damage as Cairngorms wildfire burns for two weeks
News.content:
A wildfire that has burned for two weeks in the Cairngorms National Park has left an "apocalyptic" scene of devastation, say park bosses.

The fire has destroyed about 10 sq miles (25 sq km) of moorland and forestry near Aviemore since Wednesday 15 July.

Malcolm Smith, farming advisor to the Cairngorms National Park Authority (CNPA), said: "You are passing through just bare forest now and birds flying about looking for their nests."

RSPB Scotland, whose Loch Garten reserve at Abernethy has been badly burned, said it could takes weeks before the fire was extinguished.

News.title: Fix palliative care before assisted dying debate, says PM
News.content:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said that before assisted dying is considered in England and Wales, the funding of palliative and social care should be "fixed".

It is the first time Burnham has set out his position on the issue since becoming prime minister, as MPs prepare to debate it again when Parliament returns in September.

The government is likely to remain officially neutral, but Burnham's remarks suggest he personally will not back a bill being proposed by Labour MP Lauren Edwards.

The position is a shift from that of former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, who voted in favour of the previous attempt to legalise assisted dying and gave time for the issue to be debated in Parliament.

Sir Keir's support was privately cited by some Labour MPs as a reason they backed the bill last time.

Burnham told reporters: "I take the view that that debate - and I don't say that there shouldn't be a debate at some point about those issues - personally, I think there's something that needs to happen first.

"That is the fixing of the funding of palliative care and social care.

"I think it is very challenging to introduce that wider debate in a context of people not receiving that care and having the peace of mind about that care."

In 2025, MPs voted in favour of a bill proposed by Labour MP Kim Leadbeater to legalise assisted dying.

But the bill was not passed by the House of Lords, after an unprecedented number of suggested amendments delayed its progress until it ran out of time in April this year.

Its opponents argued it had substantial flaws that risked vulnerable people being pressured into ending their lives early.

The proposed law - known as the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill - would have allowed people over the age of 18 who were expected to die within six months to be given help to end their own life, subject to certain safeguards.

Labour MP Lauren Edwards plans to bring forward an identical bill in order to "finish the job" started by Leadbeater.

Following Burnham's comments, she said improving social care and legalising assisted dying was "not a case of either/or" and that the two things "can and must go hand in hand".

"The bill that has been before Parliament and thoroughly debated since October 2024 provides for a four-year implementation period - that means if my current bill becomes law next year, we would have until 2031 to fix the status quo that Andy Burnham rightly says is broken."

Jess Asato - a Labour MP and opponent of the bill - said MPs had "a responsibility to consider the safety of introducing such a flawed bill into a broken and failing care system".

"There can be no meaningful choice and no dignity at the end of life if we don't have a palliative care system that provides basic support for the vulnerable and an affordable social care system that gives everyone dignity at the end of their lives."

Burnham was asked about his views on assisted dying after he had announced plans to reform the social care system, with the view to create a national care service and to reach a political consensus on how to fund it.

In 2024, just before the first Commons vote on the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill, Burnham told BBC Manchester he would "probably vote in favour of it" if he was in Parliament.

When he was previously an MP he abstained from a 2015 vote on another bill to legalise assisted dying because of concerns over safeguards and people feeling under pressure.

But he told the BBC in 2024 that he had had "family experience in the nine years since that has changed my view".

He said: "I think we do allow people to suffer and families to suffer too much."

He caveated his support as being for the principle of assisted dying and insisted he would want a requirement before any new law was implemented that hospices would be "properly funded and sorted out".

News.title: Four deaths at homeless shelter linked to serial killer to be reviewed
News.content:
The unexplained deaths of four people who were living at a homeless shelter in Cornwall at the same time as triple killer James Desborough are being reviewed, police have said.

The 40-year-old was found guilty of murdering two other men he met while staying at Sandy Lodge in Newquay on Tuesday.

Earlier this year he was also sentenced for murdering his cellmate in Exeter Prison while on remand for the murder charges.

Det Supt Rachael Bentley, from Devon and Cornwall Police, said officers were looking at the unexpected deaths of two men and two women at the homeless shelter between December 2024 and April 2025.

She said: "As a major crime investigation team we were informed by the coroner's officer for His Majesty's Coroner that there were four deaths at Sandy Lodge.

"As part of the investigation, a detective inspector, separate to the investigation but within major crime, did a review of those deaths, and that included commissioning some more forensic work, some CCTV, and statements."

Police said inquiries were ongoing and the deaths remained unexpected at this stage.

Bentley said Desborough was "not a suspect at this time".

"We don't believe there is a link at this time, but I said it's an ongoing investigation," she said

She said police attended each of the deaths at Sandy Lodge and inquiries suggested natural causes but coronial investigations were paused when Desborough was arrested for murder.

News.title: Fifa offers $40m if nations back controversial plan
News.content:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino has written to all 211 member associations saying they will receive $40m (Â£30m) if they back his controversial plan to sell off stakes in its major competitions.

Infantino has set a deadline of 19 September for football federations to accept his plans if they want to access an initial $20m (Â£15m).

Football's world governing body has said it wants to create a commercial subsidiary to run its main events, including the World Cup, and external investors will be able to buy stakes in it.

The incentive to nations comes less than 24 hours after the bombshell statement rocked football's foundations, quickly leading to condemnation from Europe, Asia and North America.

It is understood Infantino even left some of Fifa's eight vice-presidents in the dark about his plan, which it is claimed could raise $10bn (Â£7.52bn).

Infantino has signed a five-page letter, seen by the BBC, outlining the merits of his proposal.

The letter states if member associations respond positively by the deadline, $20m will be "available immediately" from 1 January 2027.

Fifa confirms the money will come from "liquidating a minority portion" of its stake on Fifa Forward Enterprise, a subsidiary company set up to maximise commercial revenue that will include private investors.

Although Fifa suggested Infantino gave a broad outline of his proposal at a council meeting just before the World Cup final earlier this month, others who were present rejected this strongly. They say Infantino merely offered an aspirational vision for the future around maximising revenue streams.

They now believe they were duped, with the events of the past 24 hours leading them to conclude negotiations have all been completed and now they are being presented with a fait-accompli.

"It is my duty and responsibility as Fifa president to present such game-changing opportunities to you, our members," said Infantino.

"It is equally my duty and responsibility to ensure such proposals are sufficiently complete and feasible, replete with substantiated figures and clear terms to assist you in the decision-making process."

Opposition to the plan has been fierce, with many citing the lack of due process as the first point of their anger.

An FA spokeswoman said: "We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is and what conditions are attached.

"Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved.

"When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by Fifa, we will make our views clear and comment further."

News.title: Unauthorised airport car park grows despite stop notice
News.content:
Jane Fuller, from Hadleigh, Suffolk, said her daughter's car had been left unlocked for 22 hours in April.

"My daughter has an app on her phone and she managed to lock it from Croatia," she said.

"When we eventually got back to the car park, we had to hunt for it in the dark. We found it parked on top of rubble. It was a shocking experience," she added.

Deb Jordan, from Ely, Cambridgeshire, said the transport to the car park from the airport in May with her family had been "an absolute hazard".

She said passengers had been left stranded at Stansted Airport for more than three hours after landing.

"They piled two busloads of angry people onto one small transit minibus," she said.

"Luggage was piled on top of passengers. I had a pushchair wedged over my head."

On arrival at the car park, Jordan said the family had been given the keys to someone else's car.

Several customers said they had been charged an additional Â£20 on arrival at the car park to pay for transport to the Radisson Blu Hotel at Stansted Airport, from where they then had to walk to the airport.

They were also told to meet at the location at the airport on their return after ringing drivers at New Farm once they had landed.

News.title: Polanski says guillotine re-post was mistake but refuses to apologise
News.content:
Zack Polanski has refused three times to apologise to Nigel Farage for re-posting a photo of a man wearing a t-shirt with an image of a guillotine and the slogan "we're only making plans for Nigel".

Reform UK's home affairs spokesperson, Zia Yusuf, said the image showed a "photo of man calling for the beheading of Nigel Farage", which he said could be an "incitement to murder".

The Green Party of England and Wales leader was reported to the Met over the photo, which he then deleted, but told the BBC he had not been contacted by police.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, he said he would not apologise for an "inadvertent mistake" that he said Farage had amplified in a "fundamentally dishonest way".

The row kicked off on Monday evening when Polanski shared the photo, which he said was the fifth image in a series of 20 from a party, having accepted a request to collaborate with the Instagram account of a photographer at the event.

Posting a screenshot on X, Reform UK leader Farage said: "If I was to post anything as inciteful then I would expect to be arrested, and so should Polanski."

Asked if he wanted to apologise to Farage, Polanski said: "Well, if I'd done it deliberately I'd be apologising but because this was a mistake I think the important thing is that I point out this was a mistake, that I also make sure that I condemn political violence, and also crucially I make a commitment to be better on social media."

Asked for a second time whether he would apologise, Polanski refused because he said Farage had cropped the image to make it look like he had posted it himself, which he said was "fundamentally dishonest" and only amplified the problem.

Saying he had received a death threat earlier on Tuesday, Polanski added: "The ramping up of the language to say 'this is incitement to murder me' feels like that's also putting me in a dangerous spot."

Given a third chance to apologise, Polanski doubled down and said: "You know as well as I do that as soon as I do that Nigel Farage would run all over social media saying he was correct about incitement to murder and this would all ramp up again.

"I think it's important that I draw a line and don't play his game... It is important that he's kept safe, it is important we condemn political violence, but I also recognise this as the political attack that it is."

"If Nigel Farage wants to apologise for all the times that he's put other people in danger then I will be happy to make an apology," Polanski added.

The Green leader explained he had not read the slogan on the T-shirt when he accepted the collaboration because "what I was seeing was people partying" and he only noticed the man was wearing a rainbow hat as he flicked through.

"It feels quite surreal to be having this conversation," he said, adding: "I think it would be odd for the police to speak to me about that because I think it's quite obvious I've not done anything wrong other than make an inadvertent mistake."

The Metropolitan Police said there was no update on the complaint they had received on Monday.

On Tuesday, Reform asked the monitoring officer from the Greater London Authority, where Polanski is an elected member, to investigate whether he had breached the code of conduct.

Keith Prince, a Reform London Assembly Member, said: "To say that he was unaware of what he was promoting is frankly risible."

A Reform UK source told BBC Newsnight: "It's truly astonishing and quite frankly sickening that Zack Polanski won't apologise for inciting murder.

"He admits it was wrong. He admits it's dangerous, but he still refuses to apologise. Mr Polanski is not fit to lead a national political party."

Asked about the row on Tuesday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there was a "duty on all politicians to be careful about what they post", especially in light of the death of former MP Ann Widdecombe earlier this month.

News.title: Brits urged to avoid dangerous plug adaptors this summer - what to watch out for
News.content:
Brits going on holiday abroad this summer have been warned to watch out for dangerous travel adaptors, after an investigation suggested thousands may be for sale online.

Consumer safety group Electrical Safety First (ESF) tested 14 products from AliExpress, Amazon Marketplace, eBay and TikTok Shop - and found they all failed to meet UK safety requirements.

It said in some instances the devices could expose users to risk of serious electric shock or electrocution.

AliExpress, Amazon, eBay and TikTok all said they had removed the products ESF flagged from sale, and that they treated product safety as a top priority.

But Giuseppe Capanna, ESF product safety engineer, urged those "heading abroad this summer to think before they buy".

"What looks like a bargain could come at a much higher cost," he warned.

Capanna also said shoppers should buy travel adaptors from trusted retailers "so they can travel with confidence".

ESF tested six regular travel adaptors and eight universal adaptors it suspected could pose safety concerns.

To be sold in the UK, adaptors must not have accessible live parts and only one set of pins should come out at a time.

But the charity found multiple sets could be exposed simultaneously in six out of eight of the universal adaptors it tested.

None of the eight met the required dimensions and mechanical strength, while some pins snapped off under force during tests.

ESF said anyone who tried to remove a broken pin from a socket would be at risk of electric shock.

News.title: Woman accused of breaching Donaldson victims' anonymity
News.content:
A woman has been charged with breaching an anonymity order in relation to the victims of former DUP leader and convicted paedophile Jeffrey Donaldson.

Police said the 55-year-old was arrested in the Ballynahinch area on Tuesday.

She has been charged with a breach of a lifetime ban on reporting the identity of victims, and is due to appear before Downpatrick Magistrates' Court on 24 August.

Victims of sexual offences receive lifelong legal anonymity unless they waive their right to it.

Donaldson, who was an MP from 1997 until 2024, was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

He was told by the judge that the sentence would be a lengthy one.

It has since been confirmed he is to appeal his convictions.

News.title: Chief constable resigns before misconduct tribunal
News.content:
The chief constable of Staffordshire Police has resigned, ahead of a gross misconduct hearing regarding his behaviour.

Chris Noble was suspended in August amid inquiries by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC), with the watchdog confirming in March that it had opened two more investigations regarding his behaviour.

Noble resigned on Tuesday via a letter to the Police and Crime Commissioner for Staffordshire, Ben Adams.

The misconduct hearing began on Wednesday morning in Noble's absence and has since been adjourned.

He was chosen to lead Staffordshire Police after the retirement of the previous chief constable in 2021.

Prior to this, he was the assistant chief constable of Humberside Police.

In a statement, Staffordshire Commissioner for Police, Fire & Rescue and Crime, Ben Adams said: "I can confirm that yesterday [28 July], I received Chief Constable Chris Noble's resignation, which I have accepted with immediate effect.

"Becky Riggs will remain as Staffordshire Police's acting chief constable.

"The misconduct hearing will continue today as planned, under former officer provisions."

Staffordshire Police said that it would not be appropriate to comment due to ongoing misconduct proceedings.

In a recent statement, the IOPC said: "The chair of the panel has directed that no additional information relating to the detail of the allegations can be released at this time.

"We are continuing to investigate other allegations relating to Mr Noble. Given the sensitivity of those matters, for operational reasons, no further information can be provided at this time."

News.title: Amber heat health alerts in force as heatwave reaches 35C peak
News.content:
Amber and yellow heat health alerts have come into force as parts of the UK endure the fourth widespread heatwave of the year so far.

Temperatures are forecast to peak on Wednesday with readings as high as 35C (95F) in the hottest places.

Though the heatwave will come to a quick end for many on Thursday, well above-average temperatures in the mid- to high 20s Celsius will persist into the weekend.

On Wednesday, the Environment Agency declared an official drought for more than half of England, triggered in part by the summer's unrelenting heat and significant lack of rainfall.

News.title: My 10-day headache was terminal brain cancer
News.content:
While his illness is terminal, Josh said keeping his sense of humour and making memories remained his top priorities, as well as raising awareness to boost brain tumour research funding.

In January, Josh started having "these weird feelings" but "thought nothing of it".

"I just thought I was tired," he recalled.

"February is when it started properly. I had a 10-day headache. I would be walking my dog with my wife or talking to my mum and dad, and I'd feel zoned out. I found out later it was mini seizures and I didn't realise. It's really scary to look back on."

On 9 February, his wife Kelly "dragged" him to see a GP, for the first time in about 12 years.

"I've always avoided it," he said.

"There's that societal expectation of 'man up' and get on with it. I was just popping paracetamol and getting early nights."

He said he would always be grateful that Kelly was so insistent.

"I could not have done any of this without her. If I had kept on ignoring it, I might not be here now."

Josh said the GP "found nothing wrong", prescribing more painkillers and referring him to an optician, where again no issue was found.

"I didn't have the greatest experience, it was quite dismissive," he said, adding the surgery had since apologised to him and been "so helpful".

Kelly, 33, added: "I knew something wasn't right. I remember saying there were red flags, but we were told there was nothing to worry about."

News.title: Ticket prices set to rise by 15p as Heathrow able to recover runway project money
News.content:
Heathrow Airport will be allowed to charge airlines more for its services to recover money spent on the early stages of its third runway project.

The aviation regulator is permitting the airport to claw back up to Â£320m through higher airport charges to airlines for each passenger. This is likely to end up adding 15p to ticket prices in 2028, rising to 30p in later years.

A bidder which unsuccessfully put forward a rival design involving a shorter runway, Arora Group's Heathrow West, will also be allowed to recover Â£4.1m pounds in costs.

The Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) and Heathrow said safeguards would be put in place to protect consumers from unjustified costs.

The CAA had already proposed that Heathrow's airline fees are capped at between Â£27.20 and Â£30.50 per passenger for 2027-2031.

At this stage, the costs being recovered are only for the early planning and design of the runway during 2025 and 2026.

How much the cost of actually building the runway will add to ticket prices won't be clear for some time.

Tim Johnson, the CAA's director of consumers and markets, told the BBC: "We've announced that the first tranche of costs, which is to help with the planning of this, can be recovered from passengers. That's up to a maximum of Â£320m."

Heathrow airport will also be able to collect Heathrow West's costs up to November last year by adding to its airport charges.

The CAA said allowing these costs to be recouped will result in the maximum airport charge per passenger increasing by around 15 pence in 2028, rising to an estimated 30 pence in the following years.

Rory Boland, editor of Which? Travel, said any extra costs passed onto customers were "unwelcome" when many people were struggling with the price of travel.

"These increases may seem small, but they are being added to what are already some of the highest airport charges in the world," he said.

"Heathrow has little competition on many routes, leaving travellers with few alternatives if charges continue to rise," he added.

A Heathrow spokesperson said a third runway will make "travel more affordable and giving passengers more choice, while providing a real economic boost to every region and nation of the country."

"We are carefully considering the CAA proposals and will make investment decisions accordingly," the spokesperson added.

In November, the government announced it preferred the Â£33bn scheme put forward by the airport over Arora's alternative plan.

At the time, the Department for Transport said Heathrow's own proposal offered the most deliverable option, and the "greatest likelihood" of getting a decision on planning approval within this parliament.

The CAA's director of consumers and markets, Tim Johnson, said today's decision "strikes a balance between supporting the delivery of benefits to consumers through timely progress on Heathrow expansion, whilst also protecting them from undue increases in costs".

The regulator said "safeguards" designed to monitor cost efficiency would include transparency and cost reporting requirements, and assurance by independent experts.

Airlines often complain that Heathrow is the world's most most expensive hub airport, and have repeatedly voiced concern that the airport's expansion plans will make it pricier.

The government hopes for a planning decision by 2029.

Plans for a third runway stretch back decades, with the government backing the plans in 2003.

However, the idea has also long faced opposition from climate campaigners, many local residents, and several politicians.

They worry an additional runway will increase air pollution, noise pollution, and breach the government's legally binding climate commitments.

Half of England is officially in drought after a record dry spell and high temperatures, the Environment Agency has said.

Seven areas across central, eastern and southern England have been declared as in drought, including East Anglia, Hertfordshire, London, Thames Valley, Hampshire & the Isle of Wight, Devon & Cornwall, the West Midlands and Wessex – the latter of which covers Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire, and south Gloucestershire.

July is set to be the driest month on record, with England having just 7 per cent of expected rainfall, and southern England seeing just 1 per cent.

As such, swathes of the country are now experiencing a flash drought – one which has come on swiftly despite a wet winter.

Drought map:

It comes as health alerts issued by the the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) have come into effect for large parts of the country.

An amber heat health alert is in place for the East Midlands, east of England, London and south east until Thursday, 30 July at 9am.

Meanwhile, a yellow heat health alert is in force for the West Midlands, south west and Yorkshire and the Humber during the same period.

There have been three droughts in the past five years: 2022, 2025 and 2026.

Helen Wakeham, director of water at the Environment Agency and chairwoman of the National Drought Group, said: “The hot and dry weather means we are currently using water faster than nature can replenish it.

“A second consecutive summer drought is an exceptionally serious situation and one that will have long-lasting impacts on our environment, wildlife and the economy.

“We want everyone to stay safe and hydrated during the hot weather but every drop we can save is a drop more for nature and agriculture.”

Why has a drought been declared now?

According to the Environment Agency, “droughts are natural events that cannot be defined, as every drought is different.”

It adds: “Whilst they are all caused by a shortage of rainfall, the characteristics (including timing, duration, impacts on people, the environment, agriculture and business) can vary.”

According to the Environment Agency, ‘droughts are natural events that cannot be defined, as every drought is different.’ ( Getty )

The agency lists three different main types of drought, including agricultural drought – “when there isn’t enough rainfall and moisture in soils to support crop production or farming practices” – environmental drought and water supply drought “when a lack of rainfall leads to concerns from water companies about supplies for their customers”.

Neymar has seemingly confirmed his retirement from international football, stating he no longer wishes to represent Brazil, weeks after initially hinting at the end of his national career following their World Cup last-16 defeat to Norway.

The 34-year-old forward, who is Brazil's all-time leading scorer, made the definitive comments after Santos secured a 4-2 victory over Venezuela's Universidad Central in a Copa Sudamericana match on Tuesday evening.

"I think my time with the national team has already passed. I made history there, and I'm very happy about it. I experienced a lot there, gave my blood and my life, and always fought and battled for the yellow jersey. But I don't think I want it anymore," he told reporters.

These remarks echo sentiments expressed immediately after Brazil's 2-1 World Cup loss to Norway on 5 July.

Having come on as a substitute and scored a stoppage-time penalty, Neymar suggested his international career was over during an interview with Brazilian broadcaster ge, stating: "I tried, I tried. Now it's over."

Neymar appeared to confirm his international retirement after playing for Santos on Tuesday ( Getty )

The defeat left Neymar visibly emotional, and marked Brazil's earliest World Cup exit since 1990 while prolonging the five-time champions' wait for a record-extending sixth title.

The forward, who made his World Cup debut in 2014 and competed in four global tournaments, has enjoyed a stellar club career with Santos, Barcelona, and Paris St Germain, yet secured only one senior title with the national team, the Confederations Cup in 2013.

He came back into the national team fold ahead of the World Cup after failing to play for Brazil for almost three years due to injury setbacks and loss of form.

Carlo Ancelotti opted to pick him for this summer’s tournament, but Neymar missed the opening two games due to a calf problem, and only returned as a substitute in Brazil’s 3-0 win over Scotland.

He was then an unused substitute in Brazil’s 2-1 win over Japan in the round of 32, before he came on in the second half of Brazil’s loss to Norway, with Erling Haaland’s brace sealing victory for the European nation.

Neymar’s international career concludes with an impressive 80 goals and 58 assists across 130 appearances.

The husband of a woman who was murdered in a Scottish cottage had been charged with assaulting her weeks before her death.

Stacy Mair, 35, was found dead in a cottage within the village of Houston in Renfrewshire at about 7.50am on Monday.

Her husband Jim Mair, 43, was also found dead at the property, with his death being treated as unexplained.

Police Scotland’s major investigation team is looking into the incident and the area around the cottage has been sealed off.

Jim Mair had appeared at Paisley Sheriff Court on 6 July charged with assaulting the 35-year-old mother.

The Scottish Sun reported he was granted bail on condition he did not approach her.

open image in gallery Jim Mair had appeared at Paisley Sheriff Court on 6 July charged with assaulting the 35-year-old mother ( PA )

Officers had gone to the address in the Corsliehill Road area of Houston following reports of concern for a person.

The pair were married in 2019 and Jim Mair ran a tree removal company called TRS Tree Management.

Ms Mair, who was from Falkland in Fife, had also been a director of the company but she resigned from the role in January.

Police said her death is being treated as murder while Jim Mair’s death remains unexplained.

The force said there is nothing to suggest anyone else is at risk of harm in connection with the incident.

There has been a large police presence at the scene while investigations are carried out.

Detective Chief Inspector Laura Young, of the major investigation team, said: “Our thoughts remain with the families of those affected by this incident.

“They are understandably devastated and we are providing them with support through specialist officers at this incredibly difficult time.”

Chief Inspector Iain Farmer, of Police Scotland, said: “This is a deeply upsetting incident for the families involved and the impact is felt right across the local community.

“I am grateful for the support we have received as we complete our essential inquires to ensure the families and local residents get the answers they need.”

Anyone with information or concerns regarding the incident can contact police on 101.

Former Republican congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene quietly married her fiancé, conservative journalist Brian Glenn, in Las Vegas this week, according to a report

Greene, 52, was seen in a white wedding gown while Glenn, 57, donned a tux on Tuesday as they wed at the famous Bellagio Hotel in Las Vegas, TMZ reported.

The couple was spotted holding hands as they walked through the hotel, accompanied by a cameraman who captured the entire celebration. There was also a group of children with the couple during their celebrations, according to the report.

On Monday, Glenn appeared to tease their upcoming nuptials, sharing a photo of him and Greene kissing on X and writing, “The clock is ticking.”

Neither Greene nor Glenn have publicly commented on their wedding. However, Clark County online records confirm the couple applied for a marriage license last Friday.

open image in gallery Marjorie Taylor Greene and Brian Glenn tied the knot Tuesday in Las Vegas, according to a report ( Getty )

The former Georgia congresswoman and Glenn got engaged last December after about three years of dating.

At the time, Glenn, a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump, broke the news on X, sharing an image of the two beaming at a restaurant, with Greene showing off her ring, and writing, “She said yes.”

Greene later reshared the post, adding, “Happily ever after!!! I love you @brianglenntv!!!”

Greene and Glenn were previously married, but met while they were both going through divorces in 2022, The Washington Post reported.

Greene first caught Glenn’s eye at a Trump rally, with Glenn telling the Post, “She was, like, mystical — like a unicorn or something like that, you know?”

He told the newspaper he was immediately drawn to her Georgian accent and “very gentle, almost angelic soul.”

“People don’t see the side of Marjorie that I do,” he later told the Post. “When you take her out of politics, she’s sweet. She’s sweet!”

A Reform councillor has been charged with posting a grossly offensive message on social media.

Glenn Gibbins, of Sunderland City Council, allegedly made the post, which referenced the Nigerian community, in 2024.

Northumbria Police said that he has been charged with an offence under the Communications Act 2003.

The 66-year-old, from Sunderland, is due to appear before South Tyneside Magistrates’ Court on 21 August.

The force said that it was alerted to the post in May this year.

It has now submitted a file to the Crown Prosecution Service, which has authorised a charge.

A Northumbria Police spokesperson said: “We are aware there has already been significant interest in relation to this individual and the social media post.

“We would urge people not to speculate both online and in the community in relation to this case.”

Gibbins was suspended by Reform but was later reinstated, according to reports.

Deletion is a common part of modern life. We send files and folders to the recycle bin all the time, and often get rid of unwanted personal accounts. But do you know what really happens when you hit the “delete” button?

The process of deletion is often poorly explained by tech providers. Lack of transparency around how requests are processed, and the absence of clear confirmation that data has been removed, are frequently highlighted in research.

These issues are not limited to operating systems. On social media platforms and a wide range of subscription services, deletion mechanisms are often just as unclear. Such misconceptions can have serious implications for the wellbeing of users, exposing them to security and privacy vulnerabilities.

open image in gallery On social media platforms and a wide range of subscription services, deletion mechanisms are often just as unclear ( Getty Images/iStockphoto )

A further complication is that many users fear losing data, files, photos and videos through accidental deletion – a condition dubbed “diagraphephobia”. Though this is not a recognised pathology, studies of digital hoarding behaviour show that some people get very anxious at the thought of losing or accidentally deleting personal information such as photos and music.

Such concerns extend the amount of personal data that sits untended but undeleted, ready for potential misappropriation.

Deletion vs erasure

A common misconception is thinking deletion means erasure – the idea that once a deleted item is no longer visible, it has been completely erased with no means of retrieving it. This is largely wrong.

When users delete files – moving them to the trash bin, then deleting permanently – the data isn’t actually erased. Rather, the system marks storage space as reusable and updates metadata to unlink the file. But the underlying content often remains recoverable with the right tools, especially when data is duplicated across multiple systems or devices.

More robust forms of deletion include physical destruction of the storage medium, overwriting the memory blocks with new data to bury the original, or encrypting the data and then destroying the key.

However, such methods can be expensive and may render the storage device unusable (for example, when overwriting data on magnetic media). The characteristics of cloud infrastructure also pose challenges to secure data deletion.

Similarly, content on public social networks may not really be erased after deletion due to replies, comments and internet archives which can all store the posts in some fashion. The meaning of a deleted tweet can, for example, be recreated based on replies and mentions.

Zombie accounts

Another misconception is that deleting an app from a device automatically deletes the associated account. Users often leave mobile app accounts undeleted because they are unaware of their existence, having deleted the related app.

These are called zombie accounts – abandoned profiles for a wide array of services, from shopping and storage to dating, finance and streaming. Millions of users possess zombie accounts, with personal data that is vulnerable to cyber-attacks and data breaches.

The exponential growth of AI raises a further question: can data really be deleted once it has been used to train AI models? Machine learning modules easily memorise the data they have been trained on, but “unlearning” is difficult.

In theory, people in Europe and many other countries around the world have a leagal “right to be forgotten”. This means they can request the full erasure of any personal data a platform or a company may hold. AI developers are considered data controllers under the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) laws, for example, and are subject to this obligation.

However, there are no clear guidelines on how erasure should be enforced within AI systems. Regulators may request deletion, but AI companies can argue that compliance is infeasible on account of technical constraints.

Explainable deletion

To counter the risks posed by incomplete deletion, I believe there is a pressing need for provision of concise, accessible and clear information about how deletion really works.

One potential approach is “explainable deletion” – a protocol developed by Marvin Ramokapane at the UK’s National Research Centre on Privacy, Harm Reduction and Adversarial Influence Online (Rephrain), based at the University of Bristol.

The intention is to make deletion processes more transparent and understandable without overwhelming the user with too much information in one go.

Explainable deletion breaks down information into six categories: what, how, when, who, where and why (see diagram). Each offers a user bite-size information about that part of the process.

Explainable deletion’s six categories:

open image in gallery Explainable deletion is designed to give users control over their actions ( Marvin Ramokapane and Dana Lungu, CC BY-SA )

Explainable deletion is designed to give users control over their actions, the autonomy to choose the deletion type that is right for them, and the assurance that their desired actions have been fulfilled. It may also tackle the anxiety of accidentally losing data by giving options for data recovery.

About the author Dana Lungu is a Research Associate, National Research Centre on Privacy, Harm Reduction and Adversarial Influence Online, Rephrain, University of Bristol. This article was first published by The Conversation and is republished under a Creative Commons licence. Read the original article.

While explainable deletion has not yet been adopted in practice, service providers – both platforms and developers – could heighten user trust by adopting such protocols. This framework can also be proof of compliance with GDPR regulations and the right to be forgotten.

Most of us use systems that collect and store our data on a daily basis. If these systems clearly explained what they store and what deletion really means, it could help us to spot the accounts and data that pose a real risk – and to take back control of our digital footprints.

News.title: Tottenham new boys Tonali and Robertson score in shoot-out win over Sydney FC
News.content:
Tonali was brought on as a half-time substitute, before Robertson took the captain’s armband from Archie Gray after he was introduced in the 65th minute.

The former Liverpool left-back delivered three dangerous crosses which went unconverted, something of a theme for a Spurs team who failed to make the most of long spells of dominance.

James Maddison and Mateus Fernandes were not in the match-day squad, while Pedro Porro, Marcos Senesi, Cristian Romero, Micky van de Ven and Jean Paul van Hecke have yet to join the group after the World Cup.

There was another impressive showing from 17-year-old prospect Luca Williams-Barnett, who is pushing for first-team opportunities this upcoming season.

Penalties followed the final whistle, with Spurs scoring all four of their spot kicks. Goalkeeper Martin Dubravka, signed on a free transfer this summer, saved one and Sydney FC’s Josh Lacey hit the post to give Spurs the spoils 4-2.

News.title: Recovery aids and building muscle: Welsh weightlifter Laura Hughes answers your questions
News.content:
Laura Hughes first discovered weightlifting while training at her local Crossfit gym, making the transition from amateur gym-goer to competitive lifting.

Now a member of the Welsh national weightlifting squad, the 33-year-old holds the Welsh record for both the snatch and the clean and jerk (the two official competitive lifts in weightlifting) and is currently third overall in the women’s Welsh rankings. Hughes won bronze at the 2018 Commonwealth Games in Australia and was selected again for this summer’s Games in Glasgow.

We caught up with her for our Readers Ask series, where industry specialists answer questions from our Telegraph Recommended Reader Panel.

Who inspired you to get into weightlifting?

Olamilekan, South East

Originally, it was lots of different people, particularly general gym goers who were doing weightlifting at my gym. As I’ve grown as an athlete and become more competitive, I’ve had other inspirations.

Most notably, coming into [the Commonwealth Games], it has to be Gareth [Evans], our coach. Looking back at his performance in 2018 when he won his gold medal is so inspiring. [English lifter] Emily Godley was another competitor in 2018. She won the gold medal in my category and I just remember thinking that she was on fire that day.

What are the best exercises for you to build muscle mass?

Norman, Wales

We spend a lot of time doing our main lifts, so snatches, clean and jerks, but we also do lots of pulls and squats. I spend a lot of time doing accessory work to make sure that my body stays healthy, especially being an older athlete. I’ve put on quite a lot of muscle in this last block just from going heavier and pushing my limits with my main lifts.

What advice would you give to people who want to improve their strength?

David, North West

The most important thing is consistency. As long as you’re doing something, do it regularly, even if it’s twice a week. Don’t be afraid of picking up some dumbbells. If you’ve got somebody that can teach you how to lift weights properly, that’s going to be the best option. Do it safely, do it consistently, and don’t be afraid to try new strength exercises.

News.title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
News.content:
More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country’s busiest coastal hubs.

A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses.

The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time.

“The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before,” Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph.

“Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported.”

News.title: Chelsea in 10-goal thriller as ‘Alonso ball’ brings risk and reward
News.content:
Chelsea’s first match under the management of Xabi Alonso was a 10-goal thriller in Australia, as the Premier League side eventually showed their class in a 6-4 win over Western Sydney Wanderers.

Star striker João Pedro, who was controversially left out of Brazil’s World Cup squad, scored a nine-minute hat-trick after coming off the bench with half an hour of the friendly remaining.

Alonso had selected a youthful team for the first hour before bringing nine senior players, including João Pedro, into the side in the second half. According to Transfermarkt, Chelsea’s squad is valued at over £1.3bn while their opponents a more modest £5.86m.

Teenage signing Dastan Satpayev, midfielder Dario Essugo and winger Jamie Gittens also found the net for Chelsea, who were defensively vulnerable for long spells for the game.

Here are five things Telegraph Sport learned from Alonso’s first match.

João Pedro picks up where he left off

João Pedro scored 13 goals in the second half of last season and his impressive performances resulted in the 24-year-old being named Chelsea’s player of the campaign. It was something of a surprise, then, when he was left out of Carlo Ancelotti’s Brazil squad this summer.

The good news for Chelsea is that João Pedro’s absence from the World Cup has given him plenty of time to recover ahead of the new campaign, and he looked thrillingly sharp in his second-half performance against Western Sydney Wanderers. The difference in class between João Pedro and Liam Delap, the man he replaced, was clear for all to see.

Two of the Brazilian’s three goals were classy, composed finishes — and he also created a goal for Gittens after surging past three defenders on the left wing. João Pedro looks like he means business.

News.title: China’s chip breakthrough triggers global tech rout
News.content:
China has achieved a breakthrough in developing technology crucial to the AI boom, overcoming US efforts to limit Beijing’s access to the systems.

China’s chip giant Shanghai Yuliangsheng has started production of deep ultraviolet lithography machines, according to The Information, a tech publication.

These machines, which can reach the size of a double-decker bus, use high-powered lasers to imprint designs on to silicon wafers, which are used to make chips.

Until recently, only Western companies and allies of the US had the capability to produce these machines.

The most advanced versions of the technology have largely been the preserve of companies such as Dutch giant ASML and Japan’s Nikon.

These machines have been cut off from China by US export controls, preventing their production of advanced chips as Washington seeks to slow the development of AI in the country.

Semiconductor stocks plunged on the report. Trading was briefly halted on South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index after it suffered a collapse of nearly 11pc overnight, following a bleak day on Wall Street.

Advanced semiconductors, such as those used in AI chips, rely on minuscule circuits, invisible to the naked eye. They can only be manufactured by directing tiny lasers onto microchip wafers, a process known as ultraviolet lithography.

News.title: Ramsay-Peaty ‘human first, athlete second’ as he settles for second bronze
News.content:
So a pair of bronze medals for the man who once only dealt in gold. Not that Adam Ramsay-Peaty thinks that is necessarily such a bad trade when he also computes the wider price of sporting domination.

“I’ve been that person who wins all the time, and it costs you pretty much everything, and I won’t say it’s worth it,” Ramsay-Peaty said after his return to international competition continued in his now favoured 50m breaststroke with a second podium place at these Commonwealth Games. “That period of time, where I was undefeated for eight years, it was athlete first, then human,” he added. “Now it’s human first, then athlete, which is a very fair price to pay.”

Aged 31, and with a baby girl on the way with wife Holly Ramsay, Ramsay-Peaty’s order of priorities might be understandable, but it was still another performance to raise questions over whether he can again climb to the top of a major podium.

Swimming is not kind to the over-30s – Michael Phelps was the first man in 2016 to win an Olympic gold in the pool even at the age Ramsay-Peaty is now – and we still have another two years until the Los Angeles Olympics. It would be the greatest achievement even of the Englishman’s extraordinary career to win his third individual Olympic title.

He trailed from the start here and was almost exactly a second outside his world record – set almost a decade ago – as Australia’s Sam Williamson completed a breaststroke double ahead of South Africa’s Michael Houlie in second. “As you get older, it gets harder,” said Ramsay-Peaty, before adding a crucial caveat, “but I’m enjoying it more…in my head, I’m getting fresher.”

News.title: Musk passed ‘slow death sentence’ on HIV patients by cutting US spending, says head of UNAIDS
News.content:
The world’s richest man has passed a “slow death sentence” on an untold number of people with HIV by cutting US spending on the disease, according to the head of UNAIDS.

In an interview with the Telegraph, Winnie Byanyima, executive director of the UN body, said Elon Musk’s claim that the cuts made to US aid had resulted in “zero” deaths was born of ignorance.

“I do not know where Elon Musk gets his data from, but he [is] showing ignorance of the disease”, Ms Byanyima told the Telegraph at the opening the 26th International Aids Conference in Rio de Janeiro.

“This disease is not like a bullet shot in the head and you die. This is an attack on the immune system.” Withdrawing medication is a “a slow death sentence,” she said.

Data released by UNAIDS show that reductions to international funding and cuts to HIV prevention and community services threaten a resurgence of the epidemic.

In 2025, 1.2 million more people became infected with HIV and 570 000 more people died of Aids-related illnesses as the world fell short of global targets.

Although new HIV infections and Aids-related deaths are at their lowest levels in more than 30 years, an 18 per cent cut to total international funding means previous gains are now at risk, say experts.

Sports.title: Kelly Cates makes thoughts clear on Gabby Logan and Mark Chapman as she opens up on BBC job
Sports.content:
Kelly Cates makes thoughts clear on Gabby Logan and Mark Chapman as she opens up on BBC job

Match of the Day presenter Kelly Cates has revealed what she thinks about her BBC colleagues

View 3 Images Kelly Cates has spoken about her Match of the Day colleagues (Image: The Romesh Ranganathan Show/YouTube)

Kelly Cates insisted she hadn't read any reaction to her Match of the Day appointment as she revealed her true thoughts on co-hosts Gabby Logan and Mark Chapman. Last season was the first of a new presenter line-up, with Cates, Logan and Chapman sharing hosting duties after long-running anchor Gary Lineker stepped down.

‌



The trio, who also led the BBC's World Cup coverage, host Match of the Day on a rotation basis, with Cates and Chapman continuing to work for Sky Sports and Logan and Chapman fronting the Sports Agents podcast together.

‌



Cates, the daughter of Liverpool icon Kenny Dalglish, was honoured to take on the prestigious role, especially alongside fellow respected broadcasters Logan and Chapman. She told The Romesh Ranganathan Show: "They [the BBC] just asked me. There was no big manoeuvring. Gary was leaving, which accelerated it slightly, and the process came a bit quicker.

‌



"They said, 'Do you want to come and do it, we're looking at a team of three.' I was like, 'Who are the other two?'

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

"They said it was Mark and Gabby and I said, 'That's amazing.' It's Match of the Day, so it sells itself. Also, the fact it's those two…Normally, I take the p*** out of the people I work with and it's OK.

‌



Mark Chapman's BBC colleagues have all told World Cup host exactly what they think of him READ MORE :

"But it's Mark and Gabby, and they're amazing. Being on a team with them is genuinely really exciting. I feel like I'm in a great little group."

The trio's appointment has generally gone down with viewers, not that Cates would know, as she shields herself from coverage, whether it is positive or negative. She added: "I didn't read it, and that's not hard to do.

View 3 Images Cates shares hosting duties with Mark Chapman and Gabby Logan (Image: BBC/Charlie Clift)

‌



"It's not hard to avoid the coverage. It's hard to stop people sending you the coverage but I just tell them I don't want them to send it to me, even nice stuff. I still really have no idea what people thought about it or think about it. I just do my job."

The new presenting line-up has coincided with a fall in Match of the Day's viewership. However, that is believed to be due to a change in viewing habits, with digital highlights clips of each Premier League match now available at 8pm on Saturdays.

View 3 Images The trio replaced Gary Lineker, who is now focusing on his podcast empire (Image: James Gill - Danehouse, Getty Images)

‌



Average weekly views for the highlights across the iPlayer, the BBC Sport website and the app stood at 1.52million between August and December 2025. That has more than offset the drop-off in those viewing the traditional programme.

Between August and December 2024, the average weekly viewing figures across all devices – both TV and iPlayer and the Saturday and Sunday shows – was 7.65m, but were down to 6.88m across the same period last year, a drop of around 770,000.
