Sports.title: Chelsea’s dream final month of transfer window as Alex Scott and World Cup wonderkid sign
Sports.content:
Chelsea’s dream final month of transfer window as Alex Scott and World Cup wonderkid sign

Chelsea have wasted little time splashing the cash this summer but the Xabi Alonso rebuild at Stamford Bridge is far from complete with several key pieces still needed

View 7 Images Xabi Alonso is looking to hit the ground running as Chelsea boss (Image: Getty Images)

Chelsea are entering the final stretch of the summer transfer window with plenty still to solve. Xabi Alonso has wasted little time putting his fingerprints on the squad, with the Blues beginning a significant reshaping process designed to reflect the Spaniard's tactical demands.

‌



But while formations and recruitment remain central to the rebuild, there is another area Chelsea must address - adding more experience, personality and leadership to a group that has often lacked those qualities under the current ownership.

‌



There have already been signs of the new era taking shape. The arrival of Morgan Rogers for a club-record £117million was a major statement of intent, particularly after many had expected Arsenal to secure his signature. Chelsea have also moved to strengthen their defensive options by bringing in Atalanta wing-back Marco Palestra for £43m.

‌



However, the biggest challenges of the window may still lie ahead. Chelsea need further additions if they are to build a squad capable of competing on all fronts. And it isn't just spending that will get them there, it's careful squad management, with arrivals and departures and internal man-management needed.

With that in mind, we're examining what a dream end to Chelsea's summer transfer window might look like.

FOLLOW OUR CHELSEA FB PAGE! Latest Blues news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

‌



Xabi Alonso drops telling hint over Chelsea’s Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck transfers READ MORE :

Xabi Alonso left with easy transfer decision as Chelsea win Western Sydney Wanderers goalfest READ MORE :

Get Lacroix over the line

The immediate priority should be finalising the £52m acquisition of Maxence Lacroix. The Crystal Palace centre back has been Chelsea's leading defensive target throughout the summer and would bring a level of physicality, composure and experience that has been missing from their backline.

Reports suggest an agreement has already been reached with Palace, with Lacroix completing his medical earlier this week. The French defender, who represented his country at the World Cup, has established himself as one of the Premier League's most dependable defenders since arriving at Selhurst Park from Wolfsburg in 2024.

His arrival would hand Alonso the perfect profile to anchor a back three alongside Levi Colwill. The 26-year-old is also capable of operating in a conventional four-man defence, offering Chelsea greater adaptability depending on the tactical challenge ahead.

‌



View 7 Images Maxence Lacroix is on the verge of joining Chelsea (Image: Jared C. Tilton - FIFA/FIFA via Getty Images)

Secure Welbeck and Henderson

For a squad built around emerging talent, adding experienced veterans such as Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson - both of whom Chelsea are now expected to bring in - would provide an immediate injection of maturity. Their combined experience at club and international level is exactly what the dressing room has lacked during difficult spells.

Welbeck would give Alonso a dependable attacking option who can perform multiple roles and understands the demands of Premier League football better than most. Henderson, meanwhile, would bring relentless professionalism, high standards and a commanding voice to help guide Chelsea's younger midfielders.

‌



Landing both players on short-term contracts would represent a relatively small financial commitment compared to Chelsea's usual spending, while potentially delivering huge benefits behind the scenes. More importantly, it would demonstrate that the ownership can recognise weaknesses within their project - a criticism that has followed them because of their consistent focus on developing young players.

View 7 Images Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson look set to join Chelsea (Image: Getty)

Sign a left wing-back

Following Marc Cucurella's move to Real Madrid, finding a starting-quality left wing-back remains essential to completing Alonso's tactical vision. Rayo Vallecano's Pep Chavarria has become the leading candidate after impressing in La Liga with his energy, defensive discipline and willingness to constantly push forward.

‌



However, Vallecano are refusing to budge on their valuation, insisting Chelsea activate the player's £42.4m release clause, leaving the Blues to consider alternatives if talks stall. Whether Chavarria or another target arrives, Alonso needs a player who can stretch opponents, deliver consistently from wide areas and offer a constant attacking outlet.

Completing this deal would allow Chelsea to fully embrace Alonso's preferred 3-4-2-1 shape, creating balance across both flanks after already adding Palestra on the opposite side.

View 7 Images Chelsea are still working on a deal to sign wing back Pep Chavarria (Image: Aitor Alcalde Colomer)

‌



£70m Alex Scott deal

Chelsea have reportedly already tested Bournemouth's resolve with an initial £64m offer for Alex Scott, but increasing that bid towards £70m could be enough to secure the midfielder. He has developed into one of the Premier League's most complete young central midfielders, blending the ability to escape pressure with outstanding progression of the ball.

With Andrey Santos gone and Romeo Lavia continuing to battle injury problems, Chelsea cannot afford to enter the new season lacking options in the middle of the pitch. Scott's ability to carry possession, control matches and inject energy would provide Alonso with another valuable midfield weapon.

A midfield featuring Moises Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez behind Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers would already boast exceptional quality, but depth remains a concern. Bringing in Scott would solve that issue while also underlining Chelsea's ambition, especially if they beat off competition from other Premier League clubs chasing his signature.

‌



View 7 Images Chelsea have submitted an opening bid for Alex Scott (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Sign wonderkid winger

Chelsea are also looking to strengthen their attacking depth by pursuing Bayer Leverkusen teenager Kerim Alajbegovic. Alonso knows the youngster well from his spell in Germany and will have followed his impressive development through Leverkusen's academy system.

With Alejandro Garnacho completing a loan switch to Aston Villa, signing Alajbegovic would ensure Chelsea still possess serious competition and explosiveness out wide. The Bosnian winger combines electric pace with creativity, making him the type of high-upside prospect who could develop alongside Jamie Gittens, Geovany Quenda and Estevao.

‌



Convincing Leverkusen to sell such a promising talent will not be straightforward, but the teenager is believed to be available for around £30m. Considering his potential, that figure could eventually look like excellent business.

View 7 Images Kerim Alajbegovic impressed at the World Cup (Image: FIFA via Getty Images)

Keep Enzo Fernandez

Retaining Enzo Fernandez is arguably the most important task Chelsea face before the transfer deadline. Questions over his future have intensified after the midfielder made indications - both subtle and obvious - that he wants to move elsewhere. Losing him would represent a huge setback.

‌



Alonso will need to speak with the Argentine once he returns from his post-World Cup break and convince him that Stamford Bridge remains the ideal environment for the next stage of his career. Since arriving from Benfica in a then-British record £105m transfer in 2023, Fernandez has become one of Chelsea's central figures. Yet after three-and-a-half years without the club establishing itself as a serious title challenger, it is understandable why the 25-year-old is questioning his future.

Chelsea remain in a strong position, however. Fernandez is tied down until 2032, while their £120m valuation would likely scare away all but the richest clubs. Real Madrid, once considered the most likely destination, have also reportedly eased their pursuit in recent weeks.

View 7 Images Enzo Fernandez has made it clear that he wants to leave Chelsea (Image: Harry Langer/DeFodi Images/DeFodi via Getty Images)

‌



Even so, Alonso cannot allow the uncertainty to continue. Restoring Fernandez's faith in Chelsea's direction and ensuring his attention remains fully focused on the club should be one of the manager's biggest priorities.

Shift deadwood

New arrivals must be matched by departures, and Chelsea still need to reduce the size of their squad before the window closes. They have already made progress by selling Cucurella, Santos and Tyrique George for substantial fees and sending Garnacho to Aston Villa on loan, but the clear-out is far from finished.

Welbeck's arrival would create further congestion in attack. Joao Pedro is expected to begin the season as Alonso's first-choice striker, leaving Welbeck, Liam Delap, Nicolas Jackson and new arrival Emmanuel Emegha - signed from Strasbourg last year - competing for limited opportunities.

‌



With Emegha likely to leave on loan, Chelsea should consider permanently moving on either Delap or Jackson. Jackson would probably attract the higher fee following his productive loan spell at Bayern Munich last season, but after Delap's underwhelming debut campaign at Stamford Bridge, selling the English forward could arguably be the cleaner solution.

The defence also requires attention. Benoit Badiashile, Wesley Fofana and Axel Disasi all have uncertain futures, and removing at least two of them would lower the wage bill, raise additional funds and leave Alonso with a more streamlined squad capable of challenging across every competition.

Sports.title: Sir Geoff Hurst and England fans recall 1966 World Cup glory exactly 60 years on
Sports.content:
Sir Geoff Hurst and England fans recall 1966 World Cup glory exactly 60 years on

Sir Geoff, 84, told the Mirror: "I still get stopped all the time by fans who tell me what they were doing on the day we won the World Cup"

View 4 Images The moment we will never forget - England captain Bobby Moore holds the Jules Rimet trophy aloft (Image: Mirrorpix via Getty Images)

It is 60 years since the greatest moment in our footballing history - and one man can remember it like it was yesterday.

‌



Hat-trick hero Sir Geoff Hurst says he is still stopped everywhere he goes with people keen to share their memories of the World Cup final - July 30, 1966 - when his life changed forever. They remember Kenneth Wolstenholme's iconic commentary line: "Some people are on the pitch! They think it's all over... it is now!"

‌



Fans, the families of the '66 heroes, and legends of the game have told the Mirror of their memories of the epic encounter against our old rivals. Sir Geoff met with fans from that era who are now living in Hendon Hall, a residential home, at a Budweiser event in London. Hendon Hall was the hotel where the England team stayed before the final back in '66.

‌



Sir Geoff, 84, told the Mirror: "I still get stopped all the time by fans who tell me what they were doing on the day we won the World Cup. I have such great admiration and feeling for those who remember the game and the day. I meet people on a regular basis and see how significant the day was.

View 4 Images Sir Geoff Hurst in 1974 with England team mates Martin Peters (left) and Bobby Moore (Image: Mirrorpix)

"It is an honour to meet the fans who were at Wembley on the day. You realise, even now, what a huge part it played in their lives and how they remember it."

‌



Jack and Bobby Charlton were feted with an open top limousine ride when they returned to their hometown, Ashington, Northumberland. Their dad Bob was working a shift down the pit for both the quarter-final against Argentina and the semi-final against Portugal.

For the final, the Mirror paid for Bob and his wife Cissie - the football-loving mum of the Charltons - to travel to Wembley to see the match. But their late brother Gordon, a merchant seaman, listened the final on a ship in Singapore.

View 4 Images (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

‌



Manchester Utd legend Nobby Stiles was convinced he was going to be dropped for the game, before Sir Alf Ramsey assured him that he was in the team. His wife Kay, who still lives in the family home in Manchester, was worried about him missing out right up until the day before the final.

Nobby's son John, 62, of Doncaster, said his dad saw a sign held up by fans saying 'Nobby for Prime Minister' on the way to Wembley, which team mate Alan Ball pointed out to him.

He recalled: "He told my mum that he was convinced he was going to be dropped. The TV pundits were all saying that he should be dropped after the Argentina game. He thought the country was against him.

‌



"Then at training Sir Alf came up to him, and Dad was convinced he was going to be dropped. But he just said: "You are playing tomorrow.' He later discovered the FA had called him in and told him to drop my dad, but he refused and said he would resign.

View 4 Images Sir Geoff says he is stopped everywhere he goes by people wanting to share their memories of 1966 (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

"On the way to Wembley, Alan Ball nudged him and about 100 Cockneys held a sign that read, 'Nobby for Prime Minister'. So he felt 10ft tall when Alan pointed that sign out to him."

‌



John added: "Wherever dad went on the after-dinner speaking circuit, people wanted to tell him what they were doing on the day that he danced with the World Cup trophy. They would say 'do you know where I was?', as if my dad was supposed to know. But he never left without signing an autograph or posing for a picture for the fans who wanted to meet him."

Peter Laurence, now a resident in Hendon Hall, was on a Dover to Calais ferry listening to the final on a transistor radio.

He recalled: "We were driving to southern Italy. I never thought that they were going to get to the final and Geoff said: 'You bloody coward!' I was very peeved when they got there." England scored the winner as they got into port in Calais.

Article continues below

"We jumped up and down like dervishes, got into a local hostelry where we proceeded to get hammered and we met some Germans. We put our arms around each other. It was the German equivalent of entente cordiale."

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino is out of control and a danger to football - he has to be stopped
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino is out of control and a danger to football - he has to be stopped

Gianni Infantino has shown his true colours in setting out his plan to sell a stake in the global game to private investors - the time has come to topple him as FIFA's president

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino wants to take FIFA's commercial powers to a new level (Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/FIFA via Getty Images)

FIFA is a not-for-profit organisation which has made $13billion (£9.6bn) in the last four years.

‌



Under Gianni Infantino’s leadership, world football’s governing body has leaned into that contradiction, pursuing all-out expansion and commercialisation.

‌



Growing the game. That has been Infantino’s oft-stated goal. More, more, more. Bigger, more frequent tournaments. Higher ticket prices. Half-time entertainment. Celebrities, influencers, dignitaries and heads of state in the stands.

‌



It has won him plenty of friends and supporters. A fourth term as FIFA president had been expected, with the various controversies of the World Cup – a denied visa for a Somali referee, Iran’s travel struggles, Donald Trump’s meddling in disciplinary proceedings – water off a duck’s back.

The Guardian reported recently that more than 200 FIFA members had endorsed Infantino for re-election. On Tuesday it became clearer why that might be.

UEFA nations could BOYCOTT World Cup in light of FIFA's plot to sell tournament READ MORE :

Gary Lineker shows FIFA disgust in four-word response to Gianni Infantino bombshell READ MORE :

Infantino wants to create a subsidiary worth $20billion (£15bn) and then sell off 20 per cent of FIFA Forward Enterprise to investors to raise $4.2bn (£3.16bn). The idea was communicated in a press release so boring, perhaps deliberately, an effort to obscure the stark reality: that he wants to sell off chunks of the global game for profit.

‌



Profit for Joshua Kushner, the brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared, who is leading the proposed investor group. Profit for Infantino himself, who according to The Times, could become commissioner of the company once he steps down as FIFA president. And profit for FIFA’s 211 members.

Infantino has sent a letter to FIFA’s member associations telling them they will each receive $40m (£30m) by January if they agree to the proposal by September 19. A source told The Times on Wednesday that it amounted to “pure bribery”.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino is using methods from Donald Trump's playbook (Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/FIFA via Getty Images)

‌



It is a brazen attempt to get his way and something straight out of the Trump playbook. Infantino has ingratiated himself with the US President, inventing the farcical FIFA Peace Prize to appeal to his ego. Bizarrely, he recently received an endorsement to become the next United Nations chief in return.

Infantino has somehow created a cult of personality, which for a career lawyer and administrator from Switzerland, is impressive. The white trademark trainers with a suit. The ludicrous “today I feel” speech. The recent rambling letter imploring his haters to “meditate or pray".

He is completely self-obsessed and, having spent the last six weeks flying around on a private jet to hold court with the world’s leaders, his ego has run out of control.

‌



For many, that could be forgiven or overlooked. But now we are seeing the dangers of having such an egomaniac in charge of world football.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino had been expected to win re-election for a fourth term (Image: Florencia Tan Jun, Getty Images)

Infantino has pressed launch on the biggest shockwave in football since the European Super League debacle five years ago. That self-interested power grab collapsed embarrassingly almost straight away, overcome by the sheer immediate force of the backlash.

‌



FIFA’s smaller members will no doubt be wooed by the promise of cash. But the bigger, more powerful nations must take a stand against Infantino’s ludicrous plot to sell off the crown jewels. The response from UEFA, the FA and Concacaf is promising.

The plot must be foiled – and it could have the added benefit of toppling Infantino from power if a rival for the presidency steps up. Football is at the top of a slippery slope. His megalomania must be challenged.

Sports.title: Geoff Hurst finally finds out how he was spotted as England potential by Alf Ramsey 60 years later
Sports.content:
1966 legend Geoff Hurst has just learnt for the very first time how he was spotted as a potential England player by manager Sir Alf Ramsey.

Incredibly, it was in a League Cup second round game for West Ham against Division Three minnows Mansfield Town on October 13, 1965 in front of just 11,590 people. Hurst said he was “completely unaware” that Ramsey was even at the game.

The match was played five months before Hurst made his England debut and, of course, later that year he became the first man to ever score a hat-trick in a World Cup final - exactly 60 years ago.

View 7 Images Eton Manor legend Graham Phillips (right) with respected author and historian Grant Bage (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



England icon was left penniless and forced to sell jumpers from his 1-bed flat READ MORE :

The extraordinary revelation was uncovered by Ramsey’s biographer Grant Bage in a series of new interviews. Ramsey told one of his closest friends, respected amateur team manager Charlie Phillips how he was impressed by how Hurst handled long balls from Bobby Moore that night.

Two of Hurst’s goals at Wembley in the 4-2 win over West Germany came from long passes from Moore. Now Bage, who spent six years researching and writing his biography The Unseen Sir Alf, has informed Hurst who had no idea Ramsey was even at that particular match.

Hurst replied: “I was completely unaware that this happened, which completely changed not only my football life, but my life. October 13th was obviously a very lucky day as I got married on that day 64 years ago. Thank you again.”

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst in his West Ham days (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

‌



Bage said: “Even sixty years on, we keep unearthing new information about Sir Alf Ramsey and the 1966 World Cup. It’s incredible that these ‘nuggets’ are coming out so many years later. It’s amazing that, on an October night at Upton Park at a League cup match against Mansfield, that Alf formulated his thoughts and plans for the World Cup.

“Football was rarely filmed in the 1960s, so the England manager slogged his way round watching hundreds of games, just to work out who the best English players were. And Hurst wasn’t even the player he was going to watch. But now we know that what he saw that night sowed the seeds of World Cup glory.

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst gave Mirrorman Andy Lines exclusive interview before World Cup (Image: Ian Vogler / Daily Mirror)

‌



"Alf Ramsey conquered world football through hard work and attention to detail. Just imagine if he hadn’t bothered to go to that game. Geoff Hurst didn’t even know about it which makes it all the remarkable.”

Bage found the new information after meeting Graham Phillips - son of Charlie Phillips the manager of East London non-league side Eton Manor. Hurst, who played 499 games for West Ham, has little memory of the match which was played almost 61 years ago. Ramsey was coaching them at the time and Charlie became a great friend and trusted confidante.

Bage said: “I can’t thank Graham enough for coming forward with all this detailed extra information. It helps us learn more about how Alf slotted together the only England team to ever win the World Cup."

View 7 Images Eton Manor legend and stalwart Graham Phillips (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

‌



Graham said: “Alf and my dad Charlie had two long telephone conversations, both instigated by Alf, in the immediate aftermath of the 1966 triumph. It was in these telephone discussions that Alf conveyed stories about the World Cup to Charlie.

“There were other conversations, but these were the main ones. But you have to understand that Charlie didn't sit us down after his chats with Alf and brief us on what had been said. The information came out from him gradually, on different occasions, like when we were sitting watching TV, or some relevant story had been in the paper.

“What I recall above all else is my father describing how Alf had, under the Upton Park floodlights, told me that he had witnessed ‘the second coming of Tommy Taylor’. That was a deeply significant comparison, which needs explaining for a modern audience.

“In March 1953 Tommy Taylor had signed for Manchester United, aged just 21. His 112 league goals, in a total of 166 league appearances, helped United win successive league championships in 1955-56, and 1956-57. In 19 senior appearances for England, he also scored 16 goals. Tragically, Tommy Taylor was then one of eight Manchester United players killed in the Munich air disaster of February 6, 1958, his 26th birthday having been reached the week before he died.

‌



View 7 Images Eton Manor legend Graham Phillips with respected author and historian Grant Bage (Image: Philip Coburn/Daily Mirror)

“Alf Ramsey was not prone to hyperbole, so for him to compare Geoff Hurst to Tommy Taylor was amazing: especially as Hurst was not even the main reason Ramsey had gone to watch this particular game. Alf told Charlie that Ronnie Boyce was the ‘intended’ prime target, and perhaps to take another look at Johnny Byrne.

“What must also be remembered by modern football fans, to make sense of this, is that in the mid-1960s there was very little filming of football. Most league games were also played either at 3pm on a Saturday, or on Tuesday or Wednesday evenings early in the season, before cup competitions had got going.

View 7 Images Geoff Hurst scores England's controversial third goal (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“Consequently, if Alf Ramsey wanted to review any promising English player, he needed to attend hundreds of games himself: which is why the England manager undertook this particular scouting mission to West Ham’s unpromising midweek, early-stage league cup game against lower-league opposition.

“Alf told his friend Charlie that, as it happened, Alf had phoned West Ham out of courtesy to tell them he would be attending. Unfortunately, he did not manage to speak to their manager, Ron Greenwood, so did not know whether his message had got through. “Ironically, HAD Ramsey talked to Greenwood, he may not even have made the trip! As things turned out, neither Ronnie Boyce nor Johnny Byrne would play that night, against Third Division Mansfield Town, in round three of the League Cup. Luckily though, Alf went anyway.”

Sports.title: Gianni Infantino's heinous plan must be stopped - but the FA should take a hard look at themselves first
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino's heinous plan must be stopped - but the FA should take a hard look at themselves first

The FIFA president's plans to sell the World Cup off to private investors has provoked widespread condemnation but the European governing body might want to take a long hard look at itself and its own commercial dealings

View 2 Images FIFA President Gianni Infantino exchanges gifts with The Football Association President Debbie Hewitt (Image: 2026 FIFA)

There is, of course, a quite stark irony in UEFA and all of us in these parts taking the high moral ground over Gianni Infantino’s proposal to sell the World Cup off to private investors. When it comes to selling out to the highest commercial bidders, UEFA and the Premier League and the Football Association and the rest of the elite European nations have been the trailblazers.

‌



Remember when the European Cup was a thing of single-tie knockout beauty? Probably not. That was before UEFA sold its name and birthright to Russian oil companies and the like, and turned it into a bloated, corporate mess with its own phoney anthem.

‌



Remember Gazprom? UEFA were not so moralistic then. Don’t forget, UEFA executives love a VIP gig and a freebie as much as FIFA executives do.

‌



On Aleksander Ceferin’s watch, the Champions League has become a commercial monstrosity. And as much as Infantino is a power-obsessed egotist who needs dethroning, he is only following a template set by those in Europe who rinse football followers for everything they’ve got.

In professional terms, Infantino is a wrong ‘un, of that there is absolutely no doubt. But since when have we been able to sermonise about the sanctity of football?

Gary Lineker shows FIFA disgust in four-word response to Gianni Infantino bombshell READ MORE :

UEFA nations could BOYCOTT World Cup in light of FIFA's plot to sell tournament READ MORE :

The Premier League has had - and continues to have - a quite spectacular disregard for the traditional match-going fan who might be a bit hard up. How about putting our own house in order? We sold our game to television.

‌



Perhaps politicians could do something meaningful instead of jumping on a bandwagon. Intoxicated with his carefully-acquired power, Andy Burnham, the professional Evertonian, has waded in.

“Football does not belong to investors,” he posted in one of his many social media missives. Really, Andy? So how come you want the Glazers and the great Sir Jim Ratcliffe to benefit in their hundreds of millions by having a new 100,000-seater stadium facilitated by local and central government?

As uncomfortable as Infantino’s plans sound, how about you concentrate on making sure your constituents can afford or have a chance to go to a game? Burnham’s social media message was truly laughable.

‌



“Dress the deal up however you like,” he said. “Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”

Mate, the World Cup was sold out an age ago. It was sold out when it went to Russia. It was sold out when it went to Qatar. Didn’t hear a peep from you then.

‌



English football has sold out, lock, stock and barrel. Look at the FA Cup, for goodness sake, a competition that has sold its birthright and traditions for a fast buck.

Do something about that, Prime Minister. Have a word with those at the FA who thought it was a good idea to present the FIFA president with an England shirt with his name on the back recently.

View 2 Images Gianni Infantino has been praised by Donald Trump for the commercial success of World Cup 2026 (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Look, Infantino’s ruse is reprehensible yet entirely predictable. And sadly, understandable. Hopefully, the backlash will be sufficient to get rid of him, but you doubt it.

After all, his idea of selling the World Cup off to private investors will have players and their agents licking their lips. Imagine how much a star player will be able to charge for a few weeks work on the grand stage.

And the chances are that the fans - ripped off at every turn by the current set-up - will not really care that much. It is still a proposal that demands opposition. Vehement opposition.

Article continues below

But maybe UEFA and the European footballing bigwigs - including our own - should have a long, hard look at themselves first. Because they have paved the way for FIFA’s greed.

Sports.title: Tottenham beat Sydney FC on penalties after stunning Tel free-kick
Sports.content:
Tottenham beat Sydney FC on penalties to earn their third victory of pre-season after being held to a 1-1 draw over 90 minutes during which Mathys Tel scored a stunning free-kick.

Tel found the top-right corner with a wonderful strike from 25 yards in the 29th minute in Sydney, but the A-League side equalised after half-time through Takahiro Sekine before Martin Dubravka saved a penalty in the shoot-out, which allowed Dane Scarlett to net the winner.

Tottenham are interested in signing Manchester City winger Savinho and Tel, who only signed for the club permanently this summer in a £30m deal from Bayern Munich, appeared to respond to those transfer links with a stand-out 45-minute display off the left.

How Spurs lined up First half (4-2-3-1): Dubravka; Tye Hall, Hardy, Davies, Kyerematen; Gray, Bergvall; Solomon, Gallagher, Tel; Richarlison.

Second half: Dubravka; Tye Hall, Hardy, Takai, Kyerematen; Gray, Tonali; Solomon, Gallagher, Williams-Barnett; Richarlison.

Roberto De Zerbi rested a host of his stars, including Mateus Fernandes, but started midfielder Lucas Bergvall, who Sky Sports News understands wants to leave the club this summer, for his first pre-season minutes before he was replaced at the break by club-record signing Sandro Tonali.

Andy Robertson made his first Spurs appearance as a second-half substitute, being handed the captain's armband and impressing in a 25-minute cameo by setting up two chances and having a shot saved before tucking away a penalty.

Who is missing from Spurs' pre-season tour? Mohammed Kudus, Xavi Simons, Dejan Kulusevski and Wilson Odobert and Guglielmo Vicario did not travel due to injury.

Rodrigo Bentancur and Pape Matar Sarr were granted extended leave following their appearances at the World Cup, while Pedro Porro, Marcos Senesi, Cristian Romero and Djed Spence won't take part having reached the latter stages of the tournament.

What we learned from Spurs' friendly with Sydney...

Sky Sports' Sam Blitz:

Tel responds to Savinho news - Spurs are after a new left winger and Man City's Savinho could be another high-profile addition to De Zerbi's squad. But Tel provided a reminder of his talents. His stunning free-kick stole the show but he was also Spurs' brightest attacker in the game. If Savinho and Tel are Spurs' two left-wing options, it shows real depth in that area.

Robertson looks energised on debut - He only got 25 minutes, but Robertson made a real impact on his first Spurs outing. The left-back should have had two assists but Min-Hyeok Yang missed from close range. De Zerbi's full-backs in this game were very attacking and often had good goalscoring chances, is the Scot in line for a new wave of attacking influence in the Premier League?

Image: Richarlison challenges for the ball

Gray could be important for De Zerbi - When the team news came out, it was a surprise to see Archie Gray named as captain for the second pre-season game in a row. More experienced players such as Conor Gallagher, Richarlison and Ben Davies also started, but it was the young midfielder with the armband. Despite all the talk about Fernandes and Tonali coming in, is Gray the final piece of that three-man midfield, on the basis of that vote of confidence from De Zerbi?

Where are Spurs' goals coming from? Yes, it's only pre-season. But you look at the Spurs attack and wonder where the goals are coming from. Spurs were wasteful against Sydney - with Gallagher missing three big first-half chances and substitute Yang missing two more after coming on. Richarlison was anonymous in his 60-minute display, while the likes of Dominic Solanke, James Maddison, Mohammad Kudus, Xavi Simons and Dejan Kulusevski are still out injured. De Zerbi has made loads of signings in defence and midfield, but more still needs to be done up front.

Sports.title: F1 season to end in Europe if Middle East unable to host final rounds
Sports.content:
The 2026 Formula 1 season will end in Europe in the event the final two scheduled races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi need to be relocated because of the ongoing conflict in the Middle East, F1 president Stefano Domenicali has confirmed.

The sport's bosses were previously forced to cancel April races in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia, and announced over the weekend that the Bahrain Grand Prix will now be hosted by Malaysia in October.

Bahrain's inability to host the event in October has raised doubts over whether the final two rounds of the season - in Qatar (Nov 27-29) and Abu Dhabi (Dec 4-6) - will be able to go ahead in their planned locations.

Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Domenicali insisted he is still hopeful of the calendar remaining as it currently stands, and that F1 will wait until its mid-September deadline before making a decision.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Formula 1 has added Malaysia to its 2026 schedule to host the Bahrain Grand Prix that was postponed earlier in the season

"With regard to the end of the season, we are in touch with all the other championships," Domenicali said. "And I know that, for example, WEC (World Endurance Championship) has announced that they will not go at the end of the year in the Middle East and they will stay in Europe.

"The way that we are structured is that we will take the maximum time for us to see how the situation will develop, and we will take the decision at the right time. That moment would be not before the middle of September.

"For us, today, the races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi are confirmed. But, of course, if the situation will not be clearer, the way that we believe it should be, before the middle of September, we will take the decision."

Formula 1 2026 remaining races Netherlands* August 21-23 USA October 23-25 Italy September 4-6 Mexico Oct 30-Nov 1 Madrid September 11-13 Brazil November 6-8 Azerbaijan September 24-26 Las Vegas November 20-22 Malaysia October 2-4 Qatar November 27-29 Singapore* October 9-11 Abu Dhabi December 4-6 *denotes Sprint weekend

Domenicali explained that the challenges of "Brexit-connected documentation" make Europe the only alternative venue for the final two races, but says there are multiple options within the continent.

"I just want to confirm to you that if this [races in the Middle East] will not be possible, the end of the season will be in Europe, because we cannot go in other places," he said.

"There are some possibilities on the table, but I don't think it's right to make some promises or anticipate certain things, but that's the situation of today.

"Even if I really hope that it will not be the case, if the situation will not allow for us to be there, we're going to finish the championship in Europe."

Imola 'an option' | Second Las Vegas race was considered

There has been speculation that Italy's historic Imola circuit is the front-runner to host if needed, but Domenicali said the track is "an option, but is not defined" as a would-be replacement venue.

It remains possible that Imola and another venue could act as replacement hosts, with Formula 1 keen to get as close to the originally planned 24-round schedule as possible. As it stands, the calendar has been reduced to 23 races with the Saudi Arabian Grand Prix lost.

Racing in Europe in late November or early December would come with the risk of cold weather, but Domenicali pointed out that expected temperatures are actually colder for the Las Vegas Grand Prix earlier in November than they are in Europe at that time of year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2025 Emilia Romagna Grand Prix from Imola

The Italian revealed holding a second race in Las Vegas had been considered but overlooked given the risk of undervaluing the event and going up against the hugely popular NFL.

He said: "The fascinating side is that if I look at the statistics of the temperature in Europe in that time, it is less cool than Las Vegas' average temperature while we are racing.

"It's definitely something that no one knows where the temperature will go and what the weather will be like. I think that actually we see in this situation of how the pollution of the climate change is happening. There's no certainty or anything about that.

"There was a possibility of having two races in Las Vegas, but we don't want to ruin a jewel that is growing by undervaluing what we are doing there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Anthony Davidson and Jenson Button talk you through the Las Vegas Grand Prix Strip Circuit

"And of course, we don't have to forget that in that period of the year, we are fighting in the US against NFL. That is a major sport that is, I don't want to say detracting, but a lot of fans are watching that, so we need to avoid any kind of situation that would put us in front of something that of course is quite still very big in the US."

Any further changes to the calendar could have implications on the title race, which Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli currently leads by 50 points from Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, with 12 scheduled rounds remaining.

Sports.title: Infantino offers £30m incentive for FIFA members to back controversial plans
Sports.content:
Gianni Infantino has given football associations until September 19 to back his plan to sell off part of FIFA to private investors - with a $40m (£30.1m) incentive to accept, a letter has revealed.

FIFA announced on Tuesday that it was seeking to launch FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE), which would bring together the sale of FIFA's commercial rights - including broadcasting, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing - with the operational delivery of its tournaments.

Under the proposal, FIFA would raise up to $4.2bn (£3.1bn) from external investors through the sale of minority, non-controlling stakes in FFE, which it says would be valued at around $20bn (£15bn).

The governing body says its plans - which need approval from member associations - could deliver more than $10bn in "football development funding" over the next four years.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gary Neville, Andy Burnham, the FA and more react to Gianni Infantino's World Cup sale plan

The FIFA president, in correspondence only sent to the 211 member associations after his secret plans were leaked and met with fierce opposition from UEFA, raised the subject of finances which would be available to access from January.

He warned that countries will have access to much less cash for development projects, grassroots football and national teams if they do not back selling off more than 20 per cent of a new commercial spin-off to oversee World Cups.

Infantino said the launch of FFE needs more than 50 per cent of members to back the plans, along with his ruling council.

He wrote: "Should neither condition be satisfied, FIFA will continue as planned with the Forward Programme 4.0 … meaning approximately $10m (£7.5m) per MA [member association] for the next cycle."

Infantino raised the prospect of associations who do not back his plans missing out on the cash if the majority of the world endorses the venture.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Prime Minister Andy Burnham disagrees with FIFA's attempts to bring in private investment for the World Cup

He wrote: "A singular and unique funding opportunity only for those Member Associations who wish to participate, with their decision to be made by September 19 2026 so we can plan ahead and with funds to be available immediately as of January 1 2027."

The letter raises the financial stakes, with FIFA previously saying on Tuesday that the new venture would provide access to funding of $20m (£15m) from 2027 to 2030 - a figure that has now doubled.

Infantino wrote: "This entity will be fully focused on one target objective; generating as much value as possible for FIFA's Member Associations."

But FIFA has not commented on how much Infantino stands to benefit financially from delivering a $20bn venture - and how he could stay on beyond 2031 when term limits require him to relinquish the presidency if re-elected next year.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky News sports correspondent Rob Harris raises the prospect of the World Cup being boycotted due to FIFA's attempts to bring in private investment

Threat of a boycott and 'deep concern' from the FA

UEFA, European football's governing body, released a furious statement on Tuesday that said the proposals "crossed a line".

UEFA nations are now expected to hold an emergency meeting virtually this week and Sky Sports News understands there is a willingness to use the threat of a boycott if Infantino pushes ahead with the plans.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham voiced his criticism on Tuesday evening, saying on X: "Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine."

On Wednesday morning, an FA spokeswoman added: "We were completely unaware of this proposal and have no substantive details, including what the proposition actually is, and what conditions are attached.

"Based on the limited information, we are deeply concerned about the lack of process and governance to get to this point, and the apparent substance and principles involved.

"When the proposal is shared in the full and transparent way now promised by FIFA, we will make our views clear, and comment further."

The Football Association of Wales (FAW) later said it had "not yet received any substantial details from FIFA concerning the reported proposals.

"Consequently, the FAW is concerned that such matters have become public prior to being shared with FIFA's Member Associations. We await receipt of FIFA's full proposal before commenting further on this matter."

'None of us are the owners of football'

Relations between UEFA and FIFA were already under severe strain, with UEFA president Aleksander Ceferin not attending the World Cup final in protest at a series of FIFA governance issues, including its handling of the Folarin Balogun case.

But the way the plans emerged, as well as the proposal itself, provoked fresh fury on Tuesday, with FIFA not raising the landmark strategy during meetings with football associations in New York on the eve of the World Cup final.

It is understood the FA was completely unaware of the plans - first reported in the Financial Times and The Times. Sky Sports News has contacted the Scottish FA for comment.

UEFA said in a statement after those reports emerged that the "soul and governance of football are not assets to trade".

"This crosses a line that football's governing institutions should never cross. UEFA takes it extremely seriously. So should every National Football Association.

"So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game.

"The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade - especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not FIFA's to sell."

'Remarkable commercial value' in football - FIFA explains proposal

FIFA later moved to clarify the proposed new structure, with a spokesperson saying it was beginning a consultation process after receiving a proposal that is currently under review.

FIFA confirmed to Sky Sports News that JP Morgan is acting as financial advisor on the project, with Thrive Capital - whose chief executive is Josh Kushner, brother of Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared - expected to lead the proposed investor group.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Gianni Infantino labels the 2026 World Cup as the greatest of all time

FIFA insists it would retain sole control over football governance, competitions, the international match calendar and all sporting and regulatory decisions, with any outside investment in a FIFA subsidiary rather than FIFA itself.

Infantino said the proposal would help "democratise football worldwide" and ensure more of the game's commercial success is reinvested into development projects around the globe.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports chief correspondent Kaveh Solhekol looks back at the World Cup and debates whether or not it will be regarded as a success

"Football is the world's most popular sport and an extraordinary engine of human and social development," said Infantino.

"Parts of the game have turned that popularity into remarkable commercial value - and we celebrate that success and want it to continue, because it lifts the whole game ... our next stage of growth needs a structure built for it, one where the commercial side of the game operates as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world."

The governing body also dismissed suggestions that Infantino could become chief executive of the new entity when his final term as president ends, saying such a move has "never been discussed".

But FIFA said both the president and the administration would need to play leading roles in any new entity to ensure FIFA retains control of any subsidiary in line with its statutes and regulations and for the benefit of member associations.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player How many goals, red cards and penalties? Take a look at the World Cup in 2026 in numbers

FIFA is a not-for-profit organisation owned by the 211 associations that make up its membership. As an association of associations, it enjoys a tax-free status in Switzerland where it is based.

Its revenue for the 2022-26 cycle is expected to be $15bn (£112.8bn), the majority of which comes from TV rights, sponsorship and ticket and hospitality sales from the men's World Cup this summer.

The next World Cup is the women's tournament in Brazil next year.

What happens to Infantino if plans collapse?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports correspondent Kavel Solhekol breaks down Gianni Infantino's latest plans after the World Cup.

Latest from Sky Sports News' Kaveh Solhekol:

"It’s shocking how nothing is shocking any more. I should be surprised, but I’m not surprised at all. I’ve just come back from the World Cup. According to FIFA, it was the most successful World Cup ever. They made more money than they know what to do with. Fans were paying outrageous prices for tickets.

"Gianni Infantino and those close to him have looked at this and said ‘this is the future.’ One way to make sure you have more tournaments like the one you’ve just had, is to set up a subsidiary of FIFA that will look after FIFA’s tournaments and to invite private investors to invest in that company.

"In the short term, there’s going to be a big pot of money potentially available for the 211 member associations of FIFA. The big question is, are they going to accept what Infantino is proposing? What happens to Infantino if these plans collapse? Are we seeing a tipping point on the horizon where a lot of people in football are saying they don’t like the way Infantino has been running football?

"I think there is such a groundswell of opposition to these plans that if I had to put money on it, I think they won’t succeed. It reminds me of what happened to the European Super League where plans came out, there was outrage and pretty quickly the plans didn’t come to fruition.

"Infantino knows everyone has got a price. FIFA have written to all 211 member associations and have said you have until September 19 to accept this plan. If you do, there is going to be a pot of £7.5bn for us to share. If you don’t, that pot will drop from £7.5bn to £2bn. How many of these member associations are going to turn down that money?"

Sports.title: Welbeck to have medical as Chelsea set to pay first fee for over-26 since 2022
Sports.content:
Chelsea have agreed an undisclosed fee with Brighton for Danny Welbeck.

The 35-year-old has been given permission to undergo a medical in the next 24 hours ahead of his imminent move to Stamford Bridge.

Chelsea have turned to Welbeck as they look to add experience to manager Xabi Alonso's squad.

The last time the west London club paid a transfer fee for a player over the age of 26 was four years ago, when they signed Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang from Barcelona.

Image: Welbeck is set for a medical ahead of a move to Chelsea

It has been two years since Chelsea selected a player over the age of 30 in any game.

Sky Sports News reported earlier this week that initial positive talks had been held regarding a move for Welbeck who has one-year left on his contract at Brighton.

Welbeck has continued to be a reliable goalscorer in the Premier League at 35 years old. Last season he scored 13 times, after scoring 10 in the previous campaign.

His potential arrival would be another example of Chelsea prioritising physically imposing players with Premier League experience this summer.

They have already signed Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa for £117m - a record fee for a British player - and are close to bringing in Crystal Palace defender Maxence Lacroix.

It would also place further doubt on the futures of strikers Nicolas Jackson, Liam Delap and Marc Guiu.

Chelsea have signed several players from Brighton in recent seasons including their main striker Joao Pedro, plus Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Robert Sanchez.

A number of Brighton staff members have also moved to Stamford Bridge over the past four years, including sporting directors Paul Winstanley and Sam Jewell.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jay Bothroyd discusses why Jordan Henderson and Welbeck would be good signings for Chelsea and will add the experience the team has been needing

Neville backs Chelsea decision to sign PL experience

Gary Neville has said signing players like Welbeck and Jordan Henderson is exactly what Chelsea's young players need in order to gain more guidance.

The former Premier League-winning captain insists the decision to bring the veterans in is not a "magical" one, but rather an example of what all top teams need to compete.

"If you watched Chelsea for the last three, four or five years you'd say there's inexperience right throughout the football club," he said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Gary Neville says Chelsea have been crying out for Premier League experience in their squad, backing any decision to sign the likes of Welbeck and Henderson

"I think putting a spine in of good, senior professionals who act as guardians of good behaviour, responsibility and discipline in the dressing room is something that's not magic. It's something all top teams have had for many decades.

"Putting in Jordan Henderson and Danny Welbeck who know how to win Premier League titles, their jobs will be as much off the pitch as it will be on it. They're still good players who can contribute 25-35 games a season, but they will make sure the young players turn up every single day and give their all.

"I didn't think the young players at Chelsea have any real leadership or guidance on and off the pitch. They've now got people who can do that."

BlueCo's drastic change in transfer policy

Analysis from Sky Sports' Callum Bishop:

The BlueCo era at Chelsea has been defined by hoarding some of the best young talent on the planet and developing them in-house. That method has had some successes, but overall, it has not panned out.

Image: Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was the last player over the age of 26 who Chelsea paid a transfer fee for

There is clearly some recognition and accountability from the top brass about that. In bringing in Alonso as manager, they know they have lucked out in getting one of the most highly-sought-after tacticians in the game. The Spaniard has clearly identified the need for experience and the club are following his lead.

The interest in Granit Xhaka earlier in the summer was among the first signs of the shift. Even making a move for Lacroix is evidence of a change in approach.

The Welbeck move is surprising, but there is some logic that can be applied to it. Is he going to start every week? No. However, Chelsea's four senior strikers have an average age of just 23. Combined, they have made 269 Premier League appearances and scored 74 goals.

Image: Thiago Silva was the last player over the age of 30 to play for Chelsea

The Brighton veteran has 400 appearances and 90 goals on his own. To have that as your back-up to the young guns you want to develop makes sense.

Henderson? That's a complete 180 degree turn. Caicedo and Enzo Fernandez are two of the more experienced players Alonso has. If you had to pick anywhere Chelsea needed a wise head, you would not say midfield.

Yet, they wanted Xhaka. They now want Henderson. Alonso may have been the man to oversee the blossoming of players like Florian Wirtz at Bayer Leverkusen. However, he clearly sees the values of opposite characters and knows Chelsea, and perhaps more importantly, he needs people ready now.

Sports.title: Langer hints at interest in England Test job
Sports.content:
Justin Langer says he hasn't heard from anyone at the ECB over the vacant England Test head coach role which he has been linked with, but the Australian hinted at being interested.

Speaking on the Stick to Cricket podcast, the former Australia head coach labelled that job, as well as India and England as the biggest in the sport, adding: "It's a career and everyone looks at all opportunities."

Brendon McCullum was removed as England's Test head coach earlier this month after a run of seven defeats in nine, while the early favourite to replace him, Andy Flower, turned down the role citing his current coaching commitments with Royal Challengers Bengaluru in the IPL and London Spirit in The Hundred.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking to Michael Atherton on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, former Australian white-ball captain Aaron Finch gives his thoughts on why Tom Moody or Justin Langer would be great candidates for the England Test coach role.

Langer, who is also involved in the The Hundred, leading the Manchester Super Giants, has also been touted as a possible successor, although The Telegraph have reported that he's not one of the ECB's shortlisted candidates and he himself insists he has yet to be contacted.

"I haven't, no," he said. "I haven't heard from anyone. It's all paper talk, all hypothetical."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Southern Brave and Australia all-rounder Marcus Stoinis says Justin Langer's work ethic would make him a good choice if selected to be England's next men's Test head coach.

Langer, who earned 105 Test caps for his country from 1993-2007, added: "I'm passionate about the game of cricket, but particularly Test cricket.

"I see now with franchise cricket, it's awesome, but we've got to have Test cricket. It must keep thriving for the health of the game - and so that's why I say about the three big countries [Australia, India, England] and why it's important they keep going strong.

"When it comes to coaching, it's a career and everyone looks at all opportunities."

Ben Stokes' retirement? I've heard all the counter arguements, but I thought 'respect'. I think when you're a player who has done what he has for England, a great warrior, I think go out however you want. That's my honest view.

McCullum has been retained as England's white-ball head coach, meaning the job will again be split from the Test team.

"My personal view has always been that if you're the head coach of Australia you should oversee all of it," Langer said.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Stuart Broad shares his thoughts on who could take over from Brendon McCullum as head coach of the England Test team.

"It can work [split jobs] if you have the right people. They've got to get on very well, be on the same page and have the same thinking. And alongside the director of cricket [Rob Key], they've got to fit like a glove.

"We've seen that with Andy Flower and Ashley Giles [for England], and McCullum and Matthew Mott to a degree.

"It's complicated, with T20 cricket, white-ball cricket. I would say there will be some teething issues for Baz and whoever he does it with.

"If they work well together, it could work, but there haven't been too many examples where it has."

Langer recorded 15 wins, 11 losses and 5 draws in his time in charge of Australia, which included retaining the Ashes in England in 2019 with a 2-2 series draw, before a 4-0 triumph in the Covid-impacted return Down Under in 2021-22.

He resigned in acrimonious circumstances in February 2022, just a few weeks after the comprehensive win over England, amid claims he fell out with senior players.

Sports.title: Harrington picked as Europe's third vice-captain for 2027 Ryder Cup
Sports.content:
Luke Donald has named Irishman Padraig Harrington as his third vice-captain for the 2027 Ryder Cup which will be played at Adare Manor in Ireland in September next year.

Harrington joins the Molinari brothers, Edoardo and Francesco, in Donald's backroom team for next year's contest, as Team Europe seek a third consecutive Ryder Cup victory following wins at Marco Simone in 2023 and Bethpage Black in 2025.

The three-time major champion, one of Ireland's most decorated and popular sporting heroes, was a player in the only previous Ryder Cup to be played in his home country in 2006.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at Harrington's heroics en route to his Open title defence in 2008

He represented Europe six times in total as a player - including being part of four triumphs - and was previously a vice-captain on three occasions before becoming captain for the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits.

"Luke and I arranged to meet up at The Open and chatted about it, and we felt we could strike up a good team again," said Harrington.

"Obviously, he was my vice-captain in 2021, and we have worked together as vice-captains in the past. And certainly, I feel I've something to give.

"Luke has a very strong team around him already and he felt that we would work well together.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports Jamie Weir explains why Luke Donald has been chosen as captain of Europe Ryder Cup team for a third time.

"It's something I didn't expect. I honestly didn't think I'd ever wear the European Ryder Cup logo again. So I'm very happy to be part of it.

"The Ryder Cup has been a special part of my life. Representing Europe has always been one of the highlights of my golfing career, and to be able to do it again in this situation, especially in Ireland, is special.

"You wouldn't want to miss out with it being in Ireland, so I'm very pleased.

"I think it will be a spectacular occasion and one of the great sporting events to be played in the country. The whole of Ireland will be behind it, watching it, enjoying it and living it.

"The fans are going to be fantastic, and I think the atmosphere will be second to none."

Donald said: "Padraig is someone I thought about quite a lot, especially with it being in Adare.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Donald expresses his gratitude to his fans, family and team-mates after being recognised in the King's Birthday Honours list with an OBE for his success with Team Europe.

"I've been around Padraig in many Ryder Cup team rooms, as a player, as a vice-captain to his captaincy, and he's been a vice-captain before in the past as well.

"So he brings a wealth of experience, and I do love the fact that there's a connection. He understands the Irish crowds and all that goes with having a Ryder Cup in Ireland. I think it's going to be very special for him.

"He's loved in Ireland with what he's achieved in the game, and that will only bring more energy to our team. We'll get the fans even more behind us, and you know I think that can only be a good thing. I'm very excited to have his expertise."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ryder Cup captain Jim Furyk is hopeful Tiger Woods will be able to play a role in the team in 2027.

Harrington made his Ryder Cup debut at The Country Club in Brookline in 1999 and was ever-present for the next five editions, helping Europe to victory in 2002, 2004, 2006 and 2010. He contributed a total of 10½ points to the European Team during that period.

He was named as vice-captain for the first time by fellow Dubliner Paul McGinley for the victory at Gleneagles in 2014, a role he returned to in 2016 at Hazeltine National under Darren Clarke and in 2018 for the victory at Le Golf National in Paris under Denmark's Thomas Bjorn.

Harrington then led Team Europe at the 2021 Ryder Cup at Whistling Straits, which was postponed by 12 months due to the Covid pandemic in 2020.
