What Pagar.me brought to the table

Pagar.me operated as the digital payments engine inside the Stone ecosystem, handling transactions for online stores, marketplaces, and SaaS businesses. It gave Stone a foothold in e-commerce that complemented its physical point-of-sale hardware business.

The gateway allowed developers to embed payments directly into websites and apps via APIs. This made it a critical tool for larger digital-native merchants who needed more than a card machine.

Why the consolidation is happening now

Stone’s leadership has made clear its ambition to become the primary financial partner for Brazilian merchants, not just a payment acquirer. A fragmented product stack with separate brands creates friction for clients who could otherwise use a single login for payments, banking, and credit.

By folding Pagar.me’s functionality into a unified Stone app, the company simplifies its offering and increases the likelihood that a merchant will adopt multiple services. The strategy aims to deepen wallet share and lock in retention through a stickier, all-in-one operating platform.

What changes for the merchant

Stone’s messaging to Pagar.me users emphasizes that the shift is largely administrative. Existing contracts, API integrations, and settlement flows remain intact, so merchants do not need to renegotiate terms or rebuild their checkout stacks.

Over time, merchants will access Pagar.me’s digital commerce tools through the same interface they use for Stone’s acquiring, Pix, and banking products. The goal is a seamless experience where a business can manage its online store payments and its physical card transactions in one place.

The bigger picture: from payments to operating system

The consolidation fits into Stone’s broader pivot toward becoming a merchant financial operating system. The company has been layering on services such as digital accounts, payroll, and credit, moving well beyond the “maquininha” card machine that built its brand.

Pagar.me covers the digital commerce side of that strategy, while Stone’s core brand and local sales infrastructure serve small and medium businesses through face-to-face distribution. Together, they give Stone a single platform that spans both physical and online commerce.

What it signals for the Brazilian payments market

Brazil’s payments sector has moved past a land-grab phase, and the major players are now competing on ecosystem depth rather than just transaction volume. Stone’s consolidation mirrors a regional trend where fintechs are bundling acquiring, banking, and software to make merchant relationships more durable.

For international investors and partners, the move underscores Stone’s focus on profitable growth and credit discipline. A unified platform reduces operational complexity and positions the company to cross-sell higher-margin financial products to an existing base of digital and physical merchants.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Pagar.me shutting down?

No. Pagar.me is being consolidated into a single Stone app experience, but its payment gateway and digital commerce capabilities will continue to operate without interruption.

Do merchants need to change their integrations?

Stone says existing contracts, APIs, and settlement processes remain unchanged. The consolidation is administrative, so merchants do not need to rebuild their integrations.

Why is Stone merging the brands?

Stone wants to become a primary financial partner for merchants by offering a unified platform that includes payments, banking, and credit. A single app reduces friction and encourages merchants to adopt more services.

Does this affect Stone’s physical card machines?

No. The consolidation brings the digital commerce layer into the same ecosystem as Stone’s physical point-of-sale business, but the card machine operations continue as before.

World.title: Plinio Apuleyo Mendoza, García Márquez Confidant, Dies
World.content:

Colombia · Culture

Key Facts —Full name. Plinio Apuleyo Mendoza —Born. January 1, 1932, in Boyacá, Colombia —Died. July 28, 2026, aged 94 —Key works. ’El olor de la guayaba’ and ’Manual del perfecto idiota latinoamericano’ —Roles. Journalist, novelist, essayist, and diplomat

*A literary witness to the Boom generation, he captured Gabriel García Márquez’s inner world before breaking dramatically with the political romance that defined his circle.*

Bogota, Colombia. (Photo internet reproduction)

The keeper of Gabo’s secrets

Plinio Apuleyo Mendoza was one of Gabriel García Márquez’s closest friends for decades, a bond forged when both were young journalists navigating Colombia’s partisan press. They traveled together, worked on the political magazine Acción Liberal, and shared the intellectual fervor of a generation that would redefine Latin American letters.

That intimacy produced El olor de la guayaba (The Fragrance of Guava) in 1982, a book-length conversation widely regarded as the essential roadmap to the Nobel laureate’s creative universe. In its pages, Mendoza coaxed García Márquez into revealing his origins, his writing rituals, his political convictions, and his ambivalent relationship with fame.

The ideological rupture

The friendship that produced a literary classic could not survive the ideological chasm that opened after the Cold War. Mendoza grew deeply disillusioned with the Cuban revolution and the Latin American left, a stance that put him at odds with García Márquez’s enduring loyalty to Fidel Castro.

That break found its most explosive expression in 1996 with Manual del perfecto idiota latinoamericano (Manual of the Perfect Latin American Idiot), a satirical polemic co-written with Cuban exile Carlos Alberto Montaner and Peruvian writer Álvaro Vargas Llosa. The book skewered the region’s intellectual left, its economic nationalism, and the romanticization of authoritarian populism, becoming a foundational text for a rising liberal counter-narrative.

A life in diplomacy and letters

Beyond his journalism, Mendoza served Colombia as a diplomat, with postings that reflected his cosmopolitan sensibility and his deep entanglement with the country’s political evolution. His career spanned the era when Colombian writers often doubled as cultural ambassadors, carrying the nation’s literary prestige abroad.

He authored novels and essays that, while overshadowed by his association with García Márquez, earned him recognition as a distinctive voice. His columns and commentary made him a fixture in Colombian public life, where he was read as a bridge between the magical realist generation and the more skeptical, market-oriented intellectuals who followed.

What he represents in Colombian letters

Mendoza embodies a specific Colombian archetype: the provincial boy from Boyacá who ascended to the highest circles of global literary culture without losing his sharp, often acerbic, national perspective. He was both insider and apostate, the confidant who helped build a myth and then dared to challenge it.

His trajectory traces the arc of a continent’s intellectual journey, from revolutionary hope to liberal disenchantment. For an international readership, Mendoza is a reminder that Latin America’s literary Boom was never just about aesthetics; it was a deeply political affair whose friendships and fractures mirrored the region’s ideological battles.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was Plinio Apuleyo Mendoza’s relationship with Gabriel García Márquez?

He was one of García Márquez’s closest friends from their youth, collaborating on journalism and co-creating the interview book ’El olor de la guayaba’ before they split over political differences.

What is ’El olor de la guayaba’ about?

Published in 1982, it is a book of extended conversations in which García Márquez discusses his life, creative process, political views, and the experience of fame, organized and introduced by Mendoza.

Why did Mendoza and García Márquez fall out?

Their friendship fractured over ideology. Mendoza became a sharp critic of the Latin American left and the Cuban revolution, while García Márquez remained a close ally of Fidel Castro.

What is ’Manual del perfecto idiota latinoamericano’?

A 1996 satirical essay co-written with Carlos Alberto Montaner and Álvaro Vargas Llosa, it critiques Latin America’s political and intellectual left from a liberal perspective.

World.title: IRB Brasil Re CVM Case: Ex-Directors Cleared in Buffett Claim
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · Markets

Key Facts —The ruling. Brazil's securities regulator CVM absolved former IRB Brasil Re directors Fernando Passos and Jose Carlos Cardoso on July 28, 2026. —The charges. Selective disclosure of material information, release of false information to the market, an irregular share buyback and approval of outsized bonuses, all relating to 2019 and 2020. —The Berkshire claim. At the centre was the false suggestion that Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway held a significant stake in the reinsurer. —The proposed penalties. The rapporteur had proposed fines of R$600,000 and R$39.96 million against Passos. The full board did not follow him. —The process. The judgment was suspended twice before the board reached its decision.

Brazil’s securities watchdog has drawn a sharp line between a rogue finance chief and his former boss, punishing the architect of a fabricated Warren Buffett investment story while clearing the chief executive who was deceived by it.

Sao Paulo. (Photo internet reproduction)

The fake Berkshire story that moved markets

In early 2020, a rumor swept through Brazilian markets that Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett’s conglomerate, had acquired a significant stake in IRB Brasil Re, then one of the world’s largest reinsurers. IRB’s stock jumped more than 6% on the news before Berkshire publicly denied any investment, triggering a collapse of over 40%.

Brazil’s securities regulator, the Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM), later concluded the story was entirely fabricated. The regulator identified then-CFO and investor relations head Fernando Passos as the source of the false information.

For a foreign reader, the CVM plays a role similar to the US. Securities and Exchange Commission. It oversees Brazil’s capital markets, investigates misconduct, and can impose fines, trading bans, and other sanctions on companies and individuals who break securities laws.

Its decisions can be appealed through the courts, but a ruling from the full board carries significant weight in setting standards for corporate behavior across Latin America’s largest economy.

CVM’s split decision: CFO cleared, CEO cleared

Former CEO José Carlos Cardoso, however, was unanimously acquitted of negligence. Director Daniel Maeda found no evidence of bad faith, noting that Cardoso was misled by deceptive tactics employed by Passos and that chief executives may delegate responsibilities.

The distinction the CVM drew here matters well beyond this single case. By absolving the CEO while penalizing the CFO, the regulator signaled that top executives are not automatically liable for every act committed by their subordinates.

A chief executive who relies on internal controls and delegated reporting lines, and who shows no sign of having knowingly participated in a scheme, can be treated differently from the person who actually orchestrated the deception. That principle is closely watched by boardrooms across Brazil, where family-controlled and publicly traded firms alike are still adapting to stricter governance expectations.

A separate 2026 case does not overturn the fraud finding

In June 2026, a different CVM proceeding evaluated other alleged infractions by the same former directors. That case examined whether Passos selectively disclosed confidential information and whether Cardoso authorized compensation payments above shareholder-approved limits.

It is important to understand that this second proceeding did not revisit the core Berkshire fraud. Instead, it focused on distinct governance questions: who knew what about internal financial data, and whether bonus approvals followed proper corporate procedures.

The fact that the board suspended its judgment twice before reaching a decision suggests the evidence was complex and the legal arguments finely balanced. Observers are now asking whether the CVM will issue formal guidance to help companies distinguish between a rogue employee’s hidden actions and a systemic control failure that should attract board-level liability.

U.S. authorities reinforce the fraud narrative

The Brazilian decision aligns with actions taken by American regulators. The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission charged Passos with fraud for planting the false story and disseminating fake documents, and he later agreed to a final consent judgment involving penalties and an officer-director bar.

The U.S. Department of Justice described Passos’s conduct as a securities fraud scheme designed to prop up IRB’s stock. IRB itself entered a non-prosecution agreement with the DOJ and agreed to pay $5 million in compensation to affected shareholders.

Cross-border coordination of this kind has become more common as Brazilian companies with American depositary receipts or U.S. investors fall under multiple jurisdictions. When the SEC and the CVM pursue parallel cases, it can strengthen the factual record, but it also raises practical questions about whether penalties imposed in one country should be credited in the other and how a company can settle with one authority without prejudicing its defense elsewhere.

The wider accounting scandal at IRB

The Berkshire rumor was part of a broader governance crisis at IRB. In early 2020, asset manager Squadra Investimentos published a report alleging IRB’s accounting profits were artificially inflated, triggering a sharp price drop and formal CVM investigations.

Internal probes by KPMG and law firm Felsberg identified former directors involved in accounting irregularities. Some former board members reached settlement agreements with the CVM, paying fixed amounts to close cases without a formal finding of guilt, a practice criticized by investor associations as too lenient.

These settlements, known in Brazil as “termos de compromisso,” allow a defendant to pay a sum and walk away without admitting or denying wrongdoing. Regulators value them because they conserve resources and deliver money to harmed investors faster than a full trial.

Critics argue they can allow serious misconduct to go unpunished and leave the market without a clear public ruling on what exactly happened. The debate over whether the CVM should use them more sparingly in high-profile fraud cases is likely to intensify as Brazil’s retail investor base continues to grow.

Frequently Asked Questions

What was the false Berkshire Hathaway claim?

In 2020, IRB Brasil Re’s then-CFO Fernando Passos planted a fabricated story that Warren Buffett’s Berkshire Hathaway had acquired a significant stake in the Brazilian reinsurer. The stock rose over 6% before Berkshire publicly denied any investment, causing shares to plummet more than 40%.

What happened in the United States over the same case?

The SEC charged Passos with fraud, and he later agreed to a consent judgment with penalties and an officer-director bar. The U.S. Department of Justice described the scheme as securities fraud, and IRB entered a non-prosecution agreement, paying $5 million in victim compensation.

World.title: Caserones Copper Outage Hits Chile Mine, Lundin Keeps Target
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Chile · Mining

Key Facts —Cause. A severe winter storm in the Atacama Region damaged two transmission towers, cutting grid power to the Caserones mine on 18 July 2026. —Duration. Lundin Mining expects a total power restoration and gradual restart within two to three weeks from its 27 July update. —Production. Analysts estimate the outage exposes roughly 8,400 to 10,900 tonnes of scheduled copper output based on daily run rates. —Guidance. Lundin has maintained its full-year 2026 production guidance of 130,000 to 140,000 tonnes of copper for Caserones. —Recovery. The company states weather-related disruptions are embedded in annual plans and expects to recover most lost output later in the year.

*A brutal Andean winter storm has tested Chile’s copper supply chain, knocking a major mine offline. Investors are watching whether lost output can be clawed back in a market hungry for metal.*

A copper mine in the Atacama Desert, northern Chile. (Photo internet reproduction)

How a winter storm paralyzed a copper mine

Heavy rain and unusually heavy snowfall from a severe winter storm battered Chile’s high-altitude Atacama Region in mid-July. Inspections revealed damage to two transmission towers that supply the Caserones mine, completely severing its grid connection on 18 July.

Backup generators are running only critical infrastructure while access roads remain blocked or impaired by snow. Site crews are being rotated safely as repair teams work to restore power and reopen logistics routes.

For readers unfamiliar with the region, the Atacama is not only one of the driest places on Earth at lower elevations but also hosts mining operations perched above 4,000 meters in the Andes. At those altitudes, winter storms can deliver sudden, heavy snow loads that overwhelm infrastructure designed for arid conditions.

Transmission towers, which carry electricity from Chile’s national grid across vast distances, are particularly exposed because they often run along ridgelines where wind and ice accumulate fasteSt When a tower fails, the entire line must be inspected and repaired in terrain that is difficult to reach even in good weather.

The production gap and the plan to close it

With Caserones producing an average of about 364 tonnes of copper per day in 2025, a 23-to-30-day outage exposes between 8,400 and 10,900 tonnes of scheduled output. That represents roughly seven to eight percent of the mine’s 2026 guidance midpoint.

Lundin describes this as exposure rather than a permanent loss. The company signals it can offset the shortfall by running the plant harder in the fourth quarter, deferring non-critical maintenance, and optimizing ore grades once grid power is fully restored.

In plain terms, “exposure” means the volume of copper that would have been produced if the mine had run normally during the outage window. It is not the same as a confirmed loss, because a mine can often catch up.

The catch-up strategy relies on what engineers call “surge capacity”—the ability of crushers, mills, and concentrators to run above their average daily rate for sustained periods. Most processing plants are designed with a margin above their nameplate capacity, and operators can tap that margin if they have enough ore stockpiled and no further interruptions.

Guidance holds steady despite market nerves

Lundin’s formal 2026 production target for Caserones remains unchanged at 130,000 to 140,000 tonnes of copper and 2,000 to 3,000 tonnes of molybdenum. The company explicitly notes that weather-related disruptions are factored into its annual operating plans.

Analysts caution that the guidance could come under pressure if the fourth-quarter recovery underperforms. For now, Lundin is betting that a gradual restart and a strong finish to the year will keep the mine within its original range.

Production guidance is a public commitment a mining company makes to its shareholders about how much metal it expects to deliver in a given year. Missing guidance can erode investor confidence and affect a company’s share price, which is why Lundin’s decision to hold its target steady is being read as a signal of confidence.

The company is essentially telling the market that its internal models show enough operational flexibility to absorb a multi-week stoppage without revising the annual number downward.

What it means in a tight copper market

The temporary loss of roughly 10,000 tonnes of Chilean supply arrives in a global copper market already grappling with low inventories and growing demand from the energy transition. Even short-lived disruptions can tighten spot availability and support prices.

Chile is the world’s largest copper producer, and any prolonged outage at a mid-tier mine like Caserones ripples through supply chains. For international investors and diplomats, the episode highlights the physical vulnerability of critical mineral assets to extreme weather in the high Andes.

Copper is often called the backbone of electrification because it is used in everything from electric vehicle wiring to wind turbines and grid upgrades. When supply tightens, the immediate effect is felt in the spot market, where buyers pay a premium for metal available right now.

Over time, sustained tightness can feed into higher long-term contract prices, affecting manufacturers and ultimately consumers. The question hanging over this outage is whether it remains a brief, localized hiccup or becomes part of a broader pattern of weather-driven supply losses that the market can no longer easily absorb.

Restart hinges on power, not plant damage

Lundin has not reported any structural damage to Caserones’ processing plant, crushers, or conveyor systems. The bottleneck is strictly power transmission and site access, not the integrity of ore-handling equipment.

The restart is described as gradual, meaning a staged ramp-up of crushing, conveying, milling, and concentrator circuits once electricity is stable. If repairs stay within the two-to-three-week window, the company expects to bring operations back to normal throughput without major equipment overhauls.

A gradual restart is standard industry practice after a full power loss. Operators bring systems back online in sequence, checking each component for faults before introducing ore.

Rushing this process can cause equipment damage or safety incidents, which would extend the outage further. The fact that no plant damage has been found is significant: it means the repair effort is focused entirely on external infrastructure, which is generally faster and cheaper to fix than rebuilding processing machinery.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the Caserones mine outage?

A severe winter storm in Chile’s Atacama Region damaged two transmission towers, cutting grid power to the mine on 18 July 2026. Heavy snow also blocked access roads.

How much copper production is affected?

Analysts estimate the outage exposes roughly 8,400 to 10,900 tonnes of scheduled copper output, based on the mine’s 2025 daily production average and a 23-to-30-day interruption.

Did Lundin Mining change its 2026 guidance?

No. Lundin maintained its full-year 2026 production guidance of 130,000 to 140,000 tonnes of copper for Caserones, stating weather disruptions are embedded in its annual plans.

When will the Caserones mine restart?

Lundin’s 27 July update guides to a full power restoration and gradual restart within approximately two to three weeks from that date, assuming repairs proceed on schedule.

Sources: Lundin Mining.

World.title: Halo BPO hiring work from home sales agents at $8.50 an hour
World.content:
Halo BPO hiring work from home sales agents at $8.50 an hour

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The work from home opportunities keep coming for Belizeans. Halo BPO is recruiting sales agents to work remotely from anywhere in Belize, with pay posted upfront at $8.50 BZD per hour and a dialing schedule of 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. Belize time.

The company says it is looking for qualified candidates only, specifically agents with appointment setting or home improvement sales experience.

The technical requirements are strict, and applicants should check them before applying. Candidates need internet with at least 40 Mbps download and 40 Mbps upload speed on a wired ethernet connection, as Wi-Fi is not allowed. The computer must have a quad core CPU of 2.0GHz or faster and at least 8GB of RAM, with an SSD preferred, and Chromebooks are not accepted. A webcam, a good quality USB headset, and a quiet, distraction free home workspace complete the list.

For those who qualify, the trade-off is attractive: steady daytime hours, no commute, no transport costs, and income earned from home.

Applications go to [email protected], and the company stresses one important instruction: include your full name in the email subject line.

World.title: Guyana ferry captain charged with murder over 73 deaths
World.content:
Guyana ferry captain charged with murder over 73 deaths

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): The MV Barima disaster has become a murder case. The captain and two crew members of the Guyanese passenger ferry that capsized with catastrophic loss of life were charged with murder on Tuesday, more than a week after the disaster killed 73 people and left 30 others still missing.

As reported by Reuters, Captain Kevin Price, 40, and crew members Rondell Dwayne Roberts, 42, and Delon Granderson, 33, appeared before a Georgetown court on the murder charges. They were not required to enter pleas, and the news agency could not immediately reach the defendants or their representatives for comment. The three were remanded to prison, with the case adjourned to August 3.

The charges attach to a tragedy whose dimensions have grown darker with each disclosure. The MV Barima, an 87-year-old ship, sank on July 18 while travelling from Georgetown to the northwestern village of Port Kaituma. Authorities say 76 passengers and crew were rescued, and believe 179 people were on board, far more than early reports indicated.

Prime Minister Mark Phillips has said that two of the crew members, including the captain, tested positive for marijuana following the accident, and that many of those on board had never been listed on the vessel’s passenger manifest. The Prime Minister maintained, however, that the vessel had been deemed seaworthy and had kept up with its maintenance schedule, an assertion the official inquiry will now test.

That inquiry carries a Belizean signature. President Irfaan Ali’s Commission of Inquiry into the disaster is chaired by Justice Godfrey Smith of Belize, the former Attorney General and CARICOM High-Level Representative for Law and Criminal Justice, leading an international panel empowered to determine whether negligence, misconduct, or institutional failures contributed to the tragedy. A wide-ranging investigation into the ferry services, run by the Transport and Harbours Department under the Ministry of Public Works, is also underway.

The political reckoning has begun in parallel. Opposition lawmakers have called for the resignations of Public Works Minister Juan Edghill and Public Utilities and Aviation Minister Deodat Indar.

As with any criminal matter, the three accused are presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty before the court.

For the families of the 73 recovered and the 30 still missing, Tuesday’s charges mark the first formal step toward accountability, with the deeper answers, how an 87-year-old ferry came to carry an uncounted crowd into disaster, resting with the courts and the Belizean-led commission. Breaking Belize News will continue to follow the case.

World.title: Security Guard fined $3,000 for drug trafficking after admitting he tried selling weed to support his parents
World.content:
Security Guard fined $3,000 for drug trafficking after admitting he tried selling weed to support his parents

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Belize City security guard avoided imprisonment on Tuesday after pleading guilty to drug trafficking involving 940 grams (a little over 2 pounds) of cannabis.

Barrington Earl Vanson was fined $3,000, along with $5 in court costs, and was given until December 30, 2026, to pay. If he fails to pay the fine by the deadline, he will serve one year in prison.

Vanson was arraigned in the Belize City Magistrate’s Court on Monday evening and pleaded guilty to possession of a controlled drug with intent to supply.

During his mitigation plea, Vanson admitted that he had attempted to sell the cannabis but claimed it was the first time he had become involved in selling drugs.

“I promise it won’t happen again because usually I do my little security work,” Vanson told the court. “I usually do handyman work too, chopping yards and cleaning garbage. I am asking for leniency.”

Vanson said he normally earns money through security and odd jobs but made the decision to sell cannabis because both of his parents were unemployed and he was trying to help support them.

“I know I messed up really big, and that was a stupid choice I made to survive because I have my ma to care for and my father. Both are not working right now,” he said. “I was just doing something on the side to help my family. This is the first time I decided to do this.”

The court imposed a non-custodial sentence after considering his guilty plea and mitigation.

According to police, at about 1:30 a.m. on Monday, July 27, members of the Violence Enforcement Team acted on information that cannabis was being kept inside Room No. 7 at a building located at the corner of Dean and Plues streets.

Officers visited the apartment and met Vanson, who identified himself as a security guard. Police informed him that they intended to search the premises for illegal firearms and ammunition and asked whether he had anything illegal to declare. He reportedly said no.

During the search, officers found a bag containing a grey plastic bag with seven smaller parcels of green, leafy material suspected to be cannabis.

Vanson was taken to the police station, where the substance was weighed in his presence and amounted to 940 grams.

This version keeps the court details while giving greater prominence to how Vanson normally earns a living and his explanation for committing the offence.

World.title: Collin Francis Jr. pleads guilty to manslaughter in Nestor Vasquez death and attempted murder in nurse stabbing
World.content:
Collin Francis Jr. pleads guilty to manslaughter in Nestor Vasquez death and attempted murder in nurse stabbing

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Collin Francis Jr. pleaded guilty in the High Court on Tuesday to manslaughter in the death of 60-year-old Nestor Vasquez and attempted murder in the stabbing of psychiatric nurse Augustina Elijio.

Justice Nigel Pilgrim accepted the pleas and scheduled sentencing for September 7, 2026, following mitigation. The court ordered a social inquiry report, prison report and victim impact statements in both cases.

Francis was initially charged with murder in Vasquez’s death, but the Crown accepted a manslaughter plea based on diminished responsibility. Medical records showed that Francis was experiencing an acute psychotic episode and had been diagnosed with schizophrenia at the time.

Elijio was attacked on June 4, 2019, at the Port Loyola Mental Health Clinic, where Francis had gone seeking treatment. She was stabbed in the right breast and rib cage, suffering injuries classified as grievous harm.

Two days later, while Francis was detained at the Queen Street Police Station, Vasquez was found badly beaten in a pool of blood inside the cell area. Vasquez died on June 8, 2019, from blunt-force traumatic injuries to the head.

Francis was previously deemed unfit to plead in 2024 and underwent psychiatric evaluations every six months. A recent evaluation found that he was stable while taking his medication and abstaining from marijuana.

He has been on remand since June 2019.

World.title: The Devil Made Me Do It: Jehovah’s Witness busted wearing tourist’s clothes after stealing his suitcase from bus
World.content:
The Devil Made Me Do It: Jehovah’s Witness busted wearing tourist’s clothes after stealing his suitcase from bus

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 36-year-old self-described Jehovah’s Witness was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after admitting that he stole a French tourist’s suitcase, wore some of the stolen clothing and sold other items because he wanted money to buy food.

Collin Burton Ramclam pleaded guilty to theft after admitting that he took the suitcase when he found it unattended on a bus travelling from Belmopan to Belize City.

The suitcase belonged to 20-year-old French national Ange Cesar Cirnevin, who reported it stolen on Friday, July 24.

Ramclam was later taken to the police station while wearing the tourist’s green polo shirt, a white, black and red scarf around his head and a silver Festina wristwatch valued at $300. Police also recovered the tourist’s grey suitcase and a bag containing clothing.

Ramclam reportedly told police, “I am sorry. I just meh wah money to buy food. I done sell the jeans pants and a wristwatch.”

Most of the property was recovered, except for one wristwatch and two pairs of jeans valued at $60.

In mitigation, Ramclam told the court that his own phone had been stolen the previous night, that he had been drinking and that he was hungry and had no money. He said a bus conductor had given him a free ride home from Belmopan after he travelled there to seek construction work.

Ramclam told the court that he fell asleep on the bus and noticed the suitcase when he awoke in Belize City. He admitted that he should have turned it over to the conductor but instead took it when he saw no one nearby.

The father of one asked the court for leniency, telling the magistrate that he attends Jehovah’s Witness services every Wednesday and Sunday and promising that the offence would not happen again.

Ramclam also admitted that he was not a first-time offender and had previously been convicted of theft in the Belmopan area. The senior magistrate remanded him while considering an appropriate sentence.

World.title: Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars crowned Champions at Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament
World.content:
Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars crowned Champions at Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament

By Zoila Palma: Belize’s Gonz Auto Stars returned home with championship honors after delivering an impressive performance at the XII Copa Cancún Basketball Tournament in Cancún, Quintana Roo, Mexico.

They competed with both its U15 and U17 teams from July 23 to 26, facing strong competition from teams across the region.

Both Gonz Auto Stars teams showcased determination, discipline and teamwork throughout the tournament, battling hard in every game and representing Belize with pride. Their performances reflected the commitment and fighting spirit that have become hallmarks of the Gonz Auto Stars basketball program.

The biggest achievement came from the U17 team, which captured first place to bring the championship title home to Belize. The victory was celebrated as a testament to the players’ hard work, dedication and belief in one another.

The team credited coaches Gabriel Taylor, Ronell Gonzalez Sr., Cordel Gonzalez Jr. and Cordel Gonzalez Sr. for their leadership, preparation and support throughout the tournament.

Gonz Auto Stars also expressed gratitude to its sponsors and everyone who supported the team’s BBQ fundraiser, which helped make the international trip possible.

World.title: Man remanded to prison after 10-year-old reports that 3-teeth man touched her inappropriately and gave her $3 not to tell anyone
World.content:
Man remanded to prison after 10-year-old reports that 3-teeth man touched her inappropriately and gave her $3 not to tell anyone

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A Lords Bank resident accused of sexually assaulting a 10-year-old girl was remanded to the Belize Central Prison after the Belize City Magistrate’s Court denied his application for bail following detailed submissions from both the prosecution and defense.

Manuel De Jesus Flores, a local mason, appeared before a Senior Magistrate in Court #5 to face two counts of sexual assault. The charges allege that on July 18, 2026, Flores intentionally and unlawfully touched the female minor—who is 10 years and 5 months old—in a sexual manner without her consent.

The allegations stem from an incident occurring around 12:30 a.m. while the child’s mother was briefly away at a neighboring home. According to court details, the child reported that an elderly man standing at a construction site two lots over motioned for her to come to him. When she refused and went inside, he later entered her yard, asked for a hug, and grabbed her left hand when she attempted to walk away. The assailant then lifted her hips, pressed his erection against her body, touched her inappropriately, and squeezed her breast. Before releasing her, he handed her a $1 coin and a $2 bill, telling her not to tell anyone. The victim threw the money back at him, ran down the street carrying her younger cousin, and met her mother on the road to report what had occurred.

During court proceedings, defense attorney Sharon Pitts-Robateau made extensive submissions advocating for her client’s release, seeking bail even after the sitting Magistrate initially indicated a denial due to the grave nature of the offense. Attorney Pitts highlighted that Flores is gainfully employed as a mason and emphasized the fundamental presumption of innocence, pointing out that the charges are strictly allegations at this stage. She argued that the essential legal purpose of bail is to ensure a defendant returns to court, a goal that could be achieved by setting strict bail conditions rather than remanding him.

Police Prosecutor Sgt. Ayala vigorously countered the application, urging the Senior Magistrate to consider several key factors against granting release. Sgt. Ayala cited the very young age of the victim, the high prevalence and seriousness of sexual assault offenses, and the likelihood that Flores might reoffend given the early morning hour of the alleged incident. The prosecution further argued that releasing the accused would present a significant risk of interference with the young victim or the ongoing police investigation.

After considering the arguments from both sides, the Senior Magistrate sustained the prosecution’s objections and refused bail. Flores was remanded in custody to the Belize Central Prison until his next scheduled court appearance on September 17, 2026.

World.title: Central Bank of Belize, FIU and Financial Services Commission sign Governance Agreements for use of Sanctions Registry
World.content:
Central Bank of Belize, FIU and Financial Services Commission sign Governance Agreements for use of Sanctions Registry

By Zoila Palma: The Central Bank of Belize (the Central Bank), the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), and the Financial Services Commission (FSC) have signed governance agreements establishing the framework for the shared use of the Sanctions Registry System (SRS).

A joint statement explained that SRS is a secure supervisory platform developed by the Central Bank, and designed to support the management of sanctions-related information and strengthen Belize’s framework for combatting money laundering, terrorist financing, and other forms of financial crime. By improving information management, data retrieval, and analytical capability, the system enables a more efficient, consistent, and risk-based approach to supervision.

“The governance agreements provide the legal and operational framework for participating authorities to access and use the SRS in support of their respective statutory responsibilities. While each institution will utilise the system independently within its own supervisory environment, the shared platform promotes greater consistency in regulatory information management and enhances opportunities for collaboration where appropriate,” it added.

The initiative reflects the continued commitment of the Central Bank, the FIU, and the FSC to strengthening inter-agency cooperation through the effective use of technological innovation, improved information sharing, and modern supervisory practices.

The Central Bank, FIU, and FSC said that they remain committed to working collaboratively to strengthen Belize’s regulatory framework, enhance supervisory effectiveness, and promote a safe, sound and resilient financial system.

World.title: No social media ban
World.content:
Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton (left) in discussion with Dr Ganesh Shetty (right), acting director, adolescent mental health, Ministry of Health & Wellness, as well as lead researcher and fellow at The University of the West Indies and consultant with the Ministry of Health Dr Stephen Johnson during Tuesday’s media briefing to present the findings from a National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

In what is said to be “one of the most comprehensive national assessments ever undertaken” on social media use by minors in Jamaica, the majority of citizens surveyed have baulked at a total ban but say Government must lead the way in implementing policy with strong parental involvement when it comes to enforcement.

“The results show overwhelming public support for some level of Government action,” said Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton.

He was delivering the main address, Tuesday, during a press conference to release findings of the National Study on Social Media Use and the Protection of Children.

The event was held at the Courtyard by Mariott Hotel in St Andrew.

According to Tufton, nine out of every 10 respondents, or 90.2 per cent, support Government regulation of minors’ social media use, while 2.9 per cent expressed opposition. In addition, he said, nearly 84 per cent believe Jamaica should establish a clear national policy framework governing minors’ use of social media.

Tufton said from reading the study he formed the opinion that the subject has been “a long-standing concern, but not talked about as much”.

“I was surprised when I saw the results. A strong message: The Jamaican people recognise that this is an issue requiring national attention, and they expect thoughtful leadership on the issue. But perhaps the most significant finding is not simply that Jamaicans support some levels of Government action; it is that they believe this responsibility must be shared, and I was very heartened at that,” the minister stated.

Citing the report, he said only 12.7 per cent of respondents believe Government should lead this effort alone.

“Again, that’s very good to know, because it means people will want to engage,” Tufton said, while adding that 40.5 per cent of respondents believe parents/guardians should play the leading role, while another 39 per cent favoured shared responsibility among parents, schools, Government, communities, and other stakeholders.

“The finding is especially important, because it reminds us of something we already know: No Government policy can replace active parenting, and that’s very important to note. No legislation can replace guidance within the home. No technology platform can replace the influence of families, teachers, and communities. Protecting children online, therefore, must be a national partnership, and that’s a very big theme. A takeaway from this: A national partnership,” said the minister.

He noted that the survey also revealed that Jamaicans favour balance rather than extremes, and the preferred approach was not simply stronger legal restrictions.

While acknowledging the positives brought by social media the health minister emphasised that the results of emerging research from 2025-2026 for Jamaica “confirms a strong link between social media use and increased anxiety, depression, and digital addiction, particularly among young persons and content creators”.

He said youth under 24 spend an average of six hours daily on social media, compared to five hours for adults and four hours for seniors.

Tufton stressed that the study is “intended for public consumption and discourse in the first instance, not any decision”, while at the same time assuring that there was no intention to “just wholesale adopt what entails elsewhere” as far as regulations are concerned.

Delving into the study during the event, Dr Stephen Johnson, lead researcher and fellow at The University of the West Indies and a consultant with the Ministry of Health, said the use of social media by minors has become a public health issue.

“We have data from the National Council on Drug Abuse [NCDA] indicating that 70 per cent of our minors sleep less than eight hours on an average school night. In terms of body image, [there is] low self-esteem; [we see] digital addiction from excessive screen time [of] three hours or more; having 68 per cent of our population being addicted. [There are issues of] online safety, cyberbullying, grooming, and being exposed to harmful content. Now, of course, there’s a need for Government not necessarily to be preventative, but to be proactive,” he said.

The sample of 1,027 individuals surveyed included Gen Zers, millennials, Gen X, and Boomers educated at the primary, vocational, and tertiary levels.

Dr Johnson emphasised that while the overwhelming majority, over 80 per cent of those interviewed, supported “a clear policy framework for minors’ social media use… the appetite for an outright ban it’s not really here… Persons are saying, while you’re doing this, be mindful that minors have rights,” the lead researcher disclosed.

Dr Ganash Shetty, acting director, adolescent mental health in the Ministry of Health, who pointed out that the algorithms behind social media platforms are created by behavioural specialists, spoke directly to youngsters in attendance.

World.title: Bounty Killer gets key to Kingston
World.content:
Rodney “Bounty Killer” Price delivering his acceptance speech Tuesday after receiving the Keys to the City of Kingston and the renaming of Wenchman Road in his honour.(Photo: Karl Mclarty)

FROM the inner-city community of Seaview Gardens in western St Andrew that raised him to conquering the global dancehall stage, Rodney “Bounty Killer” Price returned home Tuesday to receive the Keys to the City of Kingston and the renaming of a road in his honour.

“It’s official, the king of Kingston with the keys to Kingston,” a jubilant Price declared as he accepted the city’s highest civic honour during a ceremony at Seaview Gardens Primary School.

In a further tribute to the dancehall icon, Wenchman Road — where Price spent much of his youth — was officially renamed Rodney Price Drive, following a petition from Seaview Gardens’ residents and approval by the Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation (KSAMC).

Visibly moved by the recognition Price, who has also received the Order of Distinction for his invaluable contribution to Jamaica’s music scene, described the occasion as another meaningful milestone in his career, admitting that words could not fully express his gratitude.

“Today is really the unfolding of another historical chapter in my career. And this milestone is a very unusual and an uncommon accomplishment — the Keys to the City of Kingston,” he said, thanking the KSAMC, mayor of Kingston Andrew Swaby, and other officials for the honour.

Pointing to the road which now bears his name, Price recalled how his life was defined by it, noting that it had witnessed both the beginnings of his journey and some of his darkest moments. “This is more than just a ceremony. This is a celebration of troubles and trial and triumph and greatness. It’s just right round the road, that’s where I got shot when I was 16, right around there,” he said.

He thanked the KSAMC for immortalising the name, the battles, and the triumphs he carried long before he became known to the world as Bounty Killer.

“Our community is a golden garden. Hard work and dedication leads to these accomplishments and accolades in life. And then they say a king has never been crowned in his town, so what is this then?” questioned an evidently elated Price.

The entertainer who has won a Grammy award for his feature on No Doubt’s multi-platinum hit song Hey Baby and received a solo Grammy nomination, told the ceremony that the significance of the occasion far surpassed international acclamation.

“This is more than a Grammy to me. These are people who watched me emerge as a young artiste. These people are people who are personally involved in my upbringing, and for them to decide that I deserve the key to Kingston, this is something phenomenal,” he said.

For his part, Kingston Mayor Andrew Swaby congratulated Price and noted that the recognition is more than celebrating the successful musician, describing it as a statement about the values of the city and the potential that exists within communities such as Seaview Gardens.

“Too often communities like Seaview Gardens are viewed through the lens of their challenges rather than their possibilities. People sometimes make assumptions about what someone can achieve based on where they come from, but as we all should know by now an address does not determine one’s personal potential. What Bounty Killer’s life demonstrates is the clearest possible term that potential exists in every community; talent discipline and determination can emerge from anywhere for our young people,” said Swaby.

Announcing the renaming of Wenchman Road to Rodney Price Drive, Swaby said the tribute would ensure that the artiste’s legacy remains permanently etched in the community that shaped him.

“His name will remain fixed to this day, in this very community that raised him, so that anyone who passes through Seaview Gardens will know that greatness comes from these streets. So Bounty Killer, on behalf of the citizens of Kingston and St Andrew, thank you. Thank you for your music, for your mentorship, and for the contribution that you have made to Jamaica’s culture. This city is proud to recognise you as a son of Kingston, and it is an honour today to place this key in your hands,” said the mayor.

World.title: Grand day-long celebrations for Rita Marley’s 80th
World.content:
These young performers enjoyed the kids’ zone. (Photo: Rahyme McKenzie)

The Bob and Rita Marley foundations brought together supporters, partners, artistes, and community members to honour Alferita “Rita” Marley as she celebrated her 80th earthstrong under the theme ‘Thank You Jah 80’.

The day-long tribute celebrated Marley’s extraordinary legacy as a musician, philanthropist, entrepreneur, cultural advocate, and matriarch whose impact continues to inspire generations around the world.

Celebrations began at 6:30 am with Rise in Grace, a wellness and fitness experience at Bob Marley Museum that invited participants to embrace healthy living while reflecting on Rita Marley’s lifelong commitment to holistic well-being.

From 11:00 am to 3:00 pm Tuff Gong International came alive with a Family Fun Day, offering free entertainment and activities for all ages. Families enjoyed interactive games, storytelling, face painting, karaoke, water attractions, creative activities for children, dominoes, ludo, and complimentary health screenings. The activation reflected Rita Marley’s lifelong commitment to strengthening families, promoting wellness, and building resilient communities.

The festivities officially began with a prayer and blessing led by the Ethiopian Orthodox Church, followed by cultural performances from students of Half-Way Tree Primary, Linstead Primary, Central Branch Primary, Meadowbrook Primary and Old Harbour Bay Culture Camp.

Music then took centre stage during the lunch hour concert, held from 1:00 pm to 2:00 pm and powered by Tapedeck, an independent music streaming and digital download platform.

Through a partnership with the Jamaica Cultural Development Commission (JCDC), the concert also provided a national stage for the 2026 Festival Song Competition finalists, reinforcing both organisations’ shared commitment to preserving and celebrating Jamaican culture.

Tim Quirk, founder of Tapedeck, commented: “Rita Marley’s musical journey is a living blueprint for creative independence. What she and Bob Marley established through Tuff Gong by leveraging their voices to amplify other independent artistes and producers resonates strongly with us at Tapedeck. We are honoured to be a part of this milestone birthday celebration as we welcome Tuff Gong International Distributors to Tapedeck and look forward to bringing Jamaica’s creative community to our audience.”

The day’s celebrations culminated with the highly anticipated Thank You Jah 80 Digital Celebration Concert at 5:00 pm, streamed on the Tuff Gong TV YouTube channel and Bob Marley’s Tuff Gong Radio on SiriusXM Channel 19. Hosted by Kamila McDonald and Ron Muschette, the concert featured performances by Tessanne Chin, Nadine Sutherland, Romain Virgo, Alaine, and Makeda, reaching audiences around the world and allowing supporters everywhere to join in celebrating the milestone.

CEO of the Bob Marley Group of Companies Cedella Marley shared: “We celebrate mommy every day, but turning 80 is a milestone that deserves to be honoured in a truly special way. She has spent her entire life showing up for us — not just as our mother, but as a guide, a protector, and an unwavering source of love. Beyond our family, she’s poured that same love into communities around the world, serving others with grace, compassion, and humility. Everything she has done has been rooted in love, so celebrating her is one small way for us to say thank you. She deserves every flower, every tribute, and every moment of appreciation. This celebration is our way of letting her know just how deeply she is loved.”

World.title: ‘WALK STRONG’
World.content:
Gordon Swaby, CEO of EduFocal Limited, as the Junior Market-listed company reports early operating gains from its restructuring while working to stabilise its balance sheet.

SHAREHOLDERS of loss-making EduFocal Limited will vote on September 10 on renaming the listed company Walstron Limited, widening its mandate beyond education technology and authorising directors to issue shares to executives, advisers, employees and business partners.

The renamed company would be permitted to operate across education technology, technology, commerce and real estate, but the annual general meeting (AGM) documents identify no acquisition target, property project or commerce venture. Chief Executive Officer Gordon Swaby said there was nothing in those areas to announce, while the EduFocal brand and its existing products would continue.

The vote comes as EduFocal’s auditors warn of material uncertainty over its ability to continue as a going concern. At December 2025, the group had a $163.02-million equity deficit and only $104,315 in cash.

Swaby told the Jamaica Observer in written responses that Walstron was derived from the phrase “walk strong”.

“You know how we tell people ‘walk good’ when they’re heading off? Walstron is our version of that, except it’s about how you carry yourself through the challenging parts,” he said.

The AGM resolution says the change would reflect an expanded business focus and long-term growth strategy. Swaby, however, said the broader mandate was intended to give the company room to pursue opportunities rather than signal that a transaction was imminent.

“On real estate and commerce, what the resolution does is give us room. That’s really all it is. It widens what the company is allowed to do so we’re not running back to shareholders every time something interesting comes along,” he told the Business Observer.

“But there’s nothing for me to announce today. When there is, it goes through the JSE (Jamaica Stock Exchange) first and you’ll have it the same time our shareholders do.”

He also drew a distinction between the listed company’s proposed new name and the EduFocal operating brand.

“EduFocal is still EduFocal. Same brand, same platform, same everything. Academy runs. Quizzative runs. Engage runs,” Swaby said.

He said the previously disclosed wind-down of EduFocal’s African subsidiary operations would not affect those products or the company’s customers.

Shares for obligations

More immediately for shareholders, Resolution Six would authorise EduFocal’s directors to issue unissued ordinary shares to key partners, executives, legal advisers and other employees of the company or its subsidiaries.

The shares could be issued as compensation for services or other valuable consideration, with the directors determining each allotment at their discretion.

The resolution does not state how many shares could be issued, the proposed issue price, the recipients or the value of the services and obligations involved.

Swaby confirmed that settling some obligations with shares forms part of the plan.

“Yes. Part of what we’re asking shareholders to approve is settling certain obligations by issuing new ordinary shares,” he said.

“You either service those obligations out of cash, or you convert them into equity and free that cash up for the business. I’d much rather put the money into building.”

Issuing shares instead of using cash could reduce liabilities and preserve scarce working capital. It would, however, increase the number of shares in issue and would dilute existing shareholders. The extent of any dilution cannot be determined until the company discloses the number of shares, issue price, recipients and obligations being settled.

EduFocal had 648.45 million ordinary shares in issue at December 2025. Its shares closed Tuesday at $0.18, compared with the $1 price at which the company listed in March 2022.

Rights issue must wait

EduFocal’s audited financial statements list a proposed $250-million rights issue among the measures management intends to use to address its cash-flow difficulties. The other measures include securing $200 million in large contracts and restructuring loans with creditors.

Swaby now says the rights issue will not proceed until the balance sheet has first been repaired.

“We’re not doing a rights issue until the balance sheet is fixed. Simple as that,” he said.

“You don’t go asking people for fresh money on a balance sheet that isn’t right yet. Fix it first. That’s the work we’re in the middle of, and a good chunk of what shareholders are voting on is exactly that work.”

He did not define what would constitute a repaired balance sheet or say how much of the deficit the proposed share settlements are expected to eliminate.

The sequencing is important because the audited accounts presented the rights issue as part of management’s response to the going-concern uncertainty. Existing shareholders would ordinarily be given an opportunity to participate in a rights issue, while allotments to selected parties under Resolution Six would dilute shareholders who do not receive additional shares.

EduFocal has not reported a full-year net profit since listing.

Revenue declined 28 per cent to $70.27 million in 2025, but the company recorded an operating profit of $23.9 million after sharply reducing expenses. Finance costs and impairment losses contributed to a net loss of $29.43 million, although that was an improvement on the $58-million loss recorded in 2024.

At year end, liabilities exceeded the group’s $203.14 million in assets by $163.02 million. Its accumulated deficit stood at $341.23 million.

Approximately $153.09 million, or 75 per cent, of total assets comprised intangible assets such as software and intellectual property. The auditors identified the valuation of those assets as a key audit matter because it depends partly on management’s estimates of future revenue and cash flow.

At the stand-alone company level, current liabilities exceeded current assets by $147.01 million. The auditors said continued operation depended on management’s ability to reduce costs and increase revenue. Their opinion was not modified in respect of the going-concern matter.

EduFocal subsequently reported a net profit of $368,479 for the March 2026 quarter, reversing a $1.34-million loss a year earlier. Revenue, however, declined 53 per cent to $14.11 million.

Late again

The company’s 2025 audited accounts and March 2026 quarterly report have now been published, but both were late.

The first-quarter report, due on May 15, was submitted on July 1. EduFocal was also suspended from trading in both 2024 and 2025 after failing to submit audited financial statements within the Jamaica Stock Exchange’s deadlines. Its most recent suspension lasted from early June until December 5, 2025.

“On the filings, you’re right. We’ve been late, and that’s on me,” Swaby said in his responses.

He said the company had made significant changes to its internal processes and intended to remain current with its reporting obligations.

“When you list, you take on an obligation to keep the market informed on time, and I take that seriously. We intend to be current and to stay current,” he said.

World.title: RAINY DAY BLUES
World.content:
(From bottom to top) Antigua and Barbuda’s Cejhae Greene, Australia’s Edward Nketia, Jamaica’s Ackeem Blake, Canada’s Jerome Blake, Nigeria’s Adekalu Nicholas Fakorede, South Africa’s Gift Leotlela, Lesotho’s Mojela Koneshe and Barbados’s Kuron Griffith compete in the men’s 100m semi-finals during the athletics event at the Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, on day five of the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, Scotland, on Tuesday. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica failed to add to its medal tally on the second day of track and field at the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, on Tuesday as, for the second straight staging, no Jamaican man contested the blue-ribbon 100m final.

There were hopes of adding to the two gold medals won on Monday by high jumper Romaine Beckford and sprint hurdler Demario Prince, but the Jamaicans must wait at least until today if they are to win more medals.

Lamara Distin failed to repeat her success in the women’s high jump, placing fourth, while Jodean Williams was fifth in the women’s 100m final.

Jamaicans are down to contest two finals today — the men’s long jump and women’s shot put — while the 200m events for both men and women will also start.

The afternoon session was held in heavy rain, forcing officials to take the high jumpers off the field. When the competition resumed, Distin, who led in the first half of the event, could only manage 1.87m and missed out on a medal.

Australia’s Eleanor Patterson, the silver medallist in 2022, won the gold with a games record-equalling 1.96m, beating teammate Nicola Olyslagers, who cleared 1.93m, while Nigeria’s Temitope Simbiat Adeshina took the bronze.

Jodean Williams was the only Jamaican who reported for the women’s 100m final, with Jonielle Williams, who had also qualified, withdrawing. Both had qualified on time after placing third in their respective semi-finals.

Jodean ran 11.09 seconds (1.0m/s) as New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs won with an Oceania Area record 10.93 seconds, beating England’s Amy Hunt, who ran 10.98 seconds. Australia’s Torrie Lewis lowered her national record to 10.99 seconds after running 11.00 seconds in the semi-finals.

Both Ackeem Blake and Rohan Watson failed to get past the men’s semi-finals. Blake was third in the third semi-final in 10.06 seconds (1.1m/s), behind South Africa’s Gift Leotlela, who ran 10.02 seconds, and Australia’s Edward Nketia, who clocked a personal-best 10.03 seconds.

In the first semi-final, Watson was sixth in 10.12 seconds (0.0m/s) as Emmanuel Eseme of Cameroon won in a national-record 9.89 seconds, ahead of Australia’s Lachlan Kennedy, who ran a personal-best 9.94 seconds.

Eseme returned with another national record and a Commonwealth Games record 9.83 seconds (1.3m/s) to win the gold. Kennedy was second with an Area Record 9.85 seconds, while Nigeria’s Kayinsola Ajayi was third in 9.90 seconds.

The last Jamaican to win the men’s 100m was Kemar Bailey-Cole in 2014, while Nigel Ellis was a finalist in 2018.

Nayoka Clunis came up short in the women’s hammer throw final with three fouls after throwing 64.83m in the qualifying round a day earlier.

The NACAC Senior Championships silver medallist has a personal best and national record of 72.03m, set earlier this year, which is the fifth-best mark in the Commonwealth this year.

Zandrion Barnes ran a season’s best 45.13 seconds to lead the semi-final qualifiers in the men’s 400m at the Commonwealth Games at Scotstoun Stadium in Glasgow, Scotland, on Tuesday.

Barnes is one of two Jamaican men who won their first-round heats, including Antonio Watson, as all the Jamaicans in action booked semi-final spots for Thursday.

Former world champion Watson was in total control in his first-round race, running 46.36 seconds, with Delano Kennedy also advancing after placing second in his heat in 45.82 seconds.

Both Jamaicans in the women’s 400m also advanced, with Shana Kaye Anderson placing second in her race in 52.71 seconds and Leah Anderson third in 52.74 seconds.

National men’s 800m record holder Navasky Anderson also made progress after placing third in his first-round heat in 1:48.12.

Today, Tajay Gayle and Jordan Turner are down to contest the men’s long jump, while Lloydricia Cameron will carry the Jamaican flag in the women’s shot put.

Christopher Taylor, Roshawn Clarke and Jevaughn Powell will start their quest for medals in the men’s 200m, with Alana Reid and Lavanya Williams lining up in the women’s heats.

Assinie Wilson will contest the men’s 400m hurdles, while Sanique Walker and Shiann Salmon are in the women’s event. Kelly Ann Beckford and Adelle Tracey will compete in the women’s 800m semi-finals.

World.title: Investor residency plan edges forward
World.content:
Jamaica is moving closer to introducing economic residency for qualifying foreign investors, but the required investment, job-creation targets, and eligible assets remain undisclosed.

JAMAICA’S long-delayed plan to grant residency to qualifying foreign investors has moved closer to Parliament, more than four years after its formal implementation target and more than a decade after Jamaica Promotions Corporation (Jampro) recorded the proposal.



But the Government still has not disclosed how many applicants would have to invest, how many jobs they would have to create or which investments would qualify.

The Government’s latest annual report on Form 18-K, filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission, said draft amendments to the Immigration Restriction (Commonwealth Citizens) Act and the Aliens Act are being vetted for submission to the legislation committee.

The wording indicates progress but does not say that the committee has received the Bills or that they have been approved for tabling in Parliament.

“The proposals include the introduction of an economic residency programme which is intended to support a more enabling environment for potential investors who do not present a national security threat to Jamaica,” the report said.

It is the clearest sign of movement since the SEC filings began referring to the draft amendments in 2023. The programme nevertheless remains at a pre-parliamentary stage, with no implementation date announced.

Then Industry, Investment and Commerce Minister Audley Shaw disclosed in May 2021 that Cabinet had approved the proposal for further consultation and determination of the conditions under which permanent residency — not citizenship — would be granted.

But the proposal predates that decision. Jampro’s 2013/14 annual report described the Jamaica Economic Residency Programme as a proposed immigration-residency category for foreign investors undertaking projects involving a predefined amount of capital. It said Jampro and the Passport, Immigration and Citizenship Agency (PICA) had agreed that the programme was feasible.

The National Investment Policy, approved by Cabinet on July 18, 2022, subsequently called for a strategic economic residence programme to encourage direct investment and job creation based on specified criteria, with PICA and Jampro responsible for implementation.

The policy targeted the first quarter of fiscal year 2022/23, covering April to June 2022. That deadline had already passed when Cabinet approved the policy and is now more than four years overdue.

It compared the proposed programme with business-migration arrangements then operating in the United States and Australia, citing investments of US$1.8 million and A$1.5 million, or approximately US$1.03 million at the time. Those were international examples, not proposed Jamaican thresholds.

Successive Government filings show that the legislation remained at roughly the same stage for three years. The 2023 report said the bills were being finalised for submission to Cabinet. The 2024 report said they had been further revised and were being finalised for Cabinet approval. The 2025 report repeated that position.

The latest wording suggests movement beyond the previously stated Cabinet-preparation stage, but several features that will determine the programme’s value and credibility remain unknown.

The Government has not disclosed the minimum investment, the jobs applicants would have to create, how long the investment and jobs must be maintained or whether qualifying investments would be restricted to selected industries.

Nor has it said whether applicants could qualify through new or existing businesses, real estate, Government securities, approved development projects or investment funds. Processing fees, physical-presence requirements, provisions for dependants, renewal conditions and grounds for revoking residency also remain undisclosed.

In November 2022, then Jampro Vice-President Shullette Cox said the programme would be based on “firm, foreign direct investments that are underpinned by job creation”.

The intended applicants could include Diaspora members without Jamaican citizenship. Former State Minister for Industry, Investment and Commerce Dr Norman Dunn said in June 2022 that the programme could facilitate second- and third-generation Jamaicans ready to invest.

Permanent residency allows a foreign national to live and work in Jamaica without restrictions on the length of stay or the need for a work permit. It does not provide the same constitutional rights as citizenship or automatically give the holder a Jamaican passport.

PICA’s published permanent-residence categories cover employment, retirement, marriage and dependency, but not investment. Applicants are interviewed and must provide financial records, police certificates, medical documents and evidence of assets. Business owners must also submit company registration and tax-compliance documents, income tax returns, and audited financial statements.

Economic residency would not itself confer citizenship. Like any other qualifying non-national, a holder could later apply for naturalisation. PICA says applicants must have lived in Jamaica for at least five years in total, including the 12 months immediately before applying, and be of good character.

Because Jamaica is proposing residency rather than citizenship, the economic return would depend largely on the investment and employment attached to each approval, not the sale of a passport.

The programme could give investors greater certainty about living in Jamaica while managing local operations, remove the need for repeated work-permit and immigration applications and make the country more attractive to Diaspora investors and foreign business owners.

But its value will depend on how the Government defines an eligible investment and verifies that promised jobs and capital are maintained. Directing investors towards operating businesses and productive projects could generate employment, exports and tax revenue. Allowing passive asset purchases to qualify could produce less direct economic activity.

The legislation must also establish what happens if an investor withdraws the money, sells the qualifying asset or fails to create or maintain the promised jobs.

Residency-by-investment programmes also require strong background checks. A 2023 report by the Financial Action Task Force and the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development said the programmes can attract foreign direct investment but may also be abused to launder criminal proceeds, evade justice or misrepresent tax residence. It recommended several layers of due diligence rather than reliance on a single background check.

Jamaica’s latest filing says the programme is intended only for investors who do not present a national security threat. It does not identify which agencies would conduct the checks, how applicants’ source of wealth would be verified or whether successful applicants would be monitored after receiving residency.

The bills form part of wider amendments intended to modernise Jamaica’s immigration laws, strengthen anti-terrorism measures and increase PICA’s use of technology.

The next public test will be whether they reach the legislation committee and are subsequently approved for tabling. Until the legislation and accompanying rules are published, investors will not know the price of admission and Jamaicans will not know what economic return the country expects in exchange for residency.

World.title: Conflict shift
World.content:
Superintendent Mark Harris, commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division, speaks about the division’s changing crime landscape during an episode of the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s Force4Good podcast. x

THE St Andrew Central Police Division, which is the commercial heartbeat of the Corporate Area, where thousands of Jamaicans live and work daily, is confronting a changing crime landscape, with police saying interpersonal and domestic conflicts have become a greater concern than organised gang violence.

Commanding officer for the St Andrew Central Police Division Superintendent Mark Harris said the division has largely brought organised gang activity under control, but is now grappling with murders arising from personal disputes, many of which occur without warning and in communities not traditionally associated with violent crime. He said this shift has presented a more complex policing challenge because, unlike gang conflicts, interpersonal disputes are far less predictable.

Speaking on the Jamaica Constabulary Force’s (JCF) Force4Good podcast, Harris said the division recorded the largest reduction in murders across the Jamaica Constabulary Force last year and even went an entire month without a murder this February. However, he noted that while gang-related killings have declined significantly, police are increasingly being challenged by crimes rooted in personal and domestic disputes.

“Last year, I had gang issues, [but] this year, we don’t have a gang issue, we have criminals committing crimes, but it’s not associated with gangs, like 2024 and part of 2025, and believe it or not, gang conflict is easier to police than the interpersonal and the domestic issues,” he noted.

The St Andrew Central Police Division encompasses some of Jamaica’s busiest commercial, educational and transport hubs, including Half-Way-Tree, New Kingston, Cross Roads and Papine. It is also responsible for policing major national events, entertainment activities and sporting fixtures that are often held at the National Stadium, making it one of the JCF’s most demanding divisions.

The division also includes communities such as August Town and Nannyville, both of which have experienced persistent gang activity and periodic security operations over the years. August Town was placed under a Zone of Special Operations in 2020 following years of deadly gang violence, while Nannyville has repeatedly featured in anti-gang and anti-gun operations as police sought to dismantle organised criminal networks operating across Kingston and St Andrew.

Despite that history, Harris said the division’s greatest challenge is no longer organised gangs but the rise in deadly interpersonal conflicts.

“We know where the gangs are and where they operate and who they’re in conflict with, and we put police right there…but for the interpersonal things, even in Jack’s Hill we have murders [and] that is not normally a place where we have murders… and these are interpersonal, rather than gang conflict,” he explained.

He said the division is relying not only on intelligence-led operations but also stronger community partnerships to prevent personal disputes from escalating into violence.

“We go out there and do the hard policing, we still have our community engagement. We had to do those meetings at the Transport Centre to speak to students and parents and stakeholders,” Harris noted.

Meanwhile, Area Four Commander Assistant Commissioner of Police Michael Phipps said St Andrew Central remains critical to crime management across Kingston and St Andrew because of its concentration of commercial activity, major institutions and daily commuter traffic.

He noted that the division has also experienced a significant number of fatal attacks involving weapons other than firearms, reflecting the growing challenge posed by interpersonal violence.

“I can tell you here and now that St Andrew Central has had a very high number of murders resulting from the use of knives and other blunt-force trauma injuries that have resulted in death. So we see St Andrew Central as one of the most important divisions if we are to maintain control of crime across Area Four,” Phipps said.

Die aktuellen Umfragehochs der Partei seien einzig der eklatanten Schwäche der etablierten Parteien geschuldet. German-based workers in administrative and research and development roles will be offered a severance program.

German car manufacturer BMW is cutting thousands of jobs by the end of 2027 through a voluntary redundancy program, a corporate spokesperson told POLITICO.

The program targets German-based workers in administrative and research and development roles, the spokesperson said.

World.title: Russia charges Telegram founder Durov with facilitating terrorism
World.content:
Pavel Durov watches the bantamweight bout at UFC 321 in Abu Dhabi on Oct. 25, 2025. | Giuseppe Cacace/AFP via Getty Images

Moscow claims the platform allows Ukrainian intelligence services to recruit spies and support terrorist activities.

Russia charged Telegram co-founder and CEO Pavel Durov on Wednesday with facilitating terrorist activity and placed the Soviet-born Kremlin critic on an international wanted list.

The Federal Security Service (FSB) accused Durov’s messaging platform of supporting Ukrainian intelligence services. The agency claims a Telegram chatbot named “Daivinchik/Leo — acquaintances, communication and new friends” was used to recruit Russians “into sabotage and terrorist activities through deception and psychological manipulation.”

The FSB also accused Telegram of failing to remove numerous channels, chats and bots that it alleged were used by Ukrainian intelligence agencies and terrorist and extremist organizations to coordinate sabotage, terrorist attacks, mass killings and cyber fraud in Russia.
