See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Health technology firm Philips has received an €186 million windfall after the United States Supreme Court ordered Donald Trump’s administration to refund illegally imposed tariffs.

The figures were included in the Amsterdam-based company’s latest quarterly report, which was published this week.

Trump imposed import tariffs on products from dozens of countries, as well as the European Union, in April last year.

But in February the Supreme Court upheld a judgment by a lower court that the president had wrongly used emergency powers to introduce the tariffs.

The US government was also ordered to refund and compensate companies that had paid the tariffs or whose business had been damaged as a result.

CEO Roy Jakobs said: “We started a legal case as soon as we could, which is why we are one of the first to get our money back.” Most of the repayments have already been made.

The extra income helped Philips increase its turnover by 4% year-on-year in the second quarter of 2026. It recorded a profit of €386 million, but declining orders in both China and the US meant its share price dived by 10% on Tuesday.

Philips was founded in 1891 as a lightbulb manufacturer in Eindhoven and grew into one of the world’s largest producers of consumer electronics in the 20th century. Since 2010 it has focused on producing healthcare equipment.

World.title: Former Polish PM Morawiecki forms parliamentary caucus  rival to PiS, deepening opposition split
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Former Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki says that 40 MPs and one senator aligned with him will form their own parliamentary group, deepening a split in the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party after a dispute over party direction and loyalty declarations. The move marks the most serious internal challenge in years to PiS, which ruled Poland from 2015 to 2023, and follows months of tensions between Morawiecki’s more moderate faction and party conservatives who have pushed the group in a hard-right direction. Once formally established, Morawiecki’s caucus would become the third-largest bloc in the Sejm, Poland’s lower house of parliament. Powstanie klub parlamentarny „Rozwój Plus”. Morawiecki zdecydował#PAPInformacjehttps://t.co/IftRdgpIPw — Polska Agencja Prasowa/Polish Press Agency (PAP) (@PAPinformacje) July 29, 2026 One of Morawiecki’s allies, Marcin Horała, told reporters that the creation of the caucus did not mean they were leaving PiS, but “simply setting up a parliamentary group so that we can get on with our work”. He noted, however, that PiS’s parliamentary group “has stopped treating us as its members”. Morawiecki, meanwhile, said that his group remained ready to cooperate with PiS as a “second lung” of the party’s broader political camp, but suggested that the current leadership was moving in a different direction. He said that parts of PiS’s messaging were increasingly influenced by “dissidents and schemers” as well as hardline factions, including Sovereign Poland (Suwerenna Polska), a nationalist group that was previously a junior coalition partner of PiS and often clashed with Morawiecki when he was prime minister. Reacting to Morawiecki’s announcement, party chairman Jarosław Kaczyński said the former prime minister had carried out a planned split of the party despite his efforts to reach a deal. “Until the end I made efforts to reach an agreement, unfortunately Mateusz Morawiecki clearly had his own political plan in mind, carried out on the basis of a split in PiS,” Kaczyński wrote on X. The announcement follows a dispute that began after Morawiecki launched his Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) association in April. The former prime minister insisted the association was intended to complement PiS with a pro-development agenda rather than rival it. However, critics within PiS viewed it as an attempt by Morawiecki to build an alternative power base that could eventually evolve into a separate party ahead of the 2027 parliamentary election. Seeking to end the standoff, the party ordered PiS lawmakers to resign from all outside political associations by last Thursday, or face “consequences” including “the loss of membership in PiS”. On Friday, Kaczyński said that “around 30 MPs” had failed to comply and had therefore effectively resigned from the party, adding that Tuesday’s meeting of the party’s political committee would simply confirm this fact. Poland's right-wing opposition PiS party is set to split after a more moderate faction of over 30 MPs loyal to deputy leader @MorawieckiM refused to sign a loyalty pledge demanded by leader @OficjalnyJK, who says that means they have effectively resigned https://t.co/TuqYpGI5ak — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 24, 2026 On Tuesday, the party announced that instead, the committee had referred the cases of 44 members, who either failed to submit the required declarations or submitted them on the wrong form, to the party’s disciplinary officer for individual review, delaying a final decision. “From a formal and legal perspective, Mr Mateusz Morawiecki has not yet been removed from the list of members,” PiS spokesman Rafał Bochenek said on Tuesday. PiS disciplinary officer Karol Karski told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) he would examine each case individually. “I am open to speaking with each of them so they can present their positions,” Karski said. “At this point, I can initiate proceedings against the individual in question, refer the case to a peer disciplinary tribunal with a motion for punishment – this could include a temporary suspension or expulsion from PiS.” PiS has for the last two decades been the dominant force on the Polish right, including periods leading governments in 2005-2007 and 2015-2023. However, since losing power at elections in 2023, when the party won 35% of the vote, the party has seen its average support in polls fall to around 23-24%, the lowest level in 14 years. Support for PiS has fallen to its lowest in 14 years, as the party grapples with internal division, the rise of far-right challengers, living in President Nawrocki's shadow, and the unpopularity in Poland of PiS ally Donald Trump, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/QRScBpEQQG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 2, 2026 Meanwhile, it has been challenged by the rise of the far right, where two parties, Confederation (Konfederacja) and Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), now together poll at a similar combined level of support to PiS. In response, Kaczyński in March named a hardline figure, Przemysław Czarnek, as PiS’s candidate for prime minister in next year’s elections. Czarnek was seen as someone who could appeal to far-right voters, while also potentially working with the far right if a coalition was needed after the elections. However, there has been no rise in support for PiS since Czarnek was named, prompting growing concern from more moderate figures within the party, led by Morawiecki. The national-conservative opposition PiS party has named its candidate to be prime minister if it wins next year’s parliamentary elections. Przemysław Czarnek is a hardline conservative who played a prominent role in PiS's campaign against "LGBT ideology" https://t.co/sSJLON00hW — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2026 They argue that PiS has wrongly disowned many of the successes of its time in office before 2023, and they fear that its rightward shift damages its chances of winning over more centrist voters. Adam Szłapka, the spokesman of the current more liberal government, said Braun was “the ultimate playmaker in this whole game”, who had helped push far-right rhetoric into the political mainstream. “The worst thing about this whole situation is that Poland’s largest opposition party has, in effect, started to adopt Grzegorz Braun’s agenda from A to Z,” Szłapka told broadcaster TVN24. World.title: Polish court finds regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriage registration unconstitutional
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s Constitutional Tribunal (TK) has ruled that a new regulation allowing the registration of foreign same-sex marriage certificates in Poland was partly unconstitutional, saying it went beyond technical administrative changes and conflicted with the constitution’s definition of marriage. The regulation, introduced by the digital affairs ministry after rulings by the Court of Justice of the European Union (CJEU) and Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), was due to take effect on 23 August. The government, which considers the court to be improperly constituted, says it will not implement the ruling. The government has issued a regulation allowing foreign same-sex marriages to be entered in the civil registry The decision comes in response to an EU court order and marks a major change in a country that does not allow same-sex unions under domestic law https://t.co/2an5mGtnHl — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 22, 2026 Polish law does not allow same-sex couples to marry or enter into civil unions, and a bill that would have granted such limited rights to unmarried couples was recently vetoed by the opposition-backed president. Until this year, same-sex couples who married abroad were also unable to register their marriage certificates in Poland. After the CJEU ruled that Poland must recognise such marriages, the digital affairs ministry changed civil status forms. Instead of separate fields for “man” and “woman”, the new templates use “man/woman”, allowing registry offices to record both opposite-sex and same-sex marriages. Lawmakers from the national-conservative opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, however, challenged the regulation, arguing that the digital affairs minister had exceeded his powers because the changes were not merely technical but affected the legal definition of marriage. The tribunal, which is widely seen as being under PiS’s influence, agreed. The tribunal said the new forms allowed relationships that do not match the constitution’s definition of marriage as a union between a man and a woman to be recorded as marriages. It said regulations can only implement existing laws and cannot change matters reserved for the constitution or parliament. The tribunal also said that registering a foreign marriage certificate cannot produce legal effects that conflict with the basic principles of Polish law. It added that changing the constitutional definition of marriage would require amendments to the constitution and related laws. Some legal experts argue that, while the constitution states that a “marriage, being a union of a man and a woman… shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland,” that phrasing does not rule out other legally recognised unions receiving state protection. Poland has begun recognising foreign same-sex marriages. But the legal consequences for such couples remain unclear, especially as Polish law does not allow any form of same-sex union We asked five experts for their view on what this will mean in practice https://t.co/h2KHmW8sMI — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Shortly after the ruling, government members said they would not comply with the tribunal’s decision and that the regulation would enter into force as planned. “The illegal Constitutional Tribunal is once again attempting to obstruct a state that is enforcing the law in force and the rulings of European courts,” digital affairs minister Krzysztof Gawkowski said. “The transcription of foreign same-sex marriage certificates is and will remain legal,” he said, adding that 184 same-sex couples had so far had their foreign marriage certificates transcribed. Katarzyna Kotula, the government official responsible for equality issues, said the TK ruling on the issue of transcriptions “has no legal force whatsoever”. Nielegalny Trybunał Konstytucyjny po raz kolejny próbuje zatrzymać państwo, które wykonuje obowiązujące prawo i wyroki europejskich sądów. Transkrypcja zagranicznych aktów małżeństw jednopłciowych jest i będzie legalna. Rozporządzenie, które przyjęliśmy porządkuje dokumenty i… — Krzysztof Gawkowski (@KGawkowski) July 28, 2026 The TK has been at the heart of the rule-of-law crisis that has developed in Poland over the last decade. In 2015, former PiS-aligned President Andrzej Duda refused to swear in three judges legally chosen by the Sejm. Shortly afterwards, PiS won parliamentary elections and nominated three replacements for those judges, who were sworn in by Duda. Those three judges and their successors have been deemed illegitimate in a succession of rulings by Polish and European courts. Due to their continued presence on the court, the current government, which replaced PiS in 2023, rejects the TK’s legitimacy and refuses to recognise its rulings. Fifteen months since the change of government, Poland's rule-of-law crisis continues – indeed, many Poles think the situation has got worse.@J_Jaraczewski explains the roots of the crisis, what its impact has been, and how it might be resolved https://t.co/7KOCURV3dU — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 17, 2025 Under both Święczkowski, a former member of the PiS government, and his predecessor Julia Przyłębska, a close personal associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński, the TK has been widely seen as issuing rulings aligned with the political interests of PiS. For a long time, the government refused to appoint new judges to the Constitutional Tribunal as the terms of the previous judges expired, with some vacancies remaining unfilled for over a year. In recent months, the government has resumed appointing new judges, but President Karol Nawrocki, an ally of PiS, is refusing to administer the oath of office to some of them. World.title: Residents oppose move to add Polish village to list of protected monuments
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A decision to designate a village as a protected monument has sparked fierce opposition from residents, who have vowed to “fight until the end” against measures they say will limit their ability to renovate and build on their properties. The village in question, Ostaszów in southwestern Poland’s Lower Silesia province, was established in 1936 by Nazi Germany as an agricultural settlement of around 42 farms. At the time, the region still belonged to Germany. The Lower Silesian Provincial Conservator of Monuments argues Ostaszów has “unique, homogeneous historical architecture” requiring state protection, but local officials say that the way the decision was made, despite opposition from residents, shows “the voice of local communities has no significance”. After World War Two, most of Lower Silesia, including the village, became part of Poland. The village’s architecture has remained largely unchanged, with its residential buildings connected to barns, forming unique cohesive farmstead units. Around 250 people live there. Earlier this year, the residents were told proceedings had begun to add the village to the register of protected monuments, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. The provincial conservator said on Friday it had reached a decision. “The unique, above-standard historical, scientific and artistic value of Ostaszów as a monument cannot be questioned,” it wrote in a statement. It noted that a study by a team working under the culture ministry had found that the village was the only preserved settlement of its kind in Lower Silesia. Residents and local officials said they planned to appeal against the decision, arguing it would create additional bureaucracy and interfere with property owners’ ability to decide on building and renovation work. “We have a years-long legal battle ahead of us, but we won’t give up. We will fight until the end. We believe that decisions about the 42 homes in Ostaszów should be made by their residents, not by harmful officials,” residents wrote in a statement quoted by the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “In a cardboard state, the voice of local communities has no significance – only orders and bans count. Our future is to be decided by a heartless official from [the Lower Silesian capital of] Wrocław who does not even have time to meet with the victims of his decisions,” said the village head, Sylwia Mazur. Wieś Ostaszów wpisana do rejestru zabytków. Mieszkańcy będą się odwoływaćhttps://t.co/ZxmH2lbHnb pic.twitter.com/cPdL73PXIH — Dzieje.pl (@dziejepl) July 26, 2026 The conservator noted, however, that until the appeals process is concluded, construction works cannot proceed. It added that it planned to cooperate with locals to “develop principles of renovation and investment procedures in accordance with the regulations on the protection of monuments”. It also urged residents not to spread “scandalous narratives” about the decision leading to an “open-air museum, the impossibility of renovation, and the blocking of investments”. It said other villages in Lower Silesia were subject to similar protections without hindering their development. Gazeta Wyborcza cited some residents saying that the launch of proceedings in January had already forced them to pause work on their properties. Others complained that the decision will increase renovation costs due to strict conservation requirements. The Opole Provincial Conservator of Monuments said that, as of 2021, some 86 villages across Poland had been added to the register of monuments because of their historic layouts. Poland has joined the European Union’s plan to build artificial intelligence (AI) gigafactories with a view to hosting one of the bloc’s new computing centres. Deputy digital affairs minister Dariusz Standerski said Poland had completed a key legal step by joining the joint procurement process. The move enables Poland to bid for one of seven AI gigafactory projects planned under the EU programme, potentially attracting investment of more than 10 billion zloty (€2.3 billion) while giving businesses, researchers and public institutions access to advanced AI computing capacity. “On behalf of the Republic of Poland, I have signed the Joint Procurement Agreement, which means that Poland joins the AI gigafactory initiative,” Standerski told daily Rzeczpospolita. Under the proposed model, AI gigafactories will be designed, financed, built and operated by private consortia selected through a European tender organised by the European High Performance Computing Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU). In the first procurement round, EuroHPC JU plans to select seven projects comprising four medium-scale facilities and three large-scale sites. Poland is bidding for a medium-scale project, which would initially provide computing capacity equivalent to at least 25,000 AI accelerators before expanding to at least 75,000. The EU and its member states will support the projects by committing to purchase computing services during the initial years of operation, providing demand certainty for investors. “Poland and the EU will each buy 17% of the power, and the remaining two thirds will be made commercially available by a private consortium; Poland will commit to purchasing its own pool for five years,” Standerski said. Standerski also told the newspaper that companies’ interest in the project is “enormous”. “This means that, from the very first day the gigafactory is operational, part of its computing capacity will already have been sold,” he added. Poland’s government will spend 1.9 billion zloty (€437 million) equipping the majority of schools with so-called AI labs before the start of the next school year. The money will fund laptops, AI software and interactive displays, among other equipment https://t.co/outNQIGCv0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 19, 2026 Standerski said the government would not designate a site for the facility, with the final location to be determined by the winning consortium through the European procurement process. He said the government had previously identified 10 locations across Poland capable of hosting. Last week, the deputy minister also said Poland was preparing to sign an agreement with the Czech government, under which cooperation would involve mutual purchases of computing capacity between the two countries. He also said Lithuania had committed to a one-sided arrangement to buy computing power from a Polish AI gigafactory. Częstochowa will become the first city in Poland to use the Polish Large Language Model to support the use of AI in providing municipal services. It will help write letters, analyse inquiries from residents, and summarise long documents https://t.co/SLrmVg9VBz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 Earlier this month, Poland’s government approved a resolution enabling the country to participate in the European AI Gigafactory programme, committing more than 400 million zloty towards what the government says would be the largest computing centre in the country’s history. The government also pledged to purchase AI services worth €100 million between 2028 and 2033, with a matching contribution from the European Union. According to the government’s timetable, the European procurement process is expected to begin later this year. World.title: Poland asks US to extradite former minister Ziobro over criminal charges
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has formally asked the United States to detain and extradite former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on multiple criminal charges. Ziobro, a senior figure in the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government, is accused of offences including leading an organised criminal group and abuse of office. Having previously fled Poland to Hungary, where Viktor Orbán’s government, an ally of PiS, granted him asylum, Ziobro arrived in the United States in May following a change of government in Budapest. Wniosek o ekstradycję podejrzanego Zbigniewa Ziobro: ⬇️https://t.co/YC7T3RrIEc — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) July 27, 2026 Ziobro served as justice minister in the PiS government from 2015 to 2023. Last year, prosecutors announced that they wanted to charge him with 26 crimes, including leading a criminal group and approving the unlawful purchase of Pegasus spyware. In October, parliament approved the lifting of Ziobro’s immunity from prosecution. By then, however, he had already travelled to Hungary, and in December he was granted political asylum by the Hungarian government. In February this year, Warsaw’s district court approved a request from prosecutors to place Ziobro in pretrial detention. That decision was needed in order for the authorities to issue domestic and European arrest warrants against the suspect. However, Ziobro’s lawyers appealed against the decision. While that appeal was waiting to be heard, Orbán lost power in Hungary and, as his successor Péter Magyar was being sworn in, Ziobro left the country and flew to the United States. In July, a Warsaw court rejected Ziobro’s appeal, opening the way for Poland to seek the politician’s extradition from the US. Ziobro has no valid travel documents after Poland cancelled his passports and Budapest revoked his refugee status. The extradition request covers 19 of the 26 offences listed in the indictment, the prosecutors said. The documents submitted include the final order for Ziobro’s detention, the indictment, a wanted notice and evidence supporting the case. The request will now be sent through diplomatic channels to the US Department of Justice, where it will be assessed to determine whether it meets the formal requirements of the Polish-US extradition treaty, prosecutor Anna Adamiak said. If the request satisfies those requirements, it will be referred to a US federal court, where a judge will decide on the legal admissibility of Ziobro’s extradition to Poland. A court has upheld a request by prosecutors to bring former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro, who is wanted on 26 criminal charges, into detention. The decision paves the way for Poland to request Ziobro's extradition from the US, where he fled in May https://t.co/vIPRjvgQnA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 2, 2026 Asked how long the extradition process could take, Adamiak said previous cases suggested proceedings could last anywhere from a few months to several years, depending on their nature and complexity. Adamiak noted, however, that the extradition proceedings would not determine Ziobro’s guilt. “Its role is merely to assess whether the surrender of that person in extradition proceedings is legally permissible in light of treaty regulations and domestic law,” she told reporters, quoted by online news service Wirtualna Polska. “However, the decision on surrender is, of course, a decision made by the state, so other circumstances may also play a role,” she added. PiS, Poland’s largest opposition party, enjoys close ties with US President Donald Trump’s administration. Poland's conservative opposition enthusiastically welcomed Trump's return to the White House, but it is becoming increasingly difficult for them to maintain a tough anti-Russian line while also showing allegiance to the US president, writes @danieltilles1 https://t.co/4PW6H9nMEF — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) March 7, 2025 Asked at a news conference about the likelihood of Ziobro’s extradition and when it might take place, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said the question should be directed at “the other Donald”, reported the Polish Press Agency (PAP). “We will, in accordance with the law, seek all available means to ensure that these politicians, against whom such serious charges have been brought, appear before a Polish court sooner or later,” he added. “We are waiting for positive signals from Washington. Will they come? I don’t know.” Ziobro has long denied all accusations, saying the case against him is an act of “political revenge” by Tusk’s government. Commenting on the extradition request on the conservative television channel Republika, Ziobro said he was pleased that the case would be heard “in the United States, on American soil, and before an American court”. He claimed that the proceedings would show that the Polish government “regularly breaks the law, ignores procedures, rejects democratic principles, has taken control of the prosecutor’s office unlawfully, and is trying to destroy the opposition”. World.title: UNESCO adds Poland’s modernist port city of Gdynia to World Heritage List
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. UNESCO has added the modernist city centre of the Polish port city of Gdynia to its World Heritage List, recognising its interwar urban planning and architecture. The designation, approved during the World Heritage Committee’s 48th session in Busan, South Korea, is Poland’s 18th World Heritage site and comes as Gdynia marks the centenary of gaining city rights. In its justification, UNESCO referred to “an urban organism that harnesses a building-block-based planning approach to develop a characteristic, compact complex of modernist architecture, with robust individual architectural expressions”. Gdynia’s city centre “illustrates a critical break with historicism in the progression of turning the village of Gdynia into a new major sea gateway of the first Polish Republic between the First and Second World Wars”, it added. Granted city status in 1926, Gdynia was rapidly developed by the newly independent Polish state from a small fishing village into a major Baltic seaport, growing to more than 100,000 residents in under 20 years and providing Poland with a modern maritime gateway. It is now Poland’s 13th largest city by population, with just under 210,000 residents, and the third largest by area when including its maritime territory. Nowy tydzień zaczynamy od dobrych wieści! Komitet Światowego Dziedzictwa UNESCO oficjalnie uznał modernistyczne centrum Gdyni za dobro o wyjątkowym znaczeniu dla całego świata. Nie ma lepszego momentu niż 100-lecie Gdyni na to wyjątkowe wyróżnienie!https://t.co/L3WZZCJCAz — Gdynia (@MiastoGdynia) July 27, 2026 Oktawia Gorzeńska, Gdynia’s deputy mayor, who represented the city in Busan, celebrated the decision of the committee as “a wonderful gift for our anniversary and a tribute to the vision and determination of the people who created one of Europe’s great modernist cities”. The city’s mayor, Aleksandra Kosiorek, added that the decision “confirms that the vision which launched the history of modern Gdynia over a century ago has retained its power and universal significance.” Gdynia’s central district of Śródmieście was built largely between 1926 and 1939. Its rapid development at the time drew international attention, with a National Geographic reporter writing that “Poland dreams of building her New York”. Unlike Warsaw and nearby Gdańsk, it escaped extensive destruction during World War Two, preserving much of its original street layout and interwar architecture. According to the city authorities, UNESCO experts have recognised the Gdynia’s centre as one of the world’s most outstanding examples of early modernism in urban planning. The nomination also highlighted Gdynia’s distinctive model of modernist urban planning, setting it apart from contemporaneous developments such as Germany’s Bauhaus, Berlin’s housing estates, Kaunas in Lithuania and Tel Aviv. Gdynia’s modernist architecture is characterised by white façades and maritime-inspired details, including round windows and building forms resembling ship hulls. Gdańsk in Poland has been named a global City of Literature by @UNESCO. It is now one of only 63 such cities in the world, and the third in Poland to obtain the distinction https://t.co/QdMxlT65V4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 3, 2025 Notable examples include the so-called “bank building”, a modernist tenement block, and the Museum of Emigration, housed in the former Maritime Station, which from the 1930s until 1979 was a transit building from which thousands of Polish emigrants left for their new homelands. According to the city, the road to recognition took over 20 years, beginning in 2007, when the historic urban layout was entered into the regional register of monuments. It was designated a Monument of History in 2015, and Poland submitted the site to UNESCO’s Tentative List in 2019. Two sites in Poland were included in the inaugural World Heritage List in 1978: the Historic Centre of Kraków and the nearby Wieliczka and Bochnia Royal Salt Mines. Gdynia’s inscription is the 18th for Poland overall and the first for a Polish modernist urban complex. The most recent Polish additions before Gdynia were the Krzemionki Prehistoric Striped Flint Mining Region in 2019 and, in 2021, the beech forests in the Bieszczady Mountains. World.title: Polish president obstructs windfall tax on fuel firms’ excess profits, prompting government criticism
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Prime Minister Donald Tusk has condemned opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki’s “shocking decision” not to sign into law the government’s planned windfall tax on excess profits by fuel companies amid a sharp surge in fuel prices caused by the war in Iran. While Nawrocki did not veto the bill, he exercised his right to refuse to sign it and instead send it to the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) for assessment, a process that can take years. The president argued that the retroactive nature of the tax “raises serious constitutional concerns”. Nowy podatek nie obniża cen paliwa. Ma przede wszystkim dostarczyć pieniędzy do budżetu. Nie mogę zaakceptować sytuacji, w której próbę łatania finansów państwa przedstawia się obywatelom jako ochronę ich interesów, podczas gdy skutkiem będzie kolejna fala podwyżek – Prezydent… pic.twitter.com/LqI7Cojdrr — Kancelaria Prezydenta RP (@prezydentpl) July 24, 2026 In mid-June, the government approved a 60% tax on excess profits from liquid fuel sales, calculated as the amount that would have been generated using a company’s average 2025 fuel sales margin, increased by 20%. The measure was expected to raise around 4 billion zloty (€927 million). When announcing the plans, the finance ministry said the levy was justified by this year’s “exceptional economic and geopolitical conditions that have led to above-average financial results in a specific segment of the fuel sector, not resulting from improved operational efficiency…but from a supply shock”. The tax was intended to offset the roughly 4.7 billion zloty the government spent on keeping fuel prices lower for consumers amid the crisis in the Middle East by, among others, cutting VAT and introducing a maximum daily price. The bill was approved by parliament on 3 July. It received support from Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, but was opposed by the right-wing and far-right opposition. According to a regulatory impact assessment, state energy giant Orlen is expected to account for about 60% of the tax base for the windfall tax, with the remaining 40% generated by other market participants. Poland’s government has approved a windfall tax on fuel companies' excess profits after the surge in energy prices due to the war in Iran. It expects the measure, which still requires parliamentary and presidential approval, to raise 4bn zloty (€940m) https://t.co/DpXa8VJDjf — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 17, 2026 The legislation then passed to Nawrocki, who has vetoed a record number of bills since becoming president last year. However, this time he instead exercised his right to refer the bill to the TK without either signing or vetoing it. In a speech announcing his decision on Friday, Nawrocki said that the proposed measures “raise serious constitutional concerns”. In particular, he criticised the fact that tax would be retroactive: it would go into force in August but would apply to revenue earned from the beginning of March. “In a democratic state governed by the rule of law, citizens and businesses must know what regulations apply at the time decisions are made,” said Nawrocki. “The state cannot change the rules a few months later and send a bill for actions taken in accordance with applicable law.” The president also argued that, ultimately, the costs of the tax would be passed on to consumers, who have already been paying much higher fuel costs since the government’s protective measures expired at the end of June. “Unfortunately, it appears that the government first lowered fuel prices for propaganda purposes, and now has decided to impose a hefty bill on Poles,” declared Nawrocki. Once a bill is sent to the TK for assessment, there is generally no time limit on how long the tribunal can take to consider it. In practice, this means that some cases can can remain unresolved for years. If the TK does find a bill to be constitutional, the president must sign it into law. Currently, a majority of judges on the TK, including its chief justice, were appointed by and are regarded as aligned with the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party that ruled Poland until 2023 and which supported Nawrocki’s presidential candidacy last year. The chief justice of the constitutional court has refused to accept four new judges appointed by parliament but whom the opposition-aligned president has refused to swear in. The decision deepens an unprecedented standoff over Poland's top court https://t.co/B02DKA3uBL — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 9, 2026 Nawrocki’s decision not to approve the windfall tax was condemned by government figures, including finance minister Andrzej Domański, who accused the president of “once again striking against Poland’s public finances”. In December, Nawrocki vetoed an increased tax on alcoholic and sweet drinks. “Instead of standing on the side of Poles, he sided with fuel corporations reaping huge profits from the current situation on the fuel market,” wrote Domański on social media. Tusk, meanwhile, wrote that the president had “blocked a bill that would have allowed taxing the gigantic profits of fuel conglomerates, making it possible to fund cheaper fuel at our stations”. He told consumers to “remember this [when you are] at the fuel pumps”. In response, the head of Nawrocki’s cabinet, Paweł Szefernaker, called Tusk an “economic dilettante” for thinking that imposing a tax would somehow lower costs rather than cause prices to rise. He instead called on the government to again lower VAT and excise duty on fuels. Od dawna wiadomo, że obecny premier jest gospodarczym dyletantem. Teraz próbuje przekonać Polaków, że nałożenie nowego podatku na paliwa sprawi, iż ceny na stacjach spadną. Zamiast nakładać kolejne podatki, proszę obniżyć VAT i akcyzę, tak jak robił to rząd Prawa i… https://t.co/3xvav6Dieu — Paweł Szefernaker 🇵🇱 (@szefernaker) July 25, 2026 The dispute over the tax comes as Poland faces an increasingly difficult fiscal situation. It had the second-largest budget deficit in the European Union last year, at 7.3% of GDP. That was far higher than the 5.5% the Polish government had pledged in 2024 when it was placed under the EU’s excessive deficit procedure. Data released last week by Eurostat showed that, in the first quarter of 2026, Poland had the EU’s third-largest annual increase in debt-to-GDP ratio, at 4.5 percentage points. In March, credit rating agency Fitch, which last year switched Poland’s credit outlook to negative, warned that the “political gridlock” between the president and the government will continue to hinder policymaking, including tackling “large fiscal deficits and rapidly rising debt”. Poland’s public debt has passed 60% of GDP for the first time, thereby exceeding the limit enshrined in EU law. The country is already under the EU's excessive deficit procedure, requiring it to take steps to bring public finances under greater control https://t.co/LNJ0YrP2Ge — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2026 Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland identifies remains of legendary anti-communist resistance fighter
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s state Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) has identified the remains of Mieczysław Dziemieszkiewicz (pictured above on the right), a prominent figure in the underground resistance that fought against the Soviet-installed communist authorities in the years after World War Two. Dziemieszkiewicz, who was killed by the communist security services in 1951 and dumped in an unmarked mass grave, was identified through a combination of historical detective work and genetic testing, including exhuming the remains of his deceased mother and sister to obtain DNA samples. “Once again, we can say that the communist authorities did not win. Heroes prevail,” declared Krzysztof Szwagrzyk, deputy head of the IPN. “Even in the most difficult situations, we must seek the truth, find those of whom no trace was supposed to remain, and restore their names.” While World War Two officially came to an end in 1945, tens of thousands of Poles, known as the “cursed soldiers” (żolnierze wyklęci), continued to fight against the Soviets and the communist regime they installed in Poland. While most had laid down arms by 1947, some continued fighting well beyond then, including Dziemieszkiewicz, who operated under the nom de guerre “Rój” (meaning “swarm”). Dziemieszkiewicz, who was 20 years old when the war ended, came from a family that had been part of Poland’s wartime resistance. His anti-communist views were hardened when his elder brother, Roman, was killed by Red Army soldiers in 1945. After being conscripted that year into the Soviet-backed Polish People’s Army, Dziemieszkiewicz defected and joined the underground resistance forces, where he rose to command a unit tasked with eliminating regime officials and members of the communist Polish Workers Party (PPR). Dziemieszkiewicz’s group killed around two dozen members of the communist security services and more than 20 informants, according to the IPN. In 1950, the communist authorities intensified efforts to dismantle Dziemieszkiewicz’s unit, using threats and blackmail to recruit hundreds of agents and informants in an effort to locate the resistance fighters. Eventually, one such informant gave up Dziemieszkiewicz’s location in exchange for a promise to release her parents from captivity. Dziemieszkiewicz found himself surrounded by several hundred soldiers and was killed while trying to escape. After his body had been identified by his family, Dziemieszkiewicz was buried in a section of Powązki Cemetery in Warsaw where the remains of those killed by the communist security services were placed en masse in unmarked graves. Exhumations by the IPN, which was established after the fall of communism to investigate communist and Nazi crimes in Poland, have located over 200 complete bodies at that site as well as several thousand bone fragments. During that work, one set of remains was found buried with an eagle symbol and remnants of a black cloth. IPN researchers realised that the item was similar to a beret that appeared in posthumous photographs of Dziemieszkiewicz’s body taken by the communist security services. That prompted them to carry out genetic testing on the remains and compare them to samples taken from Dziemieszkiewicz’s mother and sister, who were buried in a cemetery in the town of Maków Mazowiecki. “We have found ‘Rój’, commander of one of the longest-fighting units of the independence underground,” declared the IPN on Friday, announcing the confirmation of his identity. They described Dziemieszkiewicz as “legend in life and a symbol of the fight against communist oppression”. The identification was announced today during a press conference at @PrzystanekH. The identification is the result of many years of work carried out by the IPN. It was preceded by extensive archival and investigative research, the analysis of forensic evidence, archaeological… https://t.co/Rcf4wemJFc pic.twitter.com/XgMUAgSQc6 — Institute of National Remembrance (@ipngovpl_eng) July 24, 2026 At a conference announcing the findings, the IPN noted that Dziemieszkiewicz’s remains had been located right next to those of another prominent anti-communist resistance fighter, Zygmunt Szendzielarz, who fought under the nom de guerre “Łupaszko”. “It is an incredible situation that two great and distinguished soldiers of the Polish underground lie next to each other in this part of the Powązki Cemetery,” said Szwagrzyk. However, Szendzielarz, who was executed by the communist authorities in 1951, has a contested legacy, given evidence that his unit was involved in the massacre of dozens of Lithuanian civilians. Some other “cursed soldiers” have faced similar accusations of war crimes. While it was often IPN historians who uncovered evidence of such actions, the institution has more recently begun to honour those figures, particularly under the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice government between 2015 and 2023. Opposition MPs walked out of parliament yesterday as the chamber commemorated an underground officer who fought against Nazi-German occupation and the imposition of communism in Poland, but has also been accused of a war crime against civilians https://t.co/MIY7krOxTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 9, 2022 Dziemieszkiewicz himself, however, like most of the cursed soldiers, has not faced such accusations. In 2007, President Lech Kaczyński posthumously awarded Dziemieszkiewicz the Commander’s Cross with Star of the Order of Polonia Restituta, one of Poland’s highest honours. In 2020, his image was featured on a commemorative silver coin issued by the National Bank of Poland. Through a combination of brutal repression and offering amnesties, the communist authorities managed to end most resistance efforts by 1947. However, the last “cursed soldier” to die in combat, Józef Franczak, was killed in 1963, 18 years after the end of the war. World.title: Hundreds of Czech Castles and Chateaus to Offer Free Entry on Two Special Days
World.content:
Visitors will be able to explore more than 100 state-managed castles, chateaus, monasteries, and other historic landmarks across Czechia free of charge on August 30 and September 27.

The initiative follows a spring pilot program that granted free admission to selected state museums and galleries. According to the Ministry, strong public interest in that campaign encouraged officials to extend the concept to historic monuments managed by the National Heritage Institute (NPÚ).

The free admission will apply to the standard sightseeing route at each participating site, along with selected additional visitor circuits where available.



Tours will operate under normal conditions, meaning visitor numbers will remain limited and capacity restrictions will continue to apply.

The National Heritage Institute is expected to publish a complete list of participating sites, opening hours, reservation requirements, and visitor information on its website in the coming days.

The latest initiative builds on an earlier trial introduced this spring.

Between April and June, visitors were granted free entry on selected Sundays to five of the country’s largest state museums: the National Museum in Prague, the Moravian Museum in Brno, the Silesian Museum in Opava, the National Technical Museum in Prague, and the Technical Museum in Brno.

According to the Ministry of Culture, attendance at those museums nearly doubled during the pilot period, with the Silesian Museum recording the largest increase in visitor numbers. Selected state galleries also participated in the program earlier this year while officials assessed the financial impact of waiving admission fees.

The ministry has said one of its long-term objectives is to help restore visitor numbers at cultural institutions to levels seen before the COVID-19 pandemic.

World.title: On this Day, in 1419: the First Defenestration of Prague
World.content:
On July 30, 1419, a Hussite procession headed by the priest Jan Želivský attacked the New Town Hall in Prague and threw the king’s representatives from the windows into the street in what came to be known as the First Defenestration of Prague.

Jan Hus spoke out against the pope for selling indulgences in Bohemia to raise money, which did not sit well with King Wenceslaus IV of Bohemia, who had received a share from indulgence sales. Without the King’s support, Jan Hus was eventually excommunicated and fled to southern Bohemia, where he stayed in exile for two years.

When the Council of Constance assembled in 1415, Jan Hus was asked to be there and present his views. But upon arrival, the Czech reformer was arrested and, refusing to recant his views, was eventually burned at the stake for heresy. Unrest in Bohemia began soon after as Hussite preachers urged their congregations to take up arms against the Catholic rulers.



The First Defenestration of Prague

People shouted over each other to break down the gates. Jan Želivský kept encouraging the invaders, saying, “Do not be afraid, children of God!

Under the onslaught of the beams brought from the enemy building, the gates burst open and everyone rushed up the staircase of the New Town Hall. At the last moment, the councillors block the door of the meeting hall with a bench, but it is of no use to them.

This is how the Hussite Revolution began on 30 July 1419, according to Jan Bauer, who wrote the book The Revolutionary Events of Czech History. “In a short time, the conseilers and the purkmister Jan Podivínský were caught and thrown out of the windows on set spears and barrels. Those who survived the fall were brutally conquered on the spot,” Bauer describes the events of the time.

The historian Petr Čornej described the events in Prague’s New Town as a carefully prepared coup. “The fact that the victims were left with their valuables, which they had with them at the time, testifies to the preparedness and perfect direction of the coup,” Čornej wrote.

Not even a shadow of suspicion of bad intentions was allowed to cling to the violent deaths of the enemies of the Hussite interpretation of the word of divine law.

But what radicalized the Czech public enough to take up arms and stand under the banner of the chalice emblem four years after the burning of Jan Hus in Constance? “After all, four years is a long time and the initial bitterness and anger must have worn off to some extent,” Bauer writes in his book.

In Bohemia at that time, there was a de facto disintegration of royal power. King Wenceslas IV, already completely overcome by alcoholism, resigned himself to ruling the country and only by occasional tantrums did he show that he was still the monarch.

“The tired, disgusted king did not seem to notice what was happening in his country at that time. All he wanted was undisturbed peace and a permanent residence in his favourite castles and the forests that surrounded them,” wrote historian Jiří Spěváček.

The defenestration of the anti-Hussite constables in Prague’s New Town simply returned the whole of Prague to Hussite hands and gave the king to understand that the Hussites would not retreat. The subsequent early demise of Wenceslas IV was the final straw that pulled down the revolutionary avalanche.

The events of 1414 to 1419 and the fact that Hussite politicians made the accession of Sigismund of Luxembourg to the Czech throne conditional on respect for the principles of the immediate reasons for the outbreak of the Hussite revolution lay in the political and ecclesiastical-religious spheres.

World.title: Czech Company Enters Fortune Global 500 for the First Time
World.content:
A Czech company has entered the Fortune Global 500 ranking for the first time in history.

Energy and industrial group EP Group (EPG), controlled by Czech businessman Daniel Křetínský, placed 179th in the latest edition of the prestigious list of the world’s largest companies by revenue.

The ranking, published annually by the U.S. business magazine Fortune, evaluates companies based on their total sales. EP Group reported revenues of $75.387 billion, equivalent to around CZK 1.6 trillion.

To put the figure into perspective, the Czech state budget expects total revenues of CZK 2.118 trillion this year.



EP Group’s portfolio includes stakes in major companies across Europe, including British postal operator Royal Mail, Slovak energy producer Slovenské elektrárne, German retail chain Metro and French energy giant TotalEnergies.

With its debut in the ranking, EP Group has also placed Prague among the headquarters of the world’s largest corporations. The Czech capital is now one of 242 cities worldwide where at least one Fortune Global 500 company is based.

Only 14 other countries in the Fortune Global 500 ranking have a single representative, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Poland, Austria and Thailand.

EP Group is also among a very small number of newcomers. Only 13 companies worldwide entered the top 500 this year for the first time, while another 11 returned after previously dropping out of the ranking.

The company’s rise reflects the growing importance of energy, infrastructure and industrial businesses in the global economy.

US companies dominate the ranking

American companies continue to lead the Fortune Global 500, with 141 firms making the list — the highest number since the global financial crisis in 2008.

World.title: Inside IAM Prague: How a Travelling Exhibition Laid the Foundation for One of the City’s Top-Rated Museums
World.content:
Just off Old Town Square, past the cafes and the crowds waiting for the Astronomical Clock, sits a museum that started almost by accident.

Today, IAM Prague has welcomed well over 1 million visitors from around the world and has held TripAdvisor’s Travelers’ Choice Award for five straight years.

From Shopping Malls to Old Town Square

The museum wasn’t originally supposed to be a… museum. Co-founder Jakub Bechyně and his partner Patrik Proško had been running a traveling illusion exhibit that moved between shopping malls, renting space for a month at a time before packing up and relocating. It worked, but it wasn’t permanent.

Then, in 2017, the owner of a building on Old Town Square approached them with an idea: turn part of it into a museum. The catch was the timeline. They wanted it open in two months.

Rather than build something from scratch, the team pulled from what they already had on the shelf, opening with one floor and sixteen exhibits in 2018. The collection has grown to more than 60 pieces since.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Illusion Art Museum Prague (@iamprague)

The museum moved to its current location in 2022 after the original building was sold. The new space, ideally located between Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square, needed walls removed and floors rebuilt to accommodate the art. The costs were substantial, but it turned out to be a good problem to have as the location dramatically increased the exhibition’s visibility to passersby on one of Prague’s busiest tourist thoroughfares.

Choosing Technique Over Fame

IAM Prague doesn’t chase famous names. It chases techniques. The team looks for a specific kind of illusion craft, one with real artistic quality, a genuine optical trick, and ideally a story behind it worth telling.

That approach led them to reverse-perspective specialist Patrick Hughes, and to artists whose work they discovered secondhand and eventually acquired outright rather than simply displaying on loan. In several cases, the museum ended up owning the pieces after renting them for years and deciding they belonged permanently in the collection.

About 80 percent of the exhibition has changed since opening. Early pieces built quickly to fill the space have gradually been replaced as the museum brought in stronger, more polished work from local and international artists.

The exhibition’s evolution continues, with four new pieces from international artists like Jonty Hurwitz and Andrej Boleslavsky, ranging from traditional mirror anamorphoses to digital art, recently unveiled in June.

History Hidden in Plain Sight

Much of what makes IAM Prague distinct is how it uses illusion as a delivery method for history. A glass-art piece featuring four endangered animals turns out to double as an environmental message.

A defenestration scene lets visitors reenact one of Prague’s most repeated historical events, tied to the 1618 uprising that helped trigger the Thirty Years’ War. Even the museum’s own opening date, a century after Czechoslovak independence in 1918, was picked on purpose.

One exhibit nods to Karel Čapek, the Czech writer who coined the word “robot,” a term that entered global use even though it comes from a Slavic word for forced labor.

Another traces the story of Tomáš Baťa, the industrialist who pioneered mass shoe manufacturing and built factories across multiple continents, including a Pakistani city that still carries his name today.

AI’s Impact on Art & Travel

Though much has been made on artificial intelligence’s impact on the world of art, the team’s biggest current concern isn’t AI-generated art replacing the exhibition’s themselves. It’s the shift in how travelers plan their trips.

For years, visibility depended on traditional guidebooks, online travel agencies, physical advertising, and street presence. Increasingly, travelers are relying on AI chat tools to create itineraries, shifting the importance of more “traditional” visibility mechanisms, which is forcing venues like Illusion Art Museum Prague to adapt.

Despite the changing landscape, the plan going forward leans further into digital and kinetic art, including new motion-based installations recently brought in from Berlin by artists like Florian Goerlitz.

For a museum that started as a temporary mall exhibit, the goal has stayed consistent since day one: make people stop, look twice, and leave with a story they didn’t expect to learn.

World.title: Nearly One in Five Prague Farmers’ Market Vendors Fail Veterinary Inspections
World.content:
Nearly one in five vendors inspected at Prague’s farmers’ markets during the first half of 2026 were found to have breached food safety or labeling regulations, according to the State Veterinary Administration (SVS).

Between January and June, veterinary inspectors checked 53 vendors across Prague and identified violations in 10 cases, representing almost 19 percent of all inspections.

Nationwide, inspectors carried out 165 inspections, with irregularities detected in 27 cases, or roughly 16 percent.

Officials said the most common problems in Prague involved improper storage temperatures for food of animal origin, incorrect or incomplete product labeling, and inadequate protection of food from contamination during sale.

Inspectors also highlighted several cases they considered particularly serious. In one instance, a vendor was found producing meat products without the legally required authorization while packaging them with the identification mark of a production facility that no longer exists. Authorities said such practices can mislead consumers about where products originate.



The SVS warned that food safety risks increase during the summer months, especially at outdoor markets where high temperatures make it more difficult to maintain proper cooling conditions.

Across the Czech Republic, labeling violations were the most frequently recorded offense this year, accounting for 26 cases. Problems related to hygiene and production practices—including incorrect storage temperatures and insufficient protection against contamination—followed with 22 cases.

Inspectors also documented 18 violations involving improper handling of food products and 12 cases where the origin of goods was unclear or could not be verified.

The SVS noted that a single inspection may uncover multiple breaches. While inspectors found violations in 27 inspections nationwide, the total number of individual offenses reached 82.

Inspection results remained largely unchanged compared with the same period last year. During the first six months of 2025, inspectors also carried out 165 inspections, finding violations in 16 percent of them. The main difference was that hygiene-related shortcomings topped the list last year, while labeling issues have become the most common problem in 2026.

Looking at the full year, the SVS carried out 380 market inspections across the Czech Republic in 2025, compared with 372 inspections in 2024. The proportion of inspections uncovering violations rose slightly from 17 percent to 18 percent.

World.title: Not an Official Visit: Petr Pavel Attends Hungarian GP as F1 Photographer
World.content:
The president of the Czech Republic, Petr Pavel, has made his way to the Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix on Sunday – but was not an official visit.

Ever wondered what world leaders do in their free time? For Czech Republic president Petr Pavel, the answer is sports photography – and he’s particularly passionate about motorsport.

This weekend, he was attending the Hungarian GP with a full photography kit – and an official FIA accreditation. He arrived at the Hungaroring for Saturday’s sessions and was already taking pictures, accompanied by Czech F1 photographer Jiri Krenek.



This wasn’t the first time he was seen at a major motorsport event as a hobby photographer. Most recently, Pavel travelled to France in June to attend the Le Mans 24 Hours, once again equipped with full camera gear.

In fact, the former NATO Military Chairman has attended several races on both two and four wheels over the years.

Within the Czech Republic, Pavel covered the MotoGP and World Superbike events at Brno, while he has travelled as far as the US and Saudi Arabia to photograph NASCAR and the Dakar Rally respectively.

Last year, he also raised nearly 30,000 euros for a charity dedicated to children, single parents and the elderly by auctioning a photo album.

While it is unusual for politicians to attend races purely for leisure, several leaders regularly appear at major motorsport events in their own countries.

Last year, then British Prime Minister Keir Starmer hosted F1 CEO Stefano Domenicali, drivers and senior team figures at a reception in 10 Downing Street ahead of the British GP.

World.title: Best Petting Zoos in Prague for Families with Kids (2026 Guide)
World.content:
Prague Zoo gets all the attention — and fair enough, it’s consistently ranked among the top zoos in the world — but the city is also full of smaller, low-key spots where kids can get hands-on with animals.

These mini farms and forest parks are perfect for a relaxed weekend outing, most are free or nearly free, and several are just a short metro ride from the centre.

Here’s our pick of the best small zoos and petting farms around Prague.

1. Milíčovský dvůr – Prague 11

Right on the edge of Milíčov forest, this outdoor farm is home to a horse, an ostrich, a fox, goats, sheep, pigs, rabbits and more. Feed dispensers let kids feed the animals directly, and there’s a sandpit, a wooden playground and a small snack stand on site. Entry costs just 20 CZK. Closed Mondays.

📍 K Milíčovu 100/8, Prague 11 — nearest metro: Háje



2. Chuchle Grove Mini Zoo – Prague 5

Set on a hillside inside the Chuchle Grove nature park, this zoo run by Prague’s city forestry service cares for injured and orphaned wildlife. Expect to see mouflons, deer, wild boar, owls, lynxes and more — though petting isn’t allowed here, since the focus is conservation and education. Free entry, open 24/7, with a playground and refreshment kiosk nearby

📍 V Lázních 8, Prague 5

3. Station of Young Biologists – Prague 5

A mix of indoor and outdoor spaces near Anděl, with a tropical terrarium (crocodiles, monkeys, boas), an aviary, and outdoor pens with kangaroos, llamas, ponies and goats. Regular workshops and interactive shows run alongside the animal exhibits. General entry is free; the terrarium and greenhouses cost a small fee (20–40 CZK).

📍 Drtinova 1A, Prague 5 — near Anděl metro

4. Toulcův dvůr – Prague 10

An 8.5-hectare environmental education centre in Hostivař with cows, horses, chickens, pigs, sheep and goats, plus a cherry orchard, wetlands and a farm-to-table restaurant. Petting and feeding aren’t permitted, but it’s a beautifully kept site for a nature walk.

📍 Kubátova 1/32, Prague 10

Honourable mentions

If you’re just after a nice walk with a chance of spotting animals, these free spots are worth a detour:

Wild Garden Hostivař (Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk.

(Prague 15) — rare white fallow deer and mouflons roam near a flooded quarry, with a playground and lakeside walk. Kunratice Forest (Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails.

(Prague 4) — sheep, dwarf goats and pigs can be fed at the “Na tý louce zelený” restaurant, with spotted deer and mouflons visible along the trails. Kamýk Forest (Prague 12) — a small goat enclosure and pheasant aviary tucked next to the gamekeeper’s lodge, surrounded by walking and cycling trails.

World.title: Stromovka: A Green Paradise in the Heart of Prague
World.content:
Stromovka is one of the largest and most popular parks in Prague, drawing visitors with its beautiful nature, rich history, and numerous activities.

Let’s explore what Stromovka offers and how to get there.

Why Visit Stromovka?

Looking for a break from the city’s hustle and bustle or the perfect spot for a picnic with friends? Stromovka is your ideal choice. This vast park features green meadows, shady alleys, and ample opportunities for sports and cultural events.

What is Stromovka?

Stromovka, officially known as Královská obora, spans more than 95 hectares, making it one of Prague’s largest green spaces. Located in Prague 7, the park is a favorite among joggers, cyclists, families, and anyone looking to escape into nature without leaving the city.

It’s perfect for walks, picnics, sports, or simply relaxing on the grass.



A Brief History

Stromovka’s history dates back to the 13th century when it was established as a royal hunting ground. Over time, it evolved and expanded, becoming a public park in the 19th century. The park is home to the original Vltava Creek and several ponds, which host various water birds.

Throughout its history, Stromovka has undergone many changes, shaping it into the popular relaxation spot it is today.

Activities in Stromovka

Stromovka offers a wide range of activities for all ages. Here are some ideas:

Walking and Running: Enjoy the scenic trails.

Cycling: Explore the park on two wheels.

Picnics: Large meadows and shady spots are perfect for a picnic.

Sports: Play football, volleyball, and other sports.

Cultural Events: Attend various events hosted in the park.

How to Get to Stromovka

By Metro: The nearest metro station is Nádraží Holešovice (line C). From there, it’s just a few minutes’ walk to Stromovka.

By Tram: Trams also reach the park. The nearest stops are Výstaviště Holešovice (lines 6, 12, 17) and Planetarium Prague (line 6).

By Bike: Cycling enthusiasts can easily access Stromovka by bike. Bike-sharing stations like Rekola and Nextbike are available around the park, allowing you to ride directly into this natural haven.

World.title: Research institute warns PM Péter Magyar risks ‘wearing himself out’
World.content:
Prime Minister Péter Magyar has dismissed criticism from political think tank Political Capital after it argued that his greatest political risk is his own constant public presence and communication style.

The debate follows the publication of Political Capital’s latest analysis, which argues that despite the government’s strong position, Magyar could gradually “wear himself out” by dominating Hungary’s political agenda.

Think tank sees risks despite government’s strong position

According to Political Capital, many Hungarian voters remain highly engaged in politics even during the summer months, meaning the governing Tisza Party cannot afford to become complacent despite the opposition’s current weakness.

The analysis points to the latest Medián opinion poll, which found that support for the governing party fell by 3–5 percentage points compared with the previous month. The researchers suggest the decline may have been linked to the government’s handling of its presidential nomination, although they stress that no direct causal relationship has been established.

Political Capital argues that the government’s first significant setback came not from the opposition but from its own communication mistakes, including the abandonment of a previously promised public consultation over the presidential nomination.

The think tank also notes that the Tisza government faces high public expectations regarding both economic performance and governance. While Hungarians remain optimistic about their own finances and the country’s economic outlook, the report says these expectations could become difficult to meet given the challenging fiscal situation inherited from the previous administration.

“Péter Magyar’s biggest political opponent is Péter Magyar”

One of the report’s central conclusions is that the prime minister currently faces little direct political competition. Instead, Political Capital argues that Magyar has become the dominant figure in Hungarian politics, with government communication largely revolving around his personal appearances and messaging.

According to the analysis, this strategy carries risks.

“For the time being, Péter Magyar’s biggest political opponent is Péter Magyar,” the report states, arguing that his constant visibility, occasional mistakes and highly active communication could eventually reduce his political appeal.

The report also notes that, unlike in previous years, Magyar did not schedule a competing political event during Viktor Orbán’s annual speech in Băile Tușnad (Tusnádfürdő), suggesting he allowed the former prime minister’s appearance to stand on its own rather than attempting to overshadow it.

PM responds: “There is plenty to wear away”

Magyar reacted directly to the analysis on Facebook after Telex shared an article summarising the report. “There is plenty to wear away,” the prime minister wrote, before adding in another comment that “polishing is not aimless wearing away.”

In a separate Facebook comment beneath another Telex post, Magyar also criticised the outlet for not highlighting one of the government’s latest policy decisions.

World.title: Elderly German man went missing near Lake Balaton
World.content:
Hungarian police have launched an extensive search for an 81-year-old German national who disappeared from his home near Tapolca on Tuesday afternoon.

According to the Veszprém County Police Headquarters, Martin Hofer left his home in the outskirts of Lesenceistvánd, near Tapolca, shortly after 3:00 PM on Tuesday, 28 July, and has not been seen since.

German man struggles with orientation and does not speak Hungarian

Police say the missing man has difficulty orienting himself in both time and place, raising concerns for his safety. He also does not speak Hungarian, which could make it more difficult for him to ask for assistance.

At the time of his disappearance, Martin Hofer was wearing:

a dark blue jacket,

light blue jeans,

and brown slippers.

Authorities have not released further details about the circumstances of his disappearance but are urging the public to remain vigilant.

Police appeal for public assistance

The Tapolca Police Department is asking anyone who may have seen the German man or has information about his whereabouts to come forward immediately.

Anyone with relevant information can report it in person at the Tapolca Police Department (2 Ady Endre Street, Tapolca) or by calling +36 30 227 3744.

Anonymous reports can also be made 24 hours a day via Hungary’s Telefontanú (Witness Hotline) on +36 80 555 111, or through the emergency number 112.

Police stress that even seemingly minor information could help locate the missing man safely.

World.title: Hungary’s powerful new Asset Recovery Office enters into force with sweeping powers to investigate public wealth
World.content:
Hungary’s Parliament has passed the law establishing the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office, granting it extensive powers to investigate suspected misuse of public assets and recover unlawfully acquired state property.

New office to recover EU funds

Hungary’s Parliament has approved legislation establishing the National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH), creating a new authority tasked with protecting public assets, investigating suspected misuse of state property and helping recover unlawfully acquired public wealth.

The bill was passed on Tuesday with 143 votes in favour and 47 against.

According to the legislation, the new office will provide the legal framework needed to safeguard public assets, uncover unlawful management of state property and facilitate asset recovery.

Wide-ranging investigative powers for asset recovery

The NVVH will be authorised to carry out public asset protection risk assessments and investigations, as well as place organisations under public asset protection supervision where necessary.

Its powers are extensive. During investigations, officials will be able to enter premises connected to an inquiry, including offices, archives, warehouses and server rooms. They will also be entitled to examine relevant documents, records, contracts and electronic data storage devices.

The National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office will also have the authority to inspect the bank accounts and financial assets of organisations placed under its supervision. In addition, it may exercise investigative and prosecutorial functions aimed at recovering and protecting public assets, while requesting assistance from the police, the prosecution service, the National Tax and Customs Administration (NAV) and other authorities when required.

The law also provides for a pre-criminal procedure phase, during which the office may conduct risk analyses before deciding whether to launch a public asset protection procedure or initiate criminal proceedings, depending on the evidence uncovered.

Acting president signs the law

Following Parliament’s approval, on Wednesday, acting President Ágnes Forsthoffer announced on Facebook that she had signed the legislation after it had undergone a constitutional review by legal experts at the Sándor Palace.

She said no constitutional concerns had been identified during the review, adding that the new office would be responsible for uncovering abuses involving public assets, supporting the recovery of unlawfully obtained wealth and helping prevent similar cases in the future.

The law entered into force on the day of her announcement, that is, on Wednesday, 29 July 2026.

Leadership to be appointed within 30 days

Under the legislation, Parliament must elect the president and deputy presidents of the NVVH within 30 days of the law entering into force.

The establishment of the office was one of the flagship campaign pledges of the governing Tisza Party, which argued that a dedicated institution was needed to strengthen the protection of public assets and improve the recovery of state property obtained unlawfully.

World.title: Hungarian military helicopter scrambled after Austrian gliders breached Hungarian airspace
World.content:
A Hungarian military helicopter took off from Pápa airbase on Tuesday after two glider pilots failed to establish radio contact with Hungarian air traffic control, Defence Minister Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi said on Facebook.

The Air Operations and Control Centre’s shift supervisor reported in the early afternoon that a glider entering Hungarian airspace from Austria had not responded to air traffic control. The Pápa search-and-rescue helicopter, which took off shortly afterward, identified two gliders in the airspace and signalled the pilots to establish contact on the emergency frequency. The pilots subsequently complied and connected with air traffic control, allowing the helicopter to return to base.

Illustration: a random glider. Photo: depositphotos.com

The minister noted that the gliders had initially filed Békéscsaba as their destination but turned toward Austria and left Hungarian airspace.

Ruszin-Szendi stressed that Hungarian forces effectively safeguard the country’s airspace, adding that scrambling fighter jets would have been unnecessary and costly, the Hungarian news agency wrote.
